title: Reductions in alcohol use following medical cannabis initiation: results from a large cross-sectional survey of medical cannabis patients in Canada.
text_ai: Evidence details how cannabis can influence the use of other psychoactive substances, including prescription medications, alcohol, tobacco and illicit drugs, but very little research has examined the factors associated with these changes in substance use patterns. This paper explores the self-reported use of cannabis as a substitute for alcohol among a Canadian medical cannabis patient population. We drew on a large cross-sectional dataset from the Canadian Cannabis Patient Survey (N = 2,032), a nationwide online questionnaire administered between July and September 2017. Participants were registered medical cannabis patients who reported using cannabis for at least one medical condition. The primary outcome was self-reported change in alcohol use frequency and quantity after initiating medical cannabis, with response options including reduction, no change, or increase. Secondary measures included demographics, cannabis use patterns (daily dose, mode of administration, cannabinoid ratios), primary medical condition, and self-rated health. Multinomial logistic regression models assessed predictors of alcohol substitution versus no change/increase, controlling for age, sex, and duration of medical cannabis use. Results indicated that 44.8% of the sample reduced their alcohol consumption after starting medical cannabis, 38.3% reported no change, and 16.9% increased use. Among those who reduced, the most frequently cited reasons were that cannabis served as a safer alternative (71.2%) and that it reduced cravings for alcohol (63.5%). Significant predictors of alcohol reduction included daily cannabis use, high-frequency administration (≥3 times/day), inhalation as the primary route, and use for chronic pain or mental health conditions. In contrast, patients using lower-potency cannabis or low-frequency administration were more likely to report no change or increases. These associations persisted after adjustment for age and sex. Findings suggest that medical cannabis initiation may be associated with substantial reductions in alcohol use for a sizeable proportion of Canadian patients, particularly those with heavier cannabis use patterns. The substitution effect appears most pronounced among individuals using cannabis to manage chronic pain or mental health symptoms. This has important implications for harm reduction and public health policy, especially given the known burdens of alcohol-related harms. However, causal inference is limited by the cross-sectional design and reliance on retrospective self-report. Future longitudinal research should examine long-term stability of substitution patterns and explore mechanisms such as symptom relief or reduced alcohol cravings. Collectively, these results support the notion that medical cannabis access may facilitate reductions in alcohol use for a clinically meaningful subset of patients.
prefix: Evidence details how cannabis can influence the use of other psychoactive substances, including prescription medications, alcohol, tobacco and illicit drugs, but very little research has examined the factors associated with these changes in substance use patterns. This paper explores the self-reported use of cannabis as a substitute for alcohol among a Canadian medical cannabis patient population.

title: Diversifying Knowledge Enhancement of Biomedical Language Models using Adapter Modules and Knowledge Graphs
text_ai: Recent advances in natural language processing (NLP) owe their success to pre-training language models on large amounts of unstructured data. Still, there is an increasing effort to combine the unstructured nature of LMs with structured knowledge and reasoning. To address this, we propose a novel framework that leverages lightweight adapter modules to inject structured knowledge from multiple biomedical knowledge graphs (KGs) into pre-trained language models. Unlike conventional fine-tuning approaches, adapters enable parameter-efficient, modular integration of diverse knowledge sources without catastrophic forgetting. In particular, we design task- and knowledge-specific adapters that capture complementary aspects of biomedical entities and relations—ranging from drug–target interactions and disease–gene associations to molecular pathways and phenotype ontologies. By training these adapters jointly with a knowledge graph embedding objective, the model learns to align its contextual representations with structured relational patterns. We evaluate our method on a suite of biomedical NLP benchmarks, including named entity recognition, relation extraction, and question answering. Results show that adapter-based knowledge enhancement yields consistent performance gains over both vanilla language models and full fine-tuning baselines, while requiring only a fraction of the parameters. Moreover, we demonstrate that combining multiple adapters—each encoding a distinct KG—further improves performance and enables knowledge transfer across tasks. This diversification of knowledge sources mitigates bias from any single KG and increases model robustness. Our work provides a scalable and modular pathway for enriching biomedical language models with structured knowledge, paving the way for more accurate and interpretable AI in healthcare.
prefix: Recent advances in natural language processing (NLP) owe their success to pre-training language models on large amounts of unstructured data. Still, there is an increasing effort to combine the unstructured nature of LMs with structured knowledge and reasoning.

title: VIVID: A Novel Approach to Remediation Prioritization in Static Application Security Testing (SAST)
text_ai: Static Application Security Testing (SAST) enables organizations to detect vulnerabilities in code early; however, major SAST platforms do not include visual aids and present little insight on correlations between tainted data chains. This gap impedes efficient remediation by obscuring the full propagation paths of vulnerabilities and their interdependencies. To address this, we introduce VIVID (VIsual Vulnerability InterDepiction), a framework that enriches SAST output with interactive taint-flow graphs and automated prioritization based on exploit likelihood and business context. VIVID constructs a weighted dependency network from data-flow and control-flow information, then applies a graph-based ranking algorithm (VIVID-Rank) that scores each tainted chain by reachability from untrusted inputs, severity of sinks, and criticality of affected code modules. Triage teams interact with a visual overlay that highlights correlated vulnerabilities, enabling rapid identification of root causes and cascading risks. In a comparative evaluation against two leading commercial SAST tools on a corpus of 12 open-source Java projects (totaling ~1.5M lines), VIVID reduced manual review time by 38% on average while increasing detection of high-priority flaws by 22%. Furthermore, VIVID’s visualizations uncovered previously hidden inter-procedural taint chains that standard reports missed, leading to the discovery of 9 previously unknown critical vulnerabilities. These results demonstrate that embedding visual analytics and connectivity-aware prioritization into SAST workflows significantly improves remediation efficiency and accuracy. VIVID thus provides a practical, scalable enhancement to existing SAST pipelines without requiring changes to the underlying analyzers.
prefix: Static Application Security Testing (SAST) enables organizations to detect vulnerabilities in code early; however, major SAST platforms do not include visual aids and present little insight on correlations between tainted data chains.

title: Partial-Information Multiple Access Protocol for Orthogonal Transmissions
text_ai: With the stringent requirements introduced by the new sixth-generation (6G) internet-of-things (IoT) use cases, traditional approaches to multiple access control have started to show their limitations. A new wave of grant-free (GF) approaches have been therefore proposed as a viable alternative. However, a definitive solution is still to be accomplished. Specifically, existing grant-free protocols often suffer from uncontrollable collisions, excessive preamble overhead, or limited scalability in massive machine-type communication (mMTC) scenarios. To address these shortcomings, this paper introduces the Partial-Information Multiple Access (PIMA) protocol for orthogonal transmission systems. PIMA leverages the intrinsic structure of orthogonal frequency-division multiple access (OFDMA) resource blocks by allowing each user to transmit a compact, non-orthogonal signature — carrying only partial information about the user’s identity and resource request — within a shared contention slot. On the receiver side, the base station employs a low-complexity compressive sensing decoder to jointly detect active users and their resource demands from the aggregated signature field. Based on the detected partial information, the base station then allocates mutually orthogonal data transmission slots to the identified users, thereby eliminating further collisions and maintaining high spectral efficiency. The protocol operates in a two-phase manner: a short contention phase using the proposed partial-information signatures, followed by a collision-free data transmission phase over orthogonal resources. We analyze the performance of PIMA in terms of successful detection probability, average access delay, and system throughput under realistic mMTC traffic models. Numerical results demonstrate that PIMA achieves a significantly lower collision probability than conventional slotted ALOHA and code-expanded random access, while incurring negligible signaling overhead compared to fully grant-based schemes. Moreover, the protocol scales gracefully with the number of active users, making it particularly suitable for 6G IoT deployments with sporadic, short-packet traffic. By strategically trading off the amount of contention information for detection complexity, PIMA bridges the gap between pure random access and fully scheduled resource allocation, offering a practical and efficient multiple access solution for orthogonal transmission systems.

title: Volatile evolution and atmospheres of Trans-Neptunian Objects
text_ai: At 30-50 K, the temperatures typical for surfaces in the Kuiper Belt (e.g. Stern & Trafton 2008), only seven species have sublimation pressures higher than 1 nbar (Fray & Schmitt 2009): Ne, N$_2$, CO, Ar, O$_2$, CH$_4$, and Kr. Of these, N$_2$, CO, and CH$_4$ have been detected or inferred on the surfaces of Trans-Neptunian Objects (TNOs). These three molecules—N$_2$, CO, and CH$_4$—are the primary drivers of atmospheric activity on TNOs, with their relative abundances determining the bulk atmospheric composition and pressure. At the low temperatures of the Kuiper Belt, sublimation of these ices creates tenuous atmospheres that respond to insolation changes, leading to seasonal cycles of condensation and sublimation. For instance, Pluto's N$_2$-dominated atmosphere exhibits strong seasonal dependence due to its orbital obliquity (e.g., Young et al. 2018). Other large TNOs like Eris and Makemake likely harbor transient atmospheres with distinct behaviors due to different volatile inventories. The evolution of these atmospheres over millions of years is modulated by stochastic processes such as impacts and cosmic ray irradiation, and the presence of less volatile species like O$_2$ and Ar, though not yet detected, may provide constraints on the origin and thermal history of TNO surfaces.

title: Generative Text-Guided 3D Vision-Language Pretraining for Unified Medical Image Segmentation
text_ai: Vision-Language Pretraining (VLP) has demonstrated remarkable capabilities in learning visual representations from textual descriptions of images without annotations. Yet, effective VLP demands large-scale image-text pairs, a resource that suffers scarcity in the medical domain. Moreover, conventional VLP is limited to 2D images while medical images encompass diverse modalities, often in 3D, making the learning process more challenging. To address these challenges, we propose Generative Text-Guided 3D Vision-Language Pretraining (GTG-3D), a novel framework that unifies medical image segmentation across diverse 3D modalities. GTG-3D leverages a generative text engine to produce dense, clinically-grounded textual descriptions from 3D medical volumes, thereby alleviating the scarcity of paired image-text data. By aligning volumetric features with these synthetic texts via a cross-modal contrastive objective, our approach learns rich 3D visual representations without requiring manual annotations. Furthermore, we introduce a unified segmentation decoder that adapts to multiple modalities—CT, MRI, and PET—by conditioning on the learned vision-language embeddings. Extensive experiments on five public benchmarks demonstrate that GTG-3D significantly outperforms existing VLP and fully-supervised methods, achieving state-of-the-art Dice scores across tasks such as organ, tumor, and lesion segmentation. Notably, our pretrained model transfers effectively to low-data regimes, improving segmentation accuracy by over 10% when only 10% of the training data is available. Ablation studies confirm the critical role of generative text guidance and the 3D volumetric context. GTG-3D offers a scalable, annotation-efficient path toward unified medical image understanding, bridging the gap between 2D VLP and the 3D multi-modal reality of clinical practice.

title: On the stability of the spherically symmetric solution to an inflow problem for an isentropic model of compressible viscous fluid
text_ai: We investigate an inflow problem for the multi-dimensional isentropic compressible Navier-Stokes equations. The fluid under consideration occupies the exterior domain of unit ball, $\Omega=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n\,\vert\, |x|\ge 1\}$, and a constant stream of mass is flowing into the domain from the boundary $\partial\Omega=\{|x|=1\}$. We focus on spherically symmetric solutions, reducing the problem to a one-dimensional system in the radial variable. Under suitable smallness conditions on the inflow rate, we establish the existence of a unique spherically symmetric stationary solution. The main result of this paper is the nonlinear asymptotic stability of this stationary solution. More precisely, we show that for small initial perturbations in suitable Sobolev spaces, the solution converges to the stationary state as time tends to infinity. The proof is based on a refined energy method that exploits the dissipative structure of the equations. We derive a priori estimates that control the growth of perturbations, using the fact that the domain is an exterior region. The analysis requires careful treatment of the boundary terms arising from the inflow condition. Furthermore, we obtain explicit decay rates depending on the dimension n. For n=3, we achieve algebraic decay, while for higher dimensions, exponential decay is possible under additional conditions. These results extend the known stability theory for bounded domains to the exterior case with inflow, and they have implications for fluid dynamics in unbounded regions with constant mass supply. The mathematical challenges include handling the singular nature of the domain and the lack of compactness, which are overcome by using weighted energy integrals and Hardy-type inequalities.

title: Bone remodeling of the proximal tibia after uncemented total knee arthroplasty: secondary endpoints analyzed from a randomized trial comparing monoblock and modular tibia traysâ??2 year follow-up of 53 cases
text_ai: Background and purpose â?? Bone remodeling as a response to bone trauma, postoperative immobilization, and device-related bone reactions can lead to loss of bone stock and increase the risk of periprosthetic fracture and aseptic loosening. This study investigates the adaptive bone remodeling of the proximal tibia after uncemented total knee arthroplasty (TKA). Methods – This secondary analysis was based on data from a prospective, randomized trial of 53 patients (mean age 66 years, 58% female) undergoing primary uncemented TKA for osteoarthritis. Patients were allocated to a monoblock (n=26) or modular (n=27) tibial tray of the same implant system, with identical femoral components and bearing surfaces. Bone mineral density (BMD) of the proximal tibia was assessed using dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) at four periprosthetic regions of interest (ROIs) corresponding to the medial and lateral condyles (ROI 1/2) and the metaphysis (ROI 3/4). Measurements were obtained preoperatively and at 6, 12, and 24 months postoperatively. Secondary endpoints comprised changes in BMD from baseline to each follow-up (absolute and percentage), clinical outcomes (Knee Society Score, Oxford Knee Score, pain visual analog scale), and radiographic evaluation for radiolucent lines, osteolysis, or component migration. Mixed linear models with repeated measures, adjusted for baseline BMD, age, sex, and body mass index, were used for between-group comparisons. Complications including periprosthetic fracture and aseptic loosening were recorded. Results – At 24 months, mean BMD decreases from baseline were observed across all ROIs in both groups. In the medial condyle (ROI 1), BMD loss was significantly smaller in the monoblock group (−4.8%, 95% CI −6.2 to −3.4) compared with the modular group (−8.1%, 95% CI −9.7 to −6.5; p=0.03). Lateral condyle (ROI 2) BMD changes did not differ (−5.9% vs −6.3%; p=0.6). Metaphyseal ROIs showed similar modest losses (approximately −3% to −4% in both arms). Clinical scores improved significantly and similarly in both groups (p>0.2). One periprosthetic tibial fracture occurred in the modular group (at 18 months), with no cases of aseptic loosening. Radiolucent lines were more frequent in the modular group (4/27 vs 1/26) but not statistically significant. Interpretation – Adaptive bone remodeling after uncemented TKA differed by tibial tray design. The monoblock tray was associated with better preservation of medial condyle bone stock at 2 years, potentially mediated by altered load transfer. Although clinical outcomes were comparable, the observed BMD difference may have implications for long-term fracture risk and implant stability. These secondary findings require confirmation with longer follow-up and larger samples.

title: Efficient Computation in Adaptive Artificial Spiking Neural Networks
text_ai: Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) are bio-inspired models of neural computation that have proven highly effective. Still, ANNs lack a natural notion of time, and neural units in ANNs exchange analog values in a frame-based manner, a computationally and energetically inefficient form of communication. Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) address these limitations by incorporating time as a fundamental computational dimension, where neurons communicate via discrete, asynchronous spikes. This event-driven paradigm mirrors biological neural processing, offering the potential for significantly reduced energy consumption and enhanced temporal processing capabilities. However, the inherent complexity of training SNNs—due to the non-differentiable nature of spike events—has hindered their widespread adoption, especially in adaptive, real-time settings. In this work, we introduce an efficient computational framework for adaptive artificial SNNs that leverages a novel synaptic plasticity rule combined with a lightweight, online learning algorithm. Our approach eschews the need for weight transport or global error signals, instead relying on local, spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) augmented with a homeostasis mechanism that dynamically adjusts firing thresholds. To further enhance computational efficiency, we propose a sparse coding strategy that minimizes unnecessary spike propagation while preserving representational fidelity. We validate our framework on a series of benchmark tasks, including temporal pattern recognition and adaptive control, demonstrating that our SNNs achieve competitive accuracy with state-of-the-art ANNs while requiring orders of magnitude fewer synaptic updates and maintaining a natural ability to process streaming data. Critically, we show that the adaptive mechanism allows the network to continuously recalibrate its parameters in response to changing input statistics, eliminating the need for retraining from scratch. Energy analysis using a custom hardware simulation reveals that our approach reduces total synaptic operations by up to 85% compared to equivalent rate-coded SNNs. These results establish that efficient, adaptive computation is not only feasible with spiking networks but can also surpass conventional ANNs in scenarios demanding temporal dynamics and energy constraints. By bridging the gap between biological plausibility and practical performance, our work provides a scalable pathway toward neuromorphic computing systems that operate efficiently at the edge.

title: Quantum entanglement between an atom and a molecule
text_ai: Conventional information processors freely convert information between different physical carriers to process, store, or transmit information. It seems plausible that quantum information will also be held by different physical carriers in applications such as tests of fundamental physics, quantum-enhanced sensors, and quantum information processing. Here we demonstrate the creation of quantum entanglement between a single atom and a single molecule in an optical cavity. The atomic qubit is encoded in the hyperfine states of a cesium atom, while the molecular qubit is encoded in the rotational states of a carbon monoxide molecule. By engineering a cavity-mediated Raman interaction, we generate a Bell state with a fidelity exceeding 0.89(4), verified through state tomography. This hybrid entanglement bridges two fundamentally different quantum systems—one with simple, well-controlled internal structure and another with rich rovibrational degrees of freedom. Our results open the door to hybrid quantum networks that leverage the long coherence times of molecules and the fast manipulation capabilities of atoms, enabling new architectures for quantum-enhanced sensing and tests of fundamental symmetries. The demonstration also provides a platform for exploring entanglement dynamics in systems with complex internal complexity, marking a key step toward scalable quantum information processing using diverse physical carriers.

title: Spot evolution on LQ Hya during 2006--2017: temperature maps based on SOFIN and FIES data
text_ai: Context. LQ Hya is one of the most frequently studied young solar analogue stars. Recently, it has been observed to show intriguing behaviour by analysing long-term photometry: during 2003--2009, a coherent spot structure migrating in the rotational frame has been reported by various authors, but since that time the star has entered a chaotic state where coherent structures seem to have disappeared and rapid phase jumps of the photometric minima occur irregularly over time. Aims. We aim to investigate the long-term evolution of surface temperature inhomogeneities on LQ Hya by applying Doppler imaging to high-resolution spectra obtained with the SOFIN (Nordic Optical Telescope) and FIES (NOT) spectrographs between 2006 and 2017. This period covers the transition from the coherent spot pattern to the chaotic state, allowing us to directly constrain the physical changes responsible for the photometric behaviour. Methods. A total of 79 SOFIN and 42 FIES spectra were inverted into surface temperature maps using a regularised maximum-entropy code. The inversion assumes a two-temperature spot model with umbra and penumbra, and incorporates local line profiles from a stellar atmosphere grid. The rotational period and inclination were fixed to previously determined values. The maps were reconstructed for 13 epochs, each spanning a few rotational cycles, yielding a temporal resolution of approximately one to two years. Results. The temperature maps reveal a dominant polar spot that persists throughout the entire interval, varying in size and temperature contrast. Mid-latitude and equatorial features show a clear evolution: from 2006 to 2009, a persistent active longitude pattern is recovered, with two active regions separated by ~180° that slowly drift in longitude. After 2010, the maps become dominated by rapidly changing, fragmented spot groups that appear at random longitudes, consistent with the photometric chaos. The transition occurs within one year around 2009–2010, suggesting a rapid change in the stellar dynamo. Conclusions. The disappearance of the coherent longitude pattern coincides with a decrease in the overall spottedness and an increase in the latitudinal spread of spots. The observed evolution supports the scenario of a cyclic dynamo that recently entered a grand minimum-like state, akin to the Maunder Minimum observed on the Sun. Continued monitoring is essential to test whether the coherent structure will reappear.

title: Scaling Universality at the Dynamic Vortex Mott Transition
text_ai: The dynamic Mott insulator-to-metal transition (DMT) is key to many intriguing phenomena in condensed matter physics yet it remains nearly unexplored. The cleanest way to observe DMT, without the interference from disorder and other effects inherent to electronic and atomic systems, is to employ the vortex Mott states formed by superconducting vortices in a regular array of pinning sites. Here we realize the DMT in a model system of vortices driven across a periodic pinning array, and demonstrate that the transition exhibits scaling universality. By measuring the voltage-current characteristics across the depinning threshold, we identify a dynamic scaling collapse onto a single universal curve, controlled by a single critical exponent. The extracted exponent is consistent with that of the static driven vortex system at the commensurate-incommensurate transition, revealing a deep connection between equilibrium and nonequilibrium critical phenomena. Our results establish the vortex Mott insulator as a clean platform for exploring dynamic universality classes, and they provide the first experimental observation of scaling at a dynamic Mott transition in any condensed matter system. The observed universality suggests that the DMT is governed by the same underlying fixed point as the static transition, despite the fundamentally different roles of time and driving force. This work opens the door to systematic studies of dynamic criticality in strongly correlated systems, where the interplay of interactions and periodic potentials gives rise to emergent nonequilibrium phases.

title: Gravitational waves constraints on post-inflationary phases stiffer than radiation
text_ai: We point out that the existence of post-inflationary phases stiffer than radiation leads to the production of stochastic gravitational waves (GW) backgrounds whose logarithmic energy spectra (in critical units) are typically "blue" at high frequencies. Such a blue tilt arises because the energy density of the universe during a stiff phase scales as a^{-3(1+w)} with w > 1/3, causing the GW relic density to increase with frequency squared relative to the radiation-dominated case. We derive the full GW spectrum as a function of the stiff-phase equation-of-state parameter w, its duration characterized by the number of e-folds, and the subsequent reheating temperature. Using current constraints from Big Bang nucleosynthesis, cosmic microwave background, and direct GW searches (LIGO/Virgo, pulsar timing arrays), we obtain upper limits on the maximum allowed length of a stiff phase before it would overproduce GWs. For the extreme case of kination (w = 1), we find that the stiff phase must end at temperatures below ∼10⁷ GeV unless the tensor-to-scalar ratio is extremely small. Conversely, future detectors such as LISA, DECIGO, and ET will be able to probe stiff phases enduring down to temperatures as low as a few GeV, potentially ruling out or confirming various post-inflationary scenarios. Our results highlight that the blue-tilted GW background provides a unique observational handle on the expansion history of the Universe between inflation and standard radiation domination, and they can be translated into stringent constraints on beyond-Standard-Model physics that predicts such stiff epochs. This analysis demonstrates the power of GW astronomy to reveal the earliest moments of our cosmic evolution.

title: H-atom bombardment of CO2, HCOOH and CH3CHO containing ices
text_ai: Context: Hydrogenation reactions are expected to be among the most important surface reactions on interstellar ices. However, solid state astrochemical laboratory data on reactions of H-atoms with common interstellar ice constituents are largely lacking. In this study, we experimentally investigate the hydrogenation of three key interstellar ice constituents—carbon dioxide (CO₂), formic acid (HCOOH), and acetaldehyde (CH₃CHO)—under ultrahigh vacuum conditions relevant to dense molecular clouds. Ice films are prepared at 10 K by vapor deposition of pure and mixed ices, then exposed to a thermal H-atom beam (T ≈ 2000 K) at fluences up to 10¹⁷ atoms cm⁻². Products are monitored in situ via reflection absorption infrared spectroscopy (RAIRS) and post-irradiation temperature-programmed desorption (TPD) coupled with quadrupole mass spectrometry. Our results reveal markedly different reactivities. For CO₂-containing ices, hydrogenation proceeds efficiently, yielding formic acid (HCOOH) as the primary product, with trace amounts of formaldehyde (H₂CO) and methanol (CH₃OH) observed at higher H-atom doses. Kinetic analysis indicates that H-atom addition to CO₂ occurs through a barrierless pathway in the solid state, consistent with quantum tunneling at low temperatures. In contrast, HCOOH ices show limited reactivity: only minor conversion to H₂CO and CO is detected, suggesting that the carboxylic acid group is relatively resistant to further hydrogenation under our conditions. For CH₃CHO, rapid and complete conversion to ethanol (CH₃CH₂OH) is observed, with no significant side products, confirming the high efficiency of aldehyde hydrogenation on interstellar ice analogues. These findings fill critical gaps in the available experimental database for H-atom reactions on interstellar ices. The efficient formation of HCOOH from CO₂ provides a plausible solid-state route to this abundant interstellar molecule, while the facile production of ethanol from acetaldehyde has direct implications for the inventory of complex organic molecules in star-forming regions. Conversely, the low reactivity of HCOOH with H atoms suggests that once formed, this species may accumulate in grain mantles, acting as a reservoir for carboxylic acids. Our results also highlight the need to incorporate competitive reaction channels and temperature-dependent tunneling efficiencies into astrochemical models. Overall, this study delivers quantitative rate constants and branching ratios that will enable more realistic simulations of grain-surface chemistry in cold environments.

title: Optimal strategies for throwing accurately
text_ai: Accuracy of throwing in games and sports is governed by how errors at projectile release are propagated by flight dynamics. To address the question of what governs the choice of throwing strategy, we use a simple model of throwing with an arm modelled as a hinged bar of fixed length that can release a projectile at any angle and angular velocity. We derive analytical expressions for the covariance matrix of landing points as a function of release parameters, assuming small independent Gaussian perturbations in release angle and angular velocity. This enables computation of the probability of hitting a circular target of given size. By minimizing the required target radius for a fixed success probability, we identify optimal release strategies. The optimal strategy depends critically on the ratio of angular to velocity noise: when angular noise dominates, steep release angles reduce sensitivity to angle errors; when velocity noise dominates, flatter trajectories minimize dispersion from flight-time variability. The model generalizes across arm lengths and target distances and is validated against empirical data from baseball pitching and dart throwing. Our findings offer a unified explanation for diverse throwing techniques, showing that the optimal trade-off is determined by the thrower’s motor noise characteristics. They also have practical implications, suggesting that novices with high angular variability should adopt steep trajectories, whereas experts with precise angular control may benefit from flatter throws.

title: Strategic Defense against Stealthy Link Flooding Attacks: A Signaling Game Approach
text_ai: With the increasing diversity of Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) attacks, it is becoming extremely challenging to design a fully protected network. For instance, Stealthy Link Flooding Attack (SLFA) is a variant of DDoS attacks that strives to block access to a target area by flooding a small set of links, and it is shown that it can bypass traditional DDoS defense mechanisms. We propose a signaling game framework to model the strategic interaction between an adversary launching a stealthy link flooding attack and a defender tasked with mitigating its impact. In this game, the attacker chooses a target link set and a level of flooding traffic that mimics legitimate congestion, while the defender observes link-state metrics—such as packet loss, latency, or traffic anomalies—and decides whether to trigger countermeasures, e.g., rerouting, capacity scaling, or scrubbing. The defender’s observations are inherently noisy because the attacker can hide malicious flows within background traffic, creating a signaling problem where the attacker’s actions convey imperfect information about its intentions. We define the game’s payoff structure by considering the attacker’s objective of degrading service to a target area (e.g., a critical server or subnet) and the defender’s goal of maintaining quality of service for legitimate users, subject to operational costs for both sides. We analyze the pure-strategy and mixed-strategy Nash equilibria of the game, identifying conditions under which the defender can deter attack by committing to a sufficiently aggressive response policy. The analysis reveals that a key determinant of equilibrium outcomes is the attacker’s ability to masquerade flood traffic as benign congestion; when this masquerading capability exceeds a threshold, the defender may be forced into a pooling equilibrium where it cannot distinguish attack from normal load. To break such pooling, we introduce a signaling mechanism: the defender intentionally injects controlled perturbations into link-state feedback—a form of “camouflage” that forces the attacker to reveal its type through observable changes in traffic patterns. We prove that under mild conditions, a separating equilibrium exists in which the defender’s strategy minimizes expected damage while bounding false-positive rates. Numerical simulations on realistic network topologies (e.g., Rockefuel and Internet2) demonstrate that our approach reduces link-flooding success probability by 40–60% compared to baseline detection algorithms, with negligible overhead. These results underscore the viability of game-theoretic defense against stealthy volumetric attacks in next-generation networks.

title: H-Alpha and Hard X-Ray Observations of a Two-Ribbon Flare Associated with a Filament Eruption
text_ai: We perform a multi-wavelength study of a two-ribbon flare on 2002 September 29 and its associated filament eruption, observed simultaneously in the H-alpha line by a ground-based imaging spectrograph and in hard X-rays by RHESSI. The flare ribbons contain several H-alpha bright kernels that show different evolutional behaviors. The kernel evolution is closely linked to the hard X-ray (HXR) emission: the earliest brightenings coincide with the onset of HXR bursts, while later kernels appear at progressively larger separations along the ribbons, consistent with a diverging reconnection site in the corona. Analysis of the H-alpha line profiles reveals strong red asymmetry in the main kernels, indicating downward-moving chromospheric plasma driven by nonthermal electron beams. Simultaneous RHESSI images in the 12–25 keV and 25–50 keV bands show that the HXR footpoint sources are cospatial with the most intense H-alpha kernels, and their centroid motions—both along and across the ribbons—correlate with the apparent expansion of the post-flare arcade. The associated filament eruption, observed as a dark absorbing feature in H-alpha, accelerates during the impulsive phase, reaching a projected plane-of-sky velocity of ~250 km s⁻¹. Its rapid rise and subsequent disappearance coincide with the formation of the two ribbons, suggesting that the erupting filament triggers the reconnection responsible for the flare. These results underscore the critical role of filament dynamics in organizing the spatial and temporal patterns of chromospheric heating and nonthermal electron precipitation in two-ribbon flares.

title: A Latent Variable Approach for Non-Hierarchical Multi-Fidelity Adaptive Sampling
text_ai: Multi-fidelity (MF) methods are gaining popularity for enhancing surrogate modeling and design optimization by incorporating data from various low-fidelity (LF) models. While most existing MF methods assume a fixed dataset, adaptive sampling methods that dynamically allocate resources among fidelity models can achieve higher efficiency in the exploring and exploiting the design space. However, existing adaptive sampling strategies for MF methods overwhelmingly rely on a hierarchical fidelity structure, which presupposes a known ordering of fidelities and often requires a high-fidelity (HF) model as the ultimate reference. This assumption severely limits applicability in many engineering contexts where multiple LF models are available but lack a clear hierarchy—for instance, simulations based on different physical approximations, reduced-order models, or experimental setups of varying but incomparable accuracy. Moreover, hierarchical approaches tend to allocate too many resources to the assumed highest-fidelity model, potentially overlooking valuable information from diverse LF sources that could jointly improve surrogate accuracy. To address these challenges, we propose a novel non-hierarchical multi-fidelity adaptive sampling framework based on a latent variable formulation. Instead of imposing a fixed fidelity ordering, we treat each fidelity level's output as an observation arising from an underlying latent process that captures the true physical phenomenon. The relationship between fidelities is modeled through a Gaussian process prior with a multi-output kernel that learns their correlations directly from data, without any a priori ranking. This enables the model to automatically discover which LF models are most informative for predicting the HF response of interest. For adaptive sampling, we develop an acquisition function that balances exploration (reducing predictive uncertainty) and exploitation (improving prediction near optima or constraints) while jointly selecting both the next input location and the fidelity level to query. The acquisition function leverages the latent variable structure to quantify the expected information gain across all fidelities in a unified manner. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several synthetic and real-world engineering test cases, comparing it against state-of-the-art hierarchical MF adaptive sampling methods. Results show that our non-hierarchical latent variable approach consistently achieves higher surrogate accuracy and faster convergence, particularly when the fidelity ordering is ambiguous or when LF models have complementary strengths. Moreover, the method naturally handles multiple fidelities beyond two levels and scales well with increasing numbers of LF sources. This work thus provides a flexible and principled alternative for multi-fidelity adaptive sampling that relaxes restrictive hierarchical assumptions, opening new possibilities for surrogate modeling in complex simulation environments.

title: Is the faint young Sun problem for Earth solved?
text_ai: Stellar evolution models predict that the solar luminosity was lower in the past, typically 20-25 % lower during the Archean (3.8-2.5 Ga). Despite the fainter Sun, there is strong evidence for the presence of liquid water on Earth's surface at that time. This apparent contradiction, known as the faint young Sun problem, has prompted numerous hypotheses. Proposed solutions include elevated atmospheric greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane. However, required CO₂ concentrations may exceed geochemical constraints from paleosols and banded iron formations. Other mechanisms involve reduced planetary albedo due to smaller continental area or different cloud distributions, but these remain uncertain. Recent coupled climate–biogeochemical models suggest that a combination of factors—including a more active Sun in terms of UV radiation and a different atmospheric composition—may resolve the discrepancy. The role of organic haze, ammonia, or other trace gases has also been explored. Despite decades of research, no single solution has been universally accepted. This review assesses the current state of the faint young Sun problem for Earth, evaluating the strengths and weaknesses of the leading hypotheses. It is concluded that while significant progress has been made, the problem is not yet fully solved; rather, it has evolved into a more nuanced understanding of early Earth's climate system, where multiple feedbacks and forcings operated in concert. Present challenges include reconciling model predictions with isotopic and mineralogical records, as well as accounting for temporal variations in solar activity and atmospheric evolution.

title: VasTSD: Learning 3D Vascular Tree-state Space Diffusion Model for Angiography Synthesis
text_ai: Angiography imaging is a medical imaging technique that enhances the visibility of blood vessels within the body by using contrast agents. Angiographic images can effectively assist in the diagnosis of vascular diseases. However, contrast agents may bring extra radiation exposure which is harmful to patients with health risks. To mitigate these risks, we propose VasTSD, a 3D vascular tree-state space diffusion model for contrast-free angiography synthesis from non-invasive imaging modalities. Our method leverages a hierarchical state space representation that captures the topological and geometric structure of vascular trees, enabling diffusion-based generation of high-fidelity angiographic volumes. Specifically, we introduce a tree-state transition kernel that operates along the vascular hierarchy, preserving branch continuity and bifurcation patterns during the denoising process. The model is trained on paired CT angiography and non-contrast CT scans, learning to map structural priors to contrast-enhanced vessel appearances. We further incorporate a vesselness-guided conditioning mechanism to enhance perceptual quality and diagnostic relevance. Experiments on a large-scale clinical dataset demonstrate that VasTSD produces synthetic angiograms with structural similarity and vessel delineation comparable to real contrast-enhanced scans, while eliminating radiation and contrast agent hazards. Quantitative evaluations show superior performance over existing generative baselines in terms of FID, vessel Dice score, and clinical interpretability. This work offers a promising direction for safe, accessible vascular imaging.

title: Clinical Significance of Cytotoxic Lesions of the Corpus Callosum in Subarachnoid Hemorrhage Patients: A Retrospective Analysis.
text_ai: Cytotoxic lesions of the corpus callosum are secondary lesions induced by significant increases in cytokine levels in the brain and are associated with subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). However, their clinical significance in SAH patients remains unclear. This retrospective study aimed to assess the clinical significance of cytotoxic lesions of the corpus callosum (CLOCCs) in a cohort of SAH patients. We analyzed clinical and imaging data from 214 SAH patients treated at our institution between 2017 and 2022. CLOCCs were identified on diffusion-weighted MRI within 14 days of ictus. Patients were divided into CLOCC-positive (n=32, 15.0%) and CLOCC-negative groups. Baseline characteristics, including age, sex, Hunt-Hess grade, and Fisher score, were comparable between groups. Primary outcomes were the incidence of angiographic vasospasm, delayed cerebral ischemia (DCI), and functional outcome assessed by modified Rankin Scale (mRS) at 3 months. Secondary outcomes included in-hospital mortality and length of stay. Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for confounders was used to determine independent associations. CLOCC-positive patients had a significantly higher incidence of vasospasm (68.8% vs. 41.2%, p=0.008) and DCI (56.3% vs. 30.8%, p=0.006). Unfavorable 3-month outcome (mRS 4-6) occurred more frequently in the CLOCC-positive group (46.9% vs. 28.0%, p=0.03). After adjustment, CLOCCs remained an independent predictor of vasospasm (OR 3.12, 95% CI 1.34-7.25, p=0.009), DCI (OR 2.88, 95% CI 1.25-6.64, p=0.013), and poor outcome (OR 2.54, 95% CI 1.09-5.92, p=0.031). No significant differences were observed in mortality or length of stay. These findings demonstrate that CLOCCs are associated with an increased risk of vasospasm, DCI, and worse functional outcome in SAH patients, suggesting that CLOCCs may serve as an early imaging biomarker for neuroinflammatory burden and adverse prognosis. Incorporating CLOCC assessment into routine neuroimaging could improve risk stratification and guide more aggressive management strategies.

title: Funnel control -- a survey
text_ai: The methodology of funnel control was introduced in the early 2000s, and it has developed since then in many respects achieving a level of mathematical maturity balanced by practical applications. Its fundamental tenet is the attainment of prescribed transient and asymptotic behaviour for continuous-time controlled dynamical processes encompassing linear and nonlinear systems described by functional differential equations, differential-algebraic systems, and partial differential equations. Its core mechanism employs a time-varying gain that adapts in response to the distance between the system output and a predefined funnel boundary, thereby guaranteeing that the tracking or regulation error remains within prescribed performance limits without requiring detailed knowledge of the system dynamics. This inherent robustness to uncertainties, such as unknown parameters, external disturbances, and unmodelled dynamics, has spurred extensive theoretical developments. The framework has been rigorously extended to cover various system classes, including functional differential equations, differential-algebraic systems, and partial differential equations, with results on existence, uniqueness, and boundedness of solutions. Practical constraints like actuator saturation, input delays, output switching, and safety-critical operations have been accommodated. Applications have proliferated across engineering domains, including autonomous vehicle control, precision manufacturing, chemical process control, and biological systems regulation. Mathematically, the approach leverages Lyapunov-based analyses, singular perturbation theory, and operator-theoretic methods to establish stability and transient bounds. Recent contributions have integrated funnel control with iterative learning, reinforcement learning, and neural network-based adaptation, yielding hybrid methods that combine prescribed performance with data-driven flexibility. Despite these advances, challenges persist, particularly in handling large-scale interconnected systems, time-varying delays, stochastic disturbances, and real-time implementation with limited computational resources. This survey synthesizes the extensive literature, categorizing results by system type, control objective, and application domain, and highlights open research questions, thereby providing a valuable resource for both practitioners and theoreticians.

title: ALMA-IMF XVI: Mass-averaged temperature of cores and protostellar luminosities in the ALMA-IMF protoclusters
text_ai: ALMA-IMF imaged 15 massive protoclusters down to a resolution of of 2 kau scales, identifying about 1000 star-forming cores. The mass and luminosity of these cores, which are fundamental physical characteristics, are difficult to determine, a problem greatly exacerbated at the distances >2 kpc of ALMA-IMF protoclusters. We therefore developed a method to estimate mass-averaged dust temperatures for each core by combining ALMA 1.3 and 3 mm continuum fluxes with a modified blackbody model, assuming a constant dust opacity index. This approach yields temperature estimates that account for both the warm inner regions and cooler outer envelopes, providing a physically motivated average over the core’s mass distribution. While individual core SEDs are poorly sampled due to limited wavelength coverage, the ensemble enables us to calibrate temperature–size and temperature–luminosity relations. Using these relations, we derive protostellar luminosities from the 1.3 mm fluxes, applying a bootstrapping method to propagate uncertainties. The resulting luminosity distribution spans ~0.1–10⁵ L⊙, with median values that vary systematically across protoclusters. We find that mass-averaged temperatures are typically 20–40 K, but exceed 50 K in the most luminous cores, consistent with significant internal heating. Crucially, we demonstrate that ignoring the temperature variation and assuming a fixed temperature (e.g., 20 K) leads to systematic overestimates of core masses by factors up to five for the warmest sources, while underestimating luminosities. By adopting our temperature-derived masses and luminosities, we construct core mass functions and protostellar luminosity functions for each protocluster. The shapes of these distributions are remarkably similar across the sample, suggesting a universal underlying mechanism for core formation and early accretion. Our results provide a robust empirical benchmark for models of massive star formation and highlight the necessity of multi-wavelength ALMA observations to overcome distance-related biases. The derived catalogs and temperature relations are made publicly available to facilitate further studies of the initial conditions of high-mass star clusters.

title: Loss Minimization for Electrical Flows over Spanning Trees on Grids
text_ai: We study the electrical distribution network reconfiguration problem, defined as follows. We are given an undirected graph with a root vertex, demand at each non-root vertex, and resistance on each edge. Then, we want to find a spanning tree of the graph that specifies the routing of power from the root to each vertex so that all the demands are satisfied and the energy loss is minimized. This problem is of practical interest in power system operation, where distribution networks are often radial (tree-structured) and reconfigurable. In this paper, we focus on the case where the underlying graph is a rectangular grid, a common model for urban distribution networks. We show that the optimization can be reformulated as a convex program over the cone of tree-structured incidence vectors, but the combinatorial constraint makes the general case NP-hard. However, for grids, we exploit the planar and regular structure to derive a polynomial-time dynamic programming algorithm. Our key insight is that the optimal spanning tree for a grid can be decomposed into independent subproblems along cuts induced by the root's row and column, leading to a state space that is only polynomial in the grid dimensions. We also prove that the energy loss on any spanning tree is a convex function of the edge currents, which allows us to apply a simple greedy heuristic that runs in near-linear time and is provably optimal for certain demand patterns. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world feeder data confirm that our algorithm finds trees with losses up to 20% lower than those produced by standard minimum-weight spanning tree heuristics, and scales to grids with over 10,000 nodes.

title: The effect of structural and magnetic disorder on the 3$d$-5$d$ exchange interactions of La$_{2-x}$Ca$_{x}$CoIrO$_{6}$
text_ai: The delicate balance between spin-orbit coupling, Coulomb repulsion and crystalline electric field interactions observed in Ir-based oxides is usually manifested as exotic magnetic behavior. Here we investigate the evolution of the exchange coupling between Co and Ir for partial La substitution by Ca in La$_{2}$CoIrO$_6$. We employ x-ray diffraction, magnetometry, and neutron spectroscopy to investigate the structural and magnetic evolution of La$_{2-x}$Ca$_{x}$CoIrO$_{6}$ for $x$ from 0 to 0.5. Hole doping from Ca$^{2+}$ substitution modifies the valence of Co and Ir, confirmed by x-ray absorption spectroscopy revealing a mix of Co$^{2+}$/Co$^{3+}$ and Ir$^{4+}$/Ir$^{5+}$. The size mismatch between Ca and La induces structural distortions, lowering symmetry from monoclinic and disrupting the antiferromagnetic order of the parent compound which has a N\'{e}el temperature around 100~K. For $x \geq 0.3$, a spin-glass phase emerges due to random Ca distribution and magnetic frustration, as confirmed by ac susceptibility measurements. Using inelastic neutron scattering and density functional theory, we evaluate the Co-Ir exchange coupling. It is highly sensitive to local structural environment and magnetic disorder: at low $x$, coupling remains strong, promoting a canted antiferromagnetic state with a finite magnetic moment; at higher $x$, dilution and structural inhomogeneities weaken the coupling, suppressing the Weiss temperature and reducing the effective paramagnetic moment in Curie-Weiss fits. The spin-orbit coupling on Ir plays a crucial role, as evidenced by deviations from simple Heisenberg behavior in magnetization isotherms. Muon spin rotation experiments further reveal the nature of the magnetic order. Our findings demonstrate that the interplay of structural and magnetic disorder can tailor exchange interactions in 3$d$-5$d$ systems, offering a pathway to design materials with tunable magnetic properties for potential spintronic applications. This study highlights the importance of considering both chemical substitution and structural effects in understanding the magnetism of complex oxides.

title: Interleukin-1beta-mediated suppression of microRNA-27a-3p activity in human cartilage via MAPK and NF-kappaB pathways: A potential mechanism of osteoarthritis pathogenesis
text_ai: The aim of the present study was to investigate the role of microRNA (miR)-27a-3p in osteoarthritis (OA). Reverse transcription-quantitative polymerase chain reaction and western blotting were performed to determine the expression of miR-27a-3p and aggrecanase-2 (ADAMTS5) in cartilage tissues from patients with OA and healthy controls, and also in interleukin (IL)-1beta-treated primary human chondrocytes. The results demonstrated that miR-27a-3p expression was significantly downregulated in OA cartilage compared with normal cartilage, correlating inversely with ADAMTS5 levels. Similarly, IL-1beta treatment of primary human chondrocytes reduced miR-27a-3p expression in a time- and dose-dependent manner, while ADAMTS5 mRNA and protein expression increased. To identify the upstream signaling mechanisms, chondrocytes were pretreated with specific inhibitors of MAPK subfamilies (p38, JNK, ERK) and NF-kappaB prior to IL-1beta stimulation. Pharmacological inhibition of p38 MAPK, JNK, and NF-kappaB, but not ERK, significantly abrogated the IL-1beta-induced suppression of miR-27a-3p, whereas activation of these pathways by IL-1beta was confirmed by phosphorylation analysis. Furthermore, luciferase reporter assays verified that miR-27a-3p directly targets the 3'-untranslated region of ADAMTS5, and overexpression of miR-27a-3p mimic in chondrocytes reduced ADAMTS5 expression and attenuated IL-1beta-induced aggrecan degradation. Conversely, inhibition of miR-27a-3p enhanced ADAMTS5 levels and exacerbated the catabolic effects of IL-1beta. Notably, chromatin immunoprecipitation revealed that IL-1beta-driven activation of NF-kappaB and MAPK pathways led to increased binding of transcription factors, including c-Jun and p65, to the miR-27a-3p promoter region, thereby repressing its transcription. Collectively, these findings elucidate a novel mechanism whereby IL-1beta suppresses miR-27a-3p activity through MAPK and NF-kappaB signaling, leading to upregulation of ADAMTS5 and subsequent cartilage matrix degradation. This pathway may represent a key molecular event in OA pathogenesis and offers potential therapeutic targets for mitigating disease progression.

title: Genetic engineering and characterisation of chlorotoxin-fused gelonin for enhanced glioblastoma therapy.
text_ai: Despite substantial advances in its treatment, brain cancer remains a life-threatening disease with a poor survival rate. The main challenges for the conventional chemotherapy include an insufficient efficacy of drugs and toxicity caused by their nonselective mode of action. Here, we report the genetic engineering of a chlorotoxin-gelonin fusion protein (CTX-Gel) for targeted glioblastoma therapy. Chlorotoxin, a scorpion venom peptide, specifically binds to glioma cells via matrix metalloproteinase-2 and annexin A2, while gelonin is a potent type I ribosome-inactivating protein. The fusion construct was expressed in E. coli, purified, and refolded. Biochemical characterization confirmed retention of both chlorotoxin binding and gelonin's N-glycosidase activity. Cytotoxicity assays demonstrated selective killing of glioblastoma cells (U87, U251) with nanomolar IC₅₀ values, while showing reduced toxicity to normal astrocytes and non-cancer cells. Confocal microscopy revealed efficient internalization via receptor-mediated endocytosis. In a 3D spheroid model, the fusion protein penetrated deeply into tumor masses and induced apoptosis. These findings indicate that CTX-Gel offers a promising strategy for enhancing the therapeutic index of gelonin by targeting glioblastoma cells specifically, thus overcoming the key limitations of conventional chemotherapy. The targeted delivery and potent cytotoxicity warrant further in vivo evaluation for clinical translation, as this approach addresses the critical need for more effective and selective brain cancer therapeutics.

title: Point-MoE: Towards Cross-Domain Generalization in 3D Semantic Segmentation via Mixture-of-Experts
text_ai: While scaling laws have transformed natural language processing and computer vision, 3D point cloud understanding has yet to reach that stage. This can be attributed to both the comparatively smaller scale of 3D datasets, as well as the disparate sources of the data itself. Despite these challenges, we argue that a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) framework can effectively bridge domain gaps by learning specialized feature representations for diverse point cloud sources. We introduce Point-MoE, a novel architecture that decomposes the semantic segmentation network into a set of expert modules, each activated via a learned gating mechanism conditioned on per-point features. This design enables the model to dynamically route different 3D structures (e.g., indoor scenes versus outdoor LiDAR scans) to different experts, thereby capturing domain-specific patterns without requiring explicit domain labels. Additionally, we incorporate a domain-invariant auxiliary loss and a sparse regularization term to encourage expert specialization while preventing collapse. Extensive experiments on seven benchmark datasets spanning autonomous driving, indoor scanning, and synthetic data demonstrate that Point-MoE achieves state-of-the-art cross-domain generalization performance, improving mIoU by 8–15% over prior domain adaptation and generalizable segmentation methods. Notably, it also exhibits strong scalability: as more experts are added, performance monotonically improves even under severe domain shifts. Our work provides a practical path toward scaling 3D point cloud understanding without the need for massive unified datasets, leveraging modular specialization to handle data heterogeneity effectively.

title: Building a Bridge Between NMDAR-Mediated Excitotoxicity and Mitochondrial Dysfunction in Chronic and Acute Diseases.
text_ai: Glutamate is the major excitatory neurotransmitter in the brain, and it is widely accepted to play a role in synaptic plasticity and excitotoxic cell death. Glutamate binds to several receptors, including ionotropic N-methyl-D-Aspartate receptor (NMDAR), which is essential in synaptic plasticity and excitotoxicity. However, overactivation of NMDARs triggers an excessive influx of Ca²⁺, initiating a cascade of downstream events that culminate in neuronal injury. This excitotoxic pathway is intimately linked to mitochondrial dysfunction, as Ca²⁺ overload disrupts mitochondrial membrane potential, impairs oxidative phosphorylation, and induces the opening of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore. Consequent release of pro-apoptotic factors and reactive oxygen species amplifies cellular damage, creating a vicious cycle that exacerbates neurodegeneration. In chronic neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s diseases, sustained low-level NMDAR hyperactivity contributes to progressive mitochondrial impairment and synaptic loss. Conversely, in acute conditions like stroke and traumatic brain injury, massive NMDAR activation precipitates rapid mitochondrial failure and necrotic cell death. Emerging evidence suggests that targeting the interface between NMDAR signaling and mitochondrial bioenergetics may offer therapeutic potential across both temporal spectra. This review synthesizes current understanding of the molecular mechanisms bridging NMDAR-mediated excitotoxicity and mitochondrial dysfunction, highlighting shared pathogenic nodes in chronic and acute diseases. We propose that a unified framework—integrating Ca²⁺ dysregulation, oxidative stress, and metabolic deficits—can inform the development of neuroprotective strategies that simultaneously mitigate excitotoxic and mitochondrial injury.

title: Comparison of space weathering spectral changes induced by solar wind and micrometeoroid impacts using ion- and femtosecond-laser-irradiated olivine and pyroxene
text_ai: Space weathering is a process that changes the surface of airless planetary bodies. Prime space weathering agents are solar wind irradiation and micrometeoroid bombardment. These processes alter planetary reflectance spectra and often modify their compositional diagnostic features. Here, we experimentally simulate these two space weathering agents under controlled laboratory conditions to isolate and compare their spectral effects on the two most abundant mafic minerals in the inner Solar System: olivine and orthopyroxene. Solar wind irradiation was simulated using broad-beam He⁺ and Ar⁺ ion bombardment at energies from 1 to 10 keV, while micrometeoroid impacts were simulated using femtosecond laser pulses (800 nm, 100 fs) at fluences of 0.1–1 J cm⁻², spanning the regime from single-pulse melting to vaporization. Reflectance spectra (0.35–2.5 µm) were measured before and after each treatment under standard conditions. Our results reveal both commonalities and distinct differences in the spectral evolution pathways. For both minerals, increasing ion fluence causes a progressive reddening (increase in spectral slope from 0.5 to 1.0 µm), a reduction in overall reflectance (darkening), and a weakening of the 1 µm and 2 µm absorption bands. These changes are consistent with the formation of nanophase iron particles (npFe⁰) in a silica-rich rind, as confirmed by scanning electron microscopy and transmission electron microscopy. In contrast, femtosecond laser irradiation produces more rapid spectral reddening and darkening at lower equivalent energy densities, and crucially, it introduces additional absorption features: broad flattening of the 1 µm band and, in pyroxene, a subtle shift of the 2 µm band center toward shorter wavelengths. These additional modifications are attributed to the formation of melt-derived amorphous phases and vapor-deposited coatings, which alter the crystal-field environment of Fe²⁺. We quantify these changes using spectral parameters (band depth, band center, spectral slope, and reflectance at 0.7 µm) and compare them to space-weathered surfaces of the Moon, Vesta, and ordinary chondrite parent bodies. Our results suggest that solar wind dominates the initial rapid darkening and npFe⁰ formation, while micrometeoroid impacts are required to produce the full range of spectral bluing (in mature lunar soils) and the suppression of pyroxene bands observed on some asteroids. The dual-agent simulation provides a framework for deconvolving the relative contributions of these two processes in remote sensing data, with direct implications for the interpretation of reflectance spectra from all airless bodies, including Mercury, asteroids, and the Moon.

title: Sedative and cardiorespiratory effects of low doses of xylazine with and without acepromazine in Nordestino donkeys.
text_ai: Information on appropriate protocols for sedation of Nordestino donkeys is scarce. To evaluate the sedative and cardiorespiratory effects of low doses of intravenous (i.v.) xylazine with and without acepromazine in 'Nordestino' donkeys. Seven healthy female Nordestino donkeys (150 ± 18 kg) were included in this blinded, randomised, crossover experiment. Each donkey received four treatments: X0.2 (xylazine 0.2 mg kg⁻¹), X0.4 (xylazine 0.4 mg kg⁻¹), XA0.2 (xylazine 0.2 mg kg⁻¹ plus acepromazine 0.02 mg kg⁻¹), and XA0.4 (xylazine 0.4 mg kg⁻¹ plus acepromazine 0.02 mg kg⁻¹) intravenously. Sedation was scored using a composite scale and cardiorespiratory variables (heart rate [HR], respiratory rate [RR], invasive mean arterial pressure [MAP], and arterial blood gases) were recorded at baseline and at 5, 10, 15, 30, 45, 60, 75, and 90 minutes post-injection. Data were analyzed using repeated measures ANOVA. All treatments induced safe, mild-to-moderate sedation, with peak effects at 5–15 minutes. XA0.4 produced significantly higher sedation scores than X0.4 (mean 5.1 vs. 4.2; P = 0.02), and sedation duration was extended with acepromazine (90 minutes versus 60 minutes). HR decreased transiently by 25–30%, with nadir at 15 minutes (33–35 beats min⁻¹), but remained above 30 beats min⁻¹. RR decreased proportionally, with no hypoxemia (PaO₂ ≥ 80 mmHg) or hypercapnia (PaCO₂ ≤ 45 mmHg). MAP declined by 10–15% in acepromazine groups, but hypotension (MAP < 65 mmHg) was absent. Arterial blood gas values remained within physiological ranges. Low doses of xylazine with or without acepromazine are safe and effective for sedation in Nordestino donkeys. Acepromazine enhances sedation depth and duration without clinically significant cardiorespiratory compromise, supporting its use for minimally invasive procedures. Further studies are warranted to optimize dosing for specific clinical contexts.

title: The Comparative Study of Cervical Shear Wave Elastography Between Twin and Singleton Pregnancy.
text_ai: To compare the cervical shear wave elastography (SWE) by using transvaginal ultrasound (TVS) between twin and singleton pregnant women. This was a prospective cohort study involving the twin and singleton pregnant women who attended the antenatal care at Ramathibodi Hospital, Bangkok, Thailand. including 50 twin and 100 singleton pregnancies matched for gestational age. All participants underwent transvaginal ultrasound with shear wave elastography at 20–24 weeks of gestation. The cervical length (CL) and SWE parameters, including mean, minimum, and maximum elasticity values (in kPa), were measured at the anterior cervical lip. Exclusion criteria included history of cervical surgery, preterm labor, rupture of membranes, or congenital anomalies. Statistical analysis was performed using independent t-tests and Mann-Whitney U tests, with significance set at p<0.05. Results showed that twin pregnancies had significantly lower mean cervical SWE values compared to singletons (mean 8.4 ± 2.1 vs. 10.9 ± 3.0 kPa, p<0.001), while cervical length did not differ significantly between groups (35.2 ± 4.5 vs. 36.1 ± 5.1 mm, p=0.28). The minimum SWE was also lower in twins (6.1 ± 1.8 vs. 8.3 ± 2.6 kPa, p<0.001). Receiver operating characteristic analysis revealed that mean SWE had an area under the curve of 0.78 for predicting twin pregnancy. These findings suggest that cervical tissue stiffness is reduced in twin compared to singleton pregnancies, independent of cervical length. In conclusion, shear wave elastography may provide additional biomechanical information for assessing cervical integrity in twin gestations, potentially aiding in the prediction of preterm birth. Further studies with longitudinal follow-up and outcome data are warranted to validate these preliminary findings.

This was a prospective cohort study involving the twin and singleton pregnant women who attended the antenatal care at Ramathibodi Hospital, Bangkok, Thailand.

title: Cladogenetic and Anagenetic Models of Chromosome Number Evolution: A Bayesian Model Averaging Approach.
text_ai: Chromosome number is a key feature of the higher-order organization of the genome, and changes in chromosome number play a fundamental role in evolution. Dysploid gains and losses in chromosome number, as well as polyploidization events, may drive reproductive isolation and lineage diversification. Despite the long-standing interest in chromosome number evolution, it remains unclear whether most changes accumulate gradually along phylogenetic branches (anagenesis) or occur in bursts at speciation events (cladogenesis). Distinguishing between these two modes is critical for understanding the tempo and drivers of genome restructuring. Here, we develop a Bayesian model-averaging framework that simultaneously evaluates anagenetic and cladogenetic models of chromosome number evolution across a phylogeny. Our approach integrates reversible-jump Markov chain Monte Carlo to sample over different rate regimes and allows the data to inform whether changes are more likely associated with speciation or with periods of phyletic stasis. We apply the method to a large empirical dataset spanning angiosperms, ferns, and insects—groups with well-documented variation in chromosome number. For each clade, we compare the posterior probabilities of pure anagenetic, pure cladogenetic, and mixed models, while accounting for polyploidization as a distinct process via a separate rate class. Results reveal strong support for mixed models in most clades, but the relative importance of cladogenesis versus anagenesis varies substantially across lineages. In angiosperms, cladogenetic changes are often favored, consistent with the hypothesis that chromosome number rearrangements contribute to reproductive isolation and rapid radiations. In contrast, ferns show a greater contribution of anagenetic changes, suggesting a different evolutionary dynamic perhaps linked to high rates of polyploidy. Our framework also quantifies the uncertainty in model selection, highlighting that a single evolutionary model may inadequately capture the complexity of chromosome number evolution. By averaging over multiple plausible models, we provide robust estimates of transition rates and ancestral states while avoiding overconfidence in any one scenario. This Bayesian model-averaging approach offers a principled way to test long-standing hypotheses about the mode of karyotypic evolution and can be extended to other discrete traits where both gradual and punctuated processes may operate.
prefix: Chromosome number is a key feature of the higher-order organization of the genome, and changes in chromosome number play a fundamental role in evolution. Dysploid gains and losses in chromosome number, as well as polyploidization events, may drive reproductive isolation and lineage diversification.

title: Tetrahedral framework nucleic acids promote scarless healing of cutaneous wounds via the AKT-signaling pathway.
text_ai: While the skin is considered the first line of defense in the human body, there are some vulnerabilities that render it susceptible to certain threats, which is an issue that is recognized by both patients and doctors. Cutaneous wound healing is a series of complex processes that involve many types of cells, such as fibroblasts and keratinocytes. Tetrahedral framework nucleic acids (tFNAs), a class of DNA nanostructures with exceptional biocompatibility and cellular internalization efficiency, have emerged as promising bioactive materials for tissue regeneration. Here, we investigated their potential to modulate scarless wound healing. tFNAs were synthesized via self-assembly of four single-stranded DNAs and topically applied to full-thickness cutaneous wounds in a murine model. Histological and immunofluorescence analyses revealed that tFNA treatment significantly accelerated re-epithelialization, reduced granulation tissue thickness, and promoted orderly collagen deposition with a higher collagen type III/I ratio, indicative of scarless repair. Mechanistically, transcriptomic profiling and western blotting demonstrated that tFNAs activated the AKT signaling pathway in both fibroblasts and keratinocytes, enhancing cell proliferation, migration, and angiogenesis while inhibiting excessive myofibroblast differentiation. Notably, pharmacological inhibition of AKT abolished these regenerative effects. These findings establish tFNAs as a potent nanomaterial for achieving scarless wound healing through AKT-mediated regulation of cellular behaviors, offering a translational strategy for improving cutaneous wound repair.
prefix: While the skin is considered the first line of defense in the human body, there are some vulnerabilities that render it susceptible to certain threats, which is an issue that is recognized by both patients and doctors. Cutaneous wound healing is a series of complex processes that involve many types of cells, such as fibroblasts and keratinocytes.

title: A GPU-accelerated viewer for HEALPix maps
text_ai: HEALPix by G\'orski et. al. (2005) is de-facto standard for Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) data storage and analysis, and is widely used in current and upcoming CMB experiments. Almost all the datasets in Legacy Archive for Microwave Background Data Analysis (LAMBDA) use HEALPix as a format of choice. Despite its ubiquity, existing visualization tools for HEALPix maps are predominantly CPU-based and often fail to deliver interactive frame rates for high-resolution maps, particularly those with Nside=8192 or larger, which contain over 800 million pixels. This performance bottleneck hinders rapid exploration and comparison of multi-frequency CMB data. To address this, we introduce a GPU-accelerated viewer that exploits the parallel processing capabilities of modern graphics cards. The viewer implements a hierarchical level-of-detail rendering scheme using HEALPix's nested ordering, dynamically subdividing the sphere into manageable tiles that are streamed to GPU memory as needed. This approach allows seamless navigation across all resolutions with minimal latency. We also incorporate efficient data structures for handling multi-component maps (temperature, Q, U polarization) and overlays such as point sources, masks, and contour lines. Performance benchmarks on a variety of datasets, including Planck, WMAP, and simulated CMB-S4 maps, demonstrate sustained rendering above 60 frames per second for maps with up to 50 million pixels, and interactivity for far larger maps through adaptive downsampling. Memory usage is reduced by an order of magnitude compared to loading full-resolution maps into system memory. The viewer supports multiple projections (mollweide, orthographic, gnomonic) and provides a Python API for scripting and integration with analysis pipelines. It is implemented in C++ using OpenGL and CUDA, and is released as open-source software to the community. We anticipate that this tool will accelerate scientific discovery by enabling in-depth visual inspection of the next generation of CMB experiments.

Almost all the datasets in Legacy Archive for Microwave Background Data Analysis (LAMBDA) use HEALPix as a format of choice.

title: Variability in Low Ionization Broad Absorption Line Outflows
text_ai: We present results of our time variability studies of Mg II and Al III absorption lines in a sample of 22 Low Ionization Broad Absorption Line QSOs (LoBAL QSOs) at 0.2 <= zem <= 2.1 using the 2m telescope at IUCAA Girawali Observatory over a time-scale of 10 days to 7.69 years in the QSO's rest frame. Our analysis reveals significant variability in the equivalent widths (EWs) and profile shapes of both Mg II and Al III absorption in 16 out of 22 sources (73%), with a typical variation amplitude of 30–60% over rest-frame timescales ranging from 0.5 to 4.2 years. The variability is more frequently detected in Mg II (14/22) than in Al III (9/22), consistent with the higher ionization potential of Al III requiring denser or more shielded gas. For 10 sources with multi-epoch data, we find no clear correlation between variability amplitude and time baseline, suggesting that the responsible physical processes—likely changes in ionization state or column density due to moving clumps across the line of sight—operate on timescales of months to years. Compared to high-ionization BAL outflows, our LoBAL sample shows a higher fraction of variable absorbers (73% vs. ~45%), hinting at more dynamic, clumpy structures closer to the central engine. We also explore the relationship between variability and other quasar properties (e.g., continuum luminosity, black hole mass, Eddington ratio) and find a mild anti-correlation with redshift, possibly due to longer rest-frame monitoring intervals for low-redshift objects. The observed variability implies that LoBAL outflows are not steady-state winds but rather exhibit significant temporal evolution, with implications for their total kinetic power and feedback efficiency. Our results support a scenario where LoBAL outflows are composed of dense, parsec-scale clouds driven by radiation pressure, with cloud crossing timescales consistent with the variability patterns. Future high-cadence monitoring and spectral modeling will further constrain the physical parameters of these intriguing outflows.
