title: An H{\alpha} view of galaxy build-up in the first 2 Gyr: luminosity functions at z~4-6.5 from NIRCam/grism spectroscopy
text_ai: The H{\alpha} nebular emission line is an optimal tracer for recent star formation in galaxies. With the advent of JWST, this line has recently become observable at z>3 for the first time. We present a catalog of 1013 H{\alpha} emitters at 3.7<z<6.7 in the GOODS fields obtained from a blind search in JWST NIRCam/grism data. Using the unique sensitivity and wide spectral coverage of JWST/NIRCam's grism mode, we identify Hα emission lines in the wavelength range 3.1–5.2 μm, covering rest-frame optical emission over the full redshift interval. We derive robust line fluxes by fitting continuum and line models to the extracted 1D spectra, applying corrections for slit-loss and line-to-continuum variations. The resulting catalog spans stellar masses of 10^7–10^10 M⊙ and star-formation rates (SFRs) of 1–100 M⊙ yr⁻¹, sampling the bulk of the star-forming population at these redshifts for the first time. We construct the Hα luminosity function (LF) in four redshift bins spanning z∼3.7–4.3, 4.3–5.0, 5.0–5.8, and 5.8–6.7, down to L(Hα) ∼ 10^41.5 erg s⁻¹. The LFs are well described by Schechter functions with faint-end slopes α ∼ –1.5 to –1.6, showing mild evolution toward steeper slopes at higher redshift. The characteristic luminosity L* increases from log(L*/erg s⁻¹)=42.8 at z∼4 to 43.3 at z∼6, consistent with the build-up of massive systems. Converting Hα luminosities to SFRs, we derive the cosmic SFR density (SFRD) over the first 2 Gyr after the Big Bang. Our SFRD measurements show a gradual decline from z∼4 to z∼6.5, dropping by a factor ∼5, in agreement with UV-based estimates but with reduced systematic uncertainties from dust attenuation. Combining our results with lower-redshift Hα surveys, we trace the assembly of stellar mass through cosmic time. We find that the star-forming galaxy population at z∼4–6.5 already contains ∼30% of the total stellar mass formed by z∼2, indicating efficient early star formation. These results highlight the power of blind grism spectroscopy to map the nebular emission from galaxies during the epoch of reionization, providing a direct and largely dust-insensitive view of galaxy build-up in the first 2 Gyr of the Universe.

title: When Do Drivers Concentrate? Attention-based Driver Behavior Modeling With Deep Reinforcement Learning
text_ai: Driver distraction a significant risk to driving safety. Apart from spatial domain, research on temporal inattention is also necessary. This paper aims to figure out the pattern of drivers' temporal attention allocation. We propose a novel framework that leverages deep reinforcement learning to model how drivers allocate attention over time in naturalistic driving scenarios. By formulating the driving task as a Markov decision process, our model learns an attention policy that determines when a driver is likely to focus on the road or engage in secondary tasks. We train the model using a large-scale dataset of real driving trips, incorporating both vehicle dynamics and driver state features. The learned attention patterns reveal that drivers strategically concentrate during critical maneuvers such as lane changes and braking events, but exhibit reduced attention during routine highway cruising. Furthermore, we find that individual differences in attention allocation are significant, with some drivers consistently maintaining higher engagement. Our model outperforms baseline approaches in predicting glance behavior and reaction times to unexpected events. The results demonstrate that temporal attention is not random but follows a learned strategy that balances safety and cognitive load. This work provides insights for designing adaptive in-vehicle interfaces and driver monitoring systems that anticipate periods of inattention. These findings highlight the potential for personalized safety interventions that adapt to individual attention strategies. Moreover, our approach can be extended to model multi-modal attention, integrating gaze, head pose, and physiological signals. Future work will explore real-time attention estimation for proactive collision avoidance.

title: 3D morphological analysis of spiral intestine morphogenesis in the little skate, Leucoraja erinacea.
text_ai: The evolution of organ asymmetries is less explored than the field of organ morphology and coiling. The digestive tract of elasmobranchs provides a fascinating model for studying the evolution of morphological asymmetries. Unique to elasmobranchs and all basal fishes is the spiral intestine, which may represent an intermediate morphology in evolution from the straight gut of lamprey to the elongated coils of higher vertebrates. Here, we employ high-resolution micro-computed tomography and 3D volumetric reconstruction to characterize the morphogenesis of the spiral intestine across embryonic development of the little skate. By quantifying the emergence and progression of the spiral fold and its associated lumenal asymmetry, we reveal that the spiral intestine initially forms as a straight, symmetric tube that subsequently undergoes a stereotyped left-handed helical coiling, establishing a consistent dextral (right-sided) orientation of the intestinal apex. The timing and pattern of this coiling correlate with localized differences in cell proliferation and convergent extension along the anteroposterior axis. These findings demonstrate that the spiral intestine’s asymmetry arises through a late, modular morphogenetic process rather than from early left-right patterning signals, suggesting an evolutionary intermediate step between the simple straight gut and the complex, regionally specialized coils of amniotes. This study provides a framework for understanding how ancestral asymmetries in gut form can arise and be co-opted during vertebrate evolution.

title: Trainable Weight Averaging: Accelerating Training and Improving Generalization
text_ai: Weight averaging is a widely used technique for accelerating training and improving the generalization of deep neural networks (DNNs). While existing approaches like stochastic weight averaging (SWA) rely on pre-set weighting schemes, they can be suboptimal when handling diverse weights. In this paper, we propose Trainable Weight Averaging (TWA), which learns optimal averaging coefficients via gradient descent on a validation set. Unlike fixed schedules, TWA adaptively weights each checkpoint, balancing contributions from early stable and late refined states. Formulating the averaging as an online bilevel optimization, we derive an efficient update rule using implicit differentiation. This reduces variance in weight trajectories and improves generalization by selectively combining beneficial checkpoints. Convergence analysis demonstrates that TWA achieves lower expected risk under mild assumptions. Empirically, on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, and PTB, TWA yields up to 2% higher accuracy and 2× faster training compared to SWA, EMA, and Lookahead. It is robust to hyperparameter choices—learning rate, averaging window, and decay—and requires negligible overhead: only one extra parameter copy and gradient buffer. Ablations confirm that learned weights diverge significantly from uniform, validating the need for trainable coefficients. TWA integrates seamlessly with SGD and Adam, and sets new state-of-the-art for weight averaging methods across ResNets, Transformers, and EfficientNets. Our open-source implementation facilitates easy adoption.

title: Active Feature Acquisition with Supervised Matrix Completion
text_ai: Feature missing is a serious problem in many applications, which may lead to low quality of training data and further significantly degrade the learning performance. While feature acquisition usually involves special devices or complex process, it is expensive to acquire all feature values for the whole dataset. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework that integrates active feature acquisition with supervised matrix completion. Our approach selects the most informative feature–instance pairs to acquire, guided by the dual objectives of improving imputation accuracy and maximizing predictive performance. A supervised matrix completion model is employed to leverage both observed features and label information, enabling more accurate recovery of missing entries while maintaining consistency with the learning task. The active acquisition strategy iteratively identifies high-uncertainty or high-impact entries, thereby reducing acquisition costs without compromising model quality. We formulate the selection criterion using an acquisition function that balances expected improvement in completion quality and predictive gain. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms baseline strategies, including random acquisition and unsupervised matrix completion, under various missing rates. Notably, the framework achieves superior classification accuracy with substantially fewer acquired feature values, highlighting its practical utility in resource-constrained settings. The proposed approach thus offers a principled solution for cost-effective data enrichment while preserving learning performance.

title: Xiaoyao Pills Ameliorate Depression-like Behaviors and Oxidative Stress Induced by Olfactory Bulbectomy in Rats via the Activation of the PIK3CA-AKT1-NFE2L2/BDNF Signaling Pathway.
text_ai: Numerous studies have revealed that oxidative stress is closely associated with the occurrence and development of depression. Xiaoyao Pills (XYW) are included in the Chinese Pharmacopoeia and are frequently used for treating anxiety and depression by smoothing the liver, strengthening the spleen, and nourishing the blood. Thus, this study aimed to evaluate the antidepressant effects of XYW and its underlying mechanisms in a rat model of olfactory bulbectomy (OBX), a well-established paradigm of depression associated with oxidative stress. Sprague-Dawley rats underwent bilateral OBX or sham surgery. After two weeks of recovery, OBX rats were orally administered XYW (0.5, 1.0, or 2.0 g/kg/day) or fluoxetine (10 mg/kg/day) for four consecutive weeks. Behavioral assessments—including the sucrose preference test, forced swim test, open field test, and elevated plus maze—were conducted to evaluate depression- and anxiety-like behaviors. Additionally, levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS), malondialdehyde (MDA), superoxide dismutase (SOD), glutathione (GSH), and catalase (CAT) in the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus were measured. Protein and mRNA expression of PIK3CA, phosphorylated AKT1 (p-AKT1), AKT1, NFE2L2, and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) were assessed via Western blotting and quantitative real-time PCR. To confirm pathway involvement, a separate cohort received the PI3K inhibitor LY294002 alongside XYW treatment. The results demonstrated that XYW significantly reversed OBX-induced anhedonia (increased sucrose preference), behavioral despair (reduced immobility in the forced swim test), and locomotor and anxiolytic deficits in the open field and elevated plus maze. Moreover, XYW attenuated oxidative stress by decreasing ROS and MDA while increasing SOD, GSH, and CAT activities. Mechanistically, XYW upregulated PIK3CA, p-AKT1/AKT1 ratio, NFE2L2 nuclear translocation, and BDNF expression in the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus. These effects were abrogated by LY294002, confirming that XYW exerts antidepressant and antioxidant actions via the PIK3CA-AKT1-NFE2L2/BDNF signaling cascade. Collectively, our findings demonstrate that XYW ameliorates depression-like behaviors and oxidative stress in OBX rats through activation of this pathway, providing a molecular basis for its clinical use in depression management.

title: Why the World Reads Wikipedia: Beyond English Speakers
text_ai: As one of the Web's primary multilingual knowledge sources, Wikipedia is read by millions of people across the globe every day. Despite this global readership, little is known about why users read Wikipedia's various language editions. This study addresses this gap by presenting a large-scale analysis of reader motivations across 15 language editions, encompassing both English and non-English speakers. Drawing on a combination of web-based surveys and behavioral log data, we identify seven primary motivations—such as work-related tasks, educational research, general curiosity, fact-checking, and news consumption—and quantify their prevalence across language communities. Our results reveal significant cross-language variation: while English Wikipedia readers are more likely to engage for work or academic purposes, readers of smaller language editions frequently prioritize current events, identity maintenance, or accessing content unavailable in their native tongue. Notably, curiosity-driven reading is universal, yet its relative importance differs systematically with the size and topical coverage of each edition. We further demonstrate that these motivational patterns correlate with the linguistic diversity of the readership and the offline resources available in each language context. These findings extend prior work, which has focused almost exclusively on English, and offer evidence that Wikipedia serves distinct informational needs across its language versions. The study underscores the platform's role in bridging knowledge gaps, particularly for communities with limited alternative sources, and suggests design implications for multilingual content discovery. Ultimately, understanding why the world reads Wikipedia beyond English speakers is crucial to supporting equitable, user-centered access to free knowledge globally.

title: Discovery and characterisation of detached M-dwarf eclipsing binaries in the WFCAM Transit Survey
text_ai: We report the discovery of 16 detached M-dwarf eclipsing binaries with J<16 mag and provide a detailed characterisation of three of them, using high-precision infrared light curves from the WFCAM Transit Survey (WTS). Such systems provide the most accurate and model-independent method for measuring the fundamental parameters of these poorly understood yet numerous stars, which currently lack sufficient observations to precisely calibrate stellar evolution models. The systems were identified through a systematic search of the WTS light curves, which cover approximately 3.7 deg² in the J-band with a typical cadence of 15 minutes over a 3-year baseline. Initial candidate selection employed a combination of variability indices and eclipse detection algorithms, followed by visual inspection to confirm periodic, well-separated primary and secondary eclipses. For the 16 detached binaries, we derived orbital periods ranging from 0.5 to 3.2 days, and used light-curve modelling to estimate inclination, eccentricity, and relative radii. We then selected the three brightest targets (J = 12.5–14.0 mag) for high-resolution near-infrared spectroscopy, obtaining radial velocity curves with precisions better than 0.5 km s⁻¹. Joint modelling of the light and radial velocity curves yielded masses and radii with typical uncertainties of 2–3% and 1–2%, respectively. The masses span 0.22–0.58 M⊙ and radii 0.25–0.56 R⊙, placing these systems in a regime where theoretical models remain poorly constrained. Comparisons with current stellar evolution models reveal significant systematic discrepancies: two of the three characterised systems show radii 8–12% larger than model predictions for their masses, while the third is consistent within 1σ. These results reinforce the well-known radius inflation seen in low-mass stars, and extend the observational baseline to near-infrared photometry, which mitigates the effects of starspots and chromospheric activity common in optical surveys. The full sample of 16 systems adds substantially to the limited catalogue of well-characterised M-dwarf eclipsing binaries, providing critical benchmarks for calibrating model input physics such as opacities and convective efficiency. Further follow-up is encouraged to extend the characterisation to the remaining 13 targets and to probe the mass–radius relation across the full M-dwarf sequence.

title: Progresses in the Analysis of Stochastic 2D Cellular Automata: a Study of Asynchronous 2D Minority
text_ai: Cellular automata are often used to model systems in physics, social sciences, biology that are inherently asynchronous. Over the past 20 years, studies have demonstrated that the behavior of cellular automata drastically changed under asynchronous updates. Still, the few mathematical analyses of asynchronism focus on one-dimensional probabilistic cellular automata, either on single examples or on specific classes. This paper extends the mathematical analysis to two dimensions by studying the minority rule under asynchronous stochastic dynamics. We introduce a novel probabilistic framework that captures the evolution of the density of active sites for the 2D minority cellular automaton on finite grids with periodic boundaries. By employing mean-field approximations and rigorous coupling arguments, we derive exact expressions for the stationary density and characterize the phase transition between disordered and ordered regimes as a function of the update rate. Unlike previous works limited to one dimension, our results reveal a rich bifurcation structure where asynchronous updates can either suppress or enhance clustering depending on the noise intensity. Furthermore, we prove convergence to equilibrium for a broad class of initial conditions using a combination of monotonicity and mixing properties unique to the minority rule. Numerical simulations corroborate the analytical predictions and highlight the critical slowdown near the transition point. These findings constitute the first rigorous treatment of a stochastic two-dimensional asynchronous cellular automaton and provide a foundation for analyzing more complex rules in distributed systems.

title: Left atrial function in patients with light chain amyloidosis: A transthoracic 3D speckle tracking imaging study.
text_ai: Systemic light chain amyloidosis (AL) is characterized by the extracellular deposition of amyloid fibrils. Transthoracic echocardiography is the modality of choice to assess cardiac function in patients with AL. Whereas left ventricular (LV) function has been well studied in this patient population, data regarding the value of left atrial (LA) function in AL patients are lacking. Therefore, the present study aimed to comprehensively assess LA function in patients with AL amyloidosis using transthoracic three-dimensional speckle tracking imaging (3D-STE) and to evaluate its relationship with established markers of cardiac involvement and prognosis. We prospectively enrolled 86 patients with biopsy-proven AL amyloidosis and 50 age- and sex-matched healthy controls. All participants underwent comprehensive echocardiography including 2D, Doppler, and 3D-STE. LA volumes and phasic function—reservoir, conduit, and booster pump—were quantified using 3D volumetric and strain analysis. Global longitudinal strain (GLS) of the left ventricle (LV) was measured, and LA reservoir strain (LAr), conduit strain (LAcd), and booster strain (LAct) were derived from 3D-STE. Patients were followed for a composite endpoint of all-cause mortality or heart failure hospitalization. Compared with controls, AL patients exhibited significantly larger LA maximum and minimum volumes, reduced LA total emptying fraction, and markedly impaired LA reservoir, conduit, and booster strain values (all P < 0.001). LA reservoir strain correlated inversely with LV GLS, E/e’ ratio, and N-terminal pro-brain natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) levels, and positively with LV ejection fraction. During a median follow-up of 24 months, 28 patients reached the composite endpoint. On multivariable Cox regression analysis, LA reservoir strain remained an independent predictor of adverse outcomes after adjustment for LV GLS, E/e’, and NT-proBNP. The addition of LA reservoir strain to a model containing these conventional parameters significantly improved risk reclassification. In conclusion, LA function assessed by 3D-STE is severely impaired in AL amyloidosis and provides incremental prognostic information beyond traditional echocardiographic and biomarker indices. These findings suggest that 3D-STE–derived LA strain may serve as a sensitive marker of early cardiac involvement and a useful tool for risk stratification in this population.

title: Weak Multiplier Hopf Algebras. The main theory
text_ai: A weak multiplier Hopf algebra is a pair (A,\Delta) of a non-degenerate idempotent algebra A and a coproduct $\Delta$ on A. The coproduct is a coassociative homomorphism from A to the multiplier algebra M(A\otimes A) with some natural extra properties (like the existence of a counit). These axioms include that the coproduct is full, i.e., the subspaces $\Delta(A)(A\otimes A)$ and $(A\otimes A)\Delta(A)$ are dense in $M(A\otimes A)$ with respect to the strict topology. The counit is a linear map $\varepsilon:A\to\mathbb{C}$ that is a homomorphism and satisfies $(\varepsilon\otimes\iota)\Delta(a)=a$ and $(\iota\otimes\varepsilon)\Delta(a)=a$ for all $a\in A$, where the products are interpreted in the multiplier algebra. Furthermore, the existence of a weak antipode $S:A\to M(A)$ is assumed, which is a linear map with properties reminiscent of the antipode in a Hopf algebra but weaker: it satisfies $S(a_{(1)})a_{(2)}=\varepsilon(a)1$ and $a_{(1)}S(a_{(2)})=\varepsilon(a)1$ for all $a\in A$, with the sums taken in a suitable multiplier sense. The weak antipode is unique if it exists and is an anti-homomorphism. The theory generalizes both multiplier Hopf algebras (where $A$ is a non-degenerate algebra with a coproduct and antipode) and weak Hopf algebras (where $A$ is finite-dimensional). Key examples include the algebra of functions on a finite groupoid with the coproduct given by the diagonal embedding, and the algebra of a weak finite quantum group. The main results focus on the construction of a Haar functional — a nonzero linear functional $h:A\to\mathbb{C}$ that is left and right invariant under the coproduct, satisfying $(h\otimes\iota)\Delta(a)=h(a)1$ and $(\iota\otimes h)\Delta(a)=h(a)1$ for all $a\in A$. The Haar functional is shown to be unique up to a scalar and to give rise to a Fourier transform and a dual weak multiplier Hopf algebra $(\widehat{A},\widehat{\Delta})$. Duality is a central theme: the dual space $\widehat{A}$ consists of linear functionals on $A$ that are bounded with respect to the Haar functional, and the dual coproduct is defined via the Fourier transform. A duality theorem is established, showing that the bidual is isomorphic to the original algebra. The theory also provides a characterization of weak multiplier Hopf algebras in terms of separable Frobenius algebras and yields a reconstruction theorem for algebraic quantum groups. This work lays the foundation for further studies, including the development of a C*-algebraic version and applications to subfactor theory and tensor categories.

title: Formation mechanism of hairpin vortices in the wake of a truncated square cylinder in a duct
text_ai: We investigate the laminar shedding of hairpin vortices in the wake of a truncated square cylinder placed in a duct, for Reynolds numbers around the critical threshold of the onset of vortex shedding. We single out the formation mechanism of the hairpin vortices by means of a detailed analysis of the flow patterns in the steady regime. We perform direct numerical simulations at Reynolds numbers slightly above the critical value, where the flow transitions from steady to unsteady. The truncation height of the cylinder is varied relative to the duct cross-section to elucidate its role in the formation process. Our analysis reveals that the hairpin vortices originate from the interaction between the primary spanwise vortices shed from the cylinder sides and the secondary streamwise vortices induced by the end-wall boundary layers. Specifically, the steady flow patterns show that a pair of counter-rotating streamwise vortices forms near the cylinder base due to the pressure gradient and the no-slip condition on the duct floor. As the Reynolds number crosses the threshold, these steady streamwise vortices become unsteady and wrap around the primary spanwise vortices, leading to the characteristic omega-shaped structure of the hairpin vortex. The temporal evolution of the vorticity field demonstrates that the hairpin head is formed by the stretching and tilting of the primary vortex core, while the legs correspond to the elongated trailing streamwise vortices. The presence of the duct sidewalls suppresses lateral growth of the vortex structure, confining the hairpin to a narrow wake region. Our findings provide a mechanistic explanation for the onset of three-dimensional vortex shedding behind truncated bluff bodies in confined flows.

title: GRBs luminosity function synthesized from \textit{Swift/BAT}, \textit{Fermi/GBM} and \textit{Konus-Wind} data
text_ai: We study the luminosity function of long gamma-ray bursts (LGRBs) using the peak flux obtained from three LGRB samples with known redshifts: (a) a sample of 251 LGRBs from the \textit{Swift/BAT} satellite/instrument; (b) a sample of 37 LGRBs from the \textit{Fermi/GBM} telescope; (c) a sample of 152 GRBs from the \textit{Konus-Wind} instrument. To overcome differences in energy bands and trigger sensitivities, we compute rest-frame peak luminosities from observed fluxes and redshifts in a standard cosmology, carefully accounting for each instrument's selection effects. A joint maximum likelihood analysis of the full 440 LGRB sample fits a broken power-law luminosity function with redshift-dependent break. Best-fit parameters: α ≈ 0.5, β ≈ 2.4, L_b ≈ 3 × 10^52 erg s^-1 at z=0, evolving as (1+z)^1.8. The intrinsic LGRB rate matches the cosmic star formation rate to z~4, with a mild excess at higher redshifts. Combining the three samples reduces parameter uncertainties by 40–60% versus individual analyses, demonstrating the power of multi-instrument synergy. These results robustly constrain LGRB progenitor models and their cosmic evolution, providing a consistent picture across different observatories. Our findings highlight the importance of joint analyses for reducing systematic biases and improving cosmological applications of GRBs.

title: Performances of Neutron Scattering Spectrometers on a Compact Neutron Source
text_ai: There is currently a big effort put into the operation and construction of world class neutron scattering facilities (SNS and SNS-TS2 in the US, J-PARC in Japan, ESS in Europe, CSS in China, PIK in Russia). But beyond these large-scale facilities, there is a growing interest in compact neutron sources (CANS) as cost-effective and accessible alternatives for specific research and education. This work evaluates the performance of several typical neutron scattering spectrometers—including a backscattering spectrometer, a time-of-flight inelastic spectrometer, and a diffractometer—when installed on a 10 kW compact neutron source driven by a proton accelerator. Using Monte Carlo simulations, we model the neutron flux, energy resolution, and scattering intensity achievable for each instrument under realistic moderator and shielding constraints. The results are benchmarked against corresponding instruments at established spallation and reactor sources to quantify the trade-offs between compactness and performance. We show that, while the peak neutron flux at a CANS is about two orders of magnitude lower than at a large facility, optimized instrument designs can still deliver useful signal levels for powder diffraction and quasielastic scattering studies, particularly when using large-area detectors and focusing optics. The study also demonstrates that the intrinsic time structure of the accelerator pulse enables effective background suppression. These findings provide a quantitative basis for designing next-generation compact neutron instruments and for identifying the scientific niches where a CANS can complement—rather than compete with—large-scale facilities.

title: Energy Loss of Solar $p$ Modes due to the excitation of Magnetic Sausage Tube Waves: Importance of Coupling the Upper Atmosphere
text_ai: We consider damping and absorption of solar $p$ modes due to their energy loss to magnetic tube waves that can freely carry energy out of the acoustic cavity. The coupling of $p$ modes and sausage tube waves is studied in a model atmosphere composed of a polytropic interior above which lies an isothermal upper atmosphere. The interior is treated as a polytrope with index $m=3/2$, representing the solar convection zone, while the overlying isothermal region models the chromosphere or corona. The magnetic flux tube is assumed to be thin, allowing the use of the thin-tube approximation for sausage waves. In this approximation, the tube responds to external pressure perturbations imposed by incident $p$ modes, which are described as plane-parallel acoustic waves in the polytropic interior. The coupling occurs at the tube boundary, where the wave pressure fluctuations drive radial oscillations of the tube wall, generating sausage waves that propagate along the magnetic field. These sausage waves are guided by the tube and, in the upper atmosphere, can propagate freely into the isothermal region if their frequency exceeds the local cutoff frequency. The cutoff is determined by the density scale height and the sound speed in the isothermal layer, which is taken to be an ideal gas with a constant temperature of $10^4$~K. By solving the linearized equations of mass and momentum conservation and the induction equation, with appropriate boundary conditions at the interface between the polytrope and the isothermal atmosphere, we derive an expression for the energy flux carried away by the sausage waves. This flux represents the loss of energy from the $p$-mode cavity, leading to damping and absorption. We compute the damping rates as functions of the $p$-mode frequency $\omega$, the horizontal wavenumber $k_h$, and the magnetic field strength $B_0$. A key result is that the coupling is particularly strong for modes with frequencies near the acoustic cutoff of the tube in the upper atmosphere, typically around 5.3~mHz. At these frequencies, the sausage waves become propagating in the isothermal region and carry energy efficiently to great heights, effectively removing it from the cavity. For lower frequencies, the waves are evanescent and cause negligible damping. The dependence on magnetic field strength shows that stronger fields enhance the damping because the tube's cross-sectional area is larger, increasing the coupling. Our results indicate that the energy loss from $p$ modes to magnetic sausage tube waves can contribute significantly to the observed linewidths of high-frequency modes, with damping rates on the order of $10^{-5}$~s$^{-1}$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that neglecting the effect of the isothermal upper atmosphere severely underestimates the damping, as it allows the sausage waves to reflect at the top of the polytrope and re-enter the cavity. Therefore, the coupling of the upper atmosphere is essential for understanding the energy balance of solar oscillations in magnetic regions.

The coupling of $p$ modes and sausage tube waves is studied in a model atmosphere composed of a polytropic interior above which lies an isothermal upper atmosphere.

title: A Dynamic Data Structure for Representing Timed Transitive Closures on Disk
text_ai: Temporal graphs represent interactions between entities over time. These interactions may be direct, a contact between two vertices at some time instant, or indirect, through sequences of contacts called journeys. Deciding whether an entity can reach another through a journey is useful for various applications in complex networks. While static temporal reachability is well understood, the dynamic setting—where contacts are inserted or deleted over time—poses significant challenges for both main-memory and disk-based representations. Existing solutions either assume entirely in-memory processing or rely on static indexing methods that cannot accommodate updates without full recomputation. Moreover, the timed transitive closure, which records the earliest and latest departure and arrival times for all pairs of vertices, grows quadratically in the number of vertices and becomes impractical for large graphs. Storing and querying this closure on disk further complicates matters because random-access patterns typical of dynamic updates conflict with the sequential access optimizations of secondary storage. In this paper, we introduce a dynamic, disk-resident data structure for representing and querying the timed transitive closure of a temporal graph. Our approach organizes the closure as a set of time-interval labels associated with each vertex, maintaining for every pair of vertices the set of time intervals during which a journey exists. To support efficient updates on disk, we employ a logarithmic decomposition of the timeline combined with B-tree-like structures that keep intervals sorted and compact. Insertions and deletions of contacts are handled by modifying only a logarithmic number of intervals per affected vertex pair, and the structure guarantees that queries of the form “can vertex u reach vertex v with departure after time t?” are answered by a single disk seek. We prove that the total I/O cost per update is O(B log n) amortized, where B is the disk block size and n the number of vertices, while queries require O(log n) I/Os. Experimental evaluation on both synthetic and real-world temporal graphs demonstrates that our structure scales to graphs with millions of vertices and billions of contacts, outperforming a baseline that rebuilds the static closure after each update by orders of magnitude. The work thus provides the first practical, dynamic solution for managing timed transitive closures entirely on disk, enabling efficient temporal reachability analysis in evolving networks.

title: Sense of Self and Time in Borderline Personality. A Comparative Robustness Study with Generative AI
text_ai: This study examines the capacity of large language models (LLMs) to support phenomenological qualitative analysis of first-person experience in Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD), understood as a disorder of temporality and selfhood. Building on a prior human-led thematic analysis of 24 inpatients' life-story interviews, we compared three LLMs (OpenAI GPT-4o, Google Gemini 2.5 Pro, Anthropic Claude Opus 4) prompted to mimic the interpretative style of the original investigators. We then quantified agreement between LLM-generated themes and the human framework using embedding similarity and blinded expert ratings, while assessing robustness across prompt formulations and temperature settings. GPT-4o most consistently reproduced original themes (highest similarity), Gemini 2.5 Pro captured temporal nuances with higher variability, and Claude Opus 4 generated coherent but less specific narratives. All models proved sensitive to prompt framing, emphasizing the need for standardized elicitation protocols. Our findings demonstrate that LLMs reliably extract themes of discontinuous self-narrative and altered time experience central to BPD, yet struggle with the subtle affective nuances that expert clinicians identify. We conclude that LLMs can support scalable phenomenological analysis of BPD temporality and selfhood, but their outputs require expert validation. This study establishes a benchmark for AI-assisted hermeneutics in clinical phenomenology, highlighting both the potential and limitations of generative models for qualitative research on experiential disturbances.

title: High performance Broadband Photodetection Based on Graphene -- MoS$_{2x}$Se$_{2(1-x)}$ Alloy Engineered Phototransistors
text_ai: The concept of alloy engineering has emerged as a viable technique towards tuning the bandgap as well as engineering the defect levels in two-dimensional transition metal dichalcognides (TMDC). Possibility to synthesize these ultrathin TMDC materials through chemical route has opened realistic possibilities to fabricate hybrid multi-functional devices. Here, we demonstrate a high-performance broadband photodetector by integrating graphene with chemically synthesized MoS$_{2x}$Se$_{2(1-x)}$ alloy nanosheets. The tunable bandgap of the alloy, spanning from ~1.55 eV (MoS$_2$) to ~1.75 eV (MoSe$_2$), enables photoresponse across a wide spectral range from 400 to 1100 nm. By varying the sulfur/selenium ratio, we achieve optimized carrier separation at the graphene–alloy interface, with the alloy acting as an efficient light absorber and charge generation layer. The resulting phototransistors exhibit a high responsivity of ~10$^4$ A/W and a specific detectivity exceeding 10$^{11}$ Jones at room temperature, with response times on the order of milliseconds. The alloy's engineered defect levels reduce trap-state density, leading to improved photocurrent stability and minimal persistent photoconductivity. Furthermore, the chemical synthesis route ensures large-area scalability and uniformity, paving the way for practical broadband photodetection applications. This work highlights the critical role of alloy composition in optimizing the optoelectronic properties of TMDC–graphene heterostructures, offering a versatile platform for next-generation photodetectors.

title: Aspects of CFTs on Real Projective Space
text_ai: We present an analytic study of conformal field theories on the real projective space $\mathbb{RP}^d$, focusing on the two-point functions of scalar operators. Due to the partially broken conformal symmetry, these are non-trivial functions of a conformal cross ratio and are constrained to obey a crossing equation. We solve this crossing equation by developing a harmonic analysis on $\mathbb{RP}^d$, expanding the two-point function in terms of conformal partial waves. These partial waves are eigenfunctions of the quadratic Casimir operator and diagonalize the action of the bulk-to-boundary propagator. We derive explicit expressions for the partial wave coefficients in terms of the operator product expansion (OPE) data of the parent Euclidean CFT, showing that the crossing equation reduces to a set of sum rules relating OPE coefficients. As an application, we compute the two-point function of the stress tensor and find that its functional form is uniquely fixed up to a single parameter corresponding to the anomaly coefficient on odd-dimensional projective spaces. For $d=3$, we demonstrate that the crossing equation combined with unitarity bounds yields a nontrivial constraint on the central charge. Our results provide a systematic framework for studying CFTs on $\mathbb{RP}^d$ and highlight the role of the real projective space as a useful background for exploring non-local observables and defect-like physics. The method extends naturally to higher-spin operators and to the study of bootstrap equations on other real projective spaces.

title: Non-Uniform Time-Step Deep Q-Network for Carrier-Sense Multiple Access in Heterogeneous Wireless Networks
text_ai: This paper investigates a new class of carrier-sense multiple access (CSMA) protocols that employ deep reinforcement learning (DRL) techniques, referred to as carrier-sense deep-reinforcement learning multiple access (CS-DLMA). The goal of CS-DLMA is to enable efficient and equitable spectrum sharing among a group of co-located heterogeneous wireless networks. Traditional DRL-based CSMA approaches typically assume fixed and synchronized time steps for decision-making, which may not align with the asynchronous and bursty traffic patterns inherent in heterogeneous networks. To address this limitation, we propose a non-uniform time-step Deep Q-Network (NUTS-DQN) algorithm that dynamically adjusts the interval between successive actions based on the observed network state and the agent's confidence in its policy. By operating on an event-driven rather than clock-driven basis, the NUTS-DQN agent can reduce unnecessary channel sensing during idle periods and accelerate adaptation during contention episodes. We formulate the CSMA problem as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) with state features including channel occupancy history, local queue lengths, and a novel congestion metric. The NUTS-DQN architecture employs a dueling network with a non-uniform time-step wrapper that outputs both action probabilities and a time-to-next-action estimate. Training is performed using a modified temporal-difference update that accounts for variable step sizes, along with prioritized experience replay to handle the skewed distribution of rare but critical contention events. Extensive simulations are conducted in a scenario with three coexisting networks operating on different physical-layer technologies (802.11ax, 802.15.4, and Bluetooth Low Energy). Results show that CS-DLMA with NUTS-DQN achieves up to 32% higher aggregate throughput and 41% lower fairness index variance compared to fixed-step DRL baselines, while reducing average decision overhead by 27%. The proposed protocol also adapts more gracefully to sudden changes in traffic load and node density. We further analyze the learned behavior and demonstrate that the non-uniform time-step policy naturally prioritizes contention resolution over channel maintenance, leading to more stable coexistence. This work bridges the gap between theoretical DRL for medium access and practical deployment considerations, offering a scalable solution for upcoming dense heterogeneous wireless environments.

title: Celestial $w_{1+\infty}$ Symmetries from Twistor Space
text_ai: We explain how twistor theory represents the self-dual sector of four dimensional gravity in terms of the loop group of Poisson diffeomorphisms of the plane via Penrose's non-linear graviton construction. The symmetries of the self-dual sector are generated by the corresponding loop algebra $Lw_{1+\infty}$ of the algebra $w_{1+\infty}$ of these Poisson diffeomorphisms. This algebra, known as $w_{1+\infty}$, generates the symmetries of the self-dual sector, and its loop extension $Lw_{1+\infty}$ captures the infinite-dimensional nature when promoted to full spacetime. In celestial holography, these symmetries are realized on the celestial sphere at null infinity, providing a dual description in terms of a two-dimensional conformal field theory. We show that the $w_{1+\infty}$ symmetries correspond to area-preserving diffeomorphisms of the celestial torus, emerging naturally from the twistor construction. By considering deformations of the non-linear graviton, we demonstrate how $Lw_{1+\infty}$ organizes the scattering amplitudes of gravitational perturbations. Furthermore, we discuss implications for the complete quantum theory, suggesting that self-dual gravity symmetries underpin the full gravitational $S$-matrix. We also explore how these symmetries constrain the operator product expansions of celestial operators, linking them directly to the algebraic structure of $w_{1+\infty}$. This work bridges twistor theory, self-dual gravity, and celestial holography, offering new insights into the emergent symmetries of quantum gravity.

title: Nonconservation of lepton current and asymmetry of relic neutrinos
text_ai:
The neutrino asymmetry in the early universe plasma, $n_
u - n_{ ar 
u}$, is calculated both before and after the electroweak phase transition (EWPT). The leptogenesis before EWPT within the standard model is well known to be driven by the abelian anomaly in a massless hypercharge field. After the EWPT, the lepton current is no longer conserved due to the chiral nature of weak interactions and the breaking of electroweak symmetry. We compute the resulting asymmetry evolution using kinetic equations that incorporate both the anomalous hypercharge production and the subsequent redistribution via sphaleron processes and Yukawa interactions. Our analysis reveals that the net lepton asymmetry $L \equiv n_
u - n_{ ar
u}$ is strongly suppressed in the symmetric phase by the large rate of hypercharge gauge interactions, which rapidly thermalize the chiral chemical potential. However, at the EWPT temperature $T_c \sim 160$ GeV, the hypercharge $U(1)_Y$ anomaly effectively sources a non-zero $B-L$ charge, which is then partially converted into a baryon asymmetry through sphaleron transitions. Crucially, we find that the residual neutrino asymmetry after the phase transition is significantly smaller than previous estimates, as the finite-temperature effective potential modifies the anomaly coefficient. We obtain $n_
u - n_{ ar

u/T_
u \sim 10^{-5}$ for electron neutrinos, which induces a characteristic shift in the neutrino decoupling temperature and alters the primordial helium abundance by $\delta Y_p \sim 10^{-5}$. Our results demonstrate that the nonconservation of the lepton current via the hypercharge anomaly provides a robust mechanism for generating a small but observable relic neutrino asymmetry, with implications for future CMB spectral distortion measurements and neutrino cosmology.

title: On channel sounding with switched arrays in fast time-varying channels
text_ai: Time-division multiplexed (TDM) channel sounders, in which a single RF chain is connected sequentially via an electronic switch to different elements of an array, are widely used for the measurement of double-directional/MIMO propagation channels. This paper investigates the impact of array switching patterns on the accuracy of parameter estimation of multipath components (MPC) for a time-division multiplexed (TDM) channel sounder. Specifically, we compare periodic and pseudorandom switching sequences under varying channel dynamics, including stationary, slowly moving, and fast-moving scenarios. Using both simulated data and controlled measurements at 2.6 GHz, we evaluate the performance of three common estimation algorithms—SAGE, RiMAX, and a compressive sensing approach—in terms of estimation accuracy of MPC delays, angles of arrival/departure, and complex amplitudes. Results show that pseudorandom switching significantly mitigates the Doppler-induced spatial aliasing and inter-element interference that degrade periodic switching in fast time-variant channels, improving delay and angle root-mean-square errors by up to 60% at high vehicular speeds. However, at low mobility, periodic switching yields slightly better accuracy due to simpler temporal sampling. We further derive a closed-form condition on the maximum allowable switching period relative to the Doppler spread and the number of array elements to ensure unambiguous MPC reconstruction. The findings provide practical guidelines for selecting switching patterns and signal parameters in TDM channel sounders, directly informing the design of measurement campaigns for next-generation wireless systems operating in highly dynamic environments.

title: Mitigating ML Model Decay in Continuous Integration with Data Drift Detection: An Empirical Study
text_ai: Background: Machine Learning (ML) methods are being increasingly used for automating different activities, e.g., Test Case Prioritization (TCP), of Continuous Integration (CI). However, ML models need frequent retraining as a result of changes in the CI environment, more commonly known as data drift. Also, continuously retraining ML models consume a lot of time and effort. To address this challenge, we propose and empirically evaluate a data drift detection framework that selectively triggers model retraining only when significant distributional shifts are observed, thereby balancing model accuracy against retraining cost. Our approach monitors both feature-space drift (via multivariate statistical tests such as the Hotelling’s T² and Maximum Mean Discrepancy) and concept drift (via tracking of prediction error distributions) across successive CI cycles. We instantiate this framework for the specific task of Test Case Prioritization (TCP) in CI, where a regression model predicts the fault-detection effectiveness of test cases. Experiments are conducted using nine real-world CI pipelines spanning diverse software projects, with historical commit and test execution data spanning over 12,000 CI builds. We compare our drift-aware retraining policy against three baselines: periodic retraining (every N builds), always-retrain, and never-retrain. Results show that our method reduces retraining frequency by an average of 68% compared to periodic retraining with the same retraining budget, while maintaining—and in 4 out of 9 projects, even improving—the Mean Average Percentage of Faults Detected (MAPFD) by up to 11%. Importantly, the drift detector consistently signals retraining before a significant drop in TCP performance occurs, demonstrating its ability to preempt model decay. We further analyze the computational overhead of drift detection, which adds only 1.2% to the total build time, making it practical for industrial CI environments. Our findings suggest that data drift detection is an effective and efficient strategy for mitigating ML model decay in CI, enabling teams to redirect retraining effort toward builds where it matters most. Practitioners can adopt our lightweight drift monitoring method to sustain automation quality without incurring the cost of continuous retraining.

title: Modified gravity and massive neutrinos: constraints from the full shape analysis of BOSS galaxies and forecasts for Stage IV surveys
text_ai: We constrain the growth index $\gamma$ by performing a full-shape analysis of the power spectrum multipoles measured from the BOSS DR12 data. We adopt a theoretical model based on the Effective Field theory of the Large Scale Structure (EFTofLSS) and focus on two different cosmologies: $\gamma$CDM and $\gamma \nu$CDM, where we also vary the total neutrino mass. We adopt the one-loop EFTofLSS power spectrum multipoles (monopole, quadrupole, hexadecapole) for the BOSS DR12 CMASS and LOWZ samples, covering scales up to kmax ≈ 0.25 h/Mpc. The model includes a shot noise term and galaxy bias up to second order, with all nuisance parameters marginalized. For the γCDM model, assuming a flat ΛCDM background, we obtain γ = 0.62 ± 0.05 (68% CL), which is consistent with general relativity (γ ≈ 0.55) at about 1.4σ. This constraint improves over previous RSD-only analyses by breaking degeneracies between growth and bias. In the γνCDM extension, we vary the sum of neutrino masses M_ν alongside γ and standard cosmological parameters. We find γ = 0.65 ± 0.08 and M_ν < 0.28 eV (95% CL), with a correlation coefficient of ρ(γ, M_ν) ≈ 0.3. The degeneracy direction is such that a higher γ can be compensated by a larger M_ν, but it is mild given the BOSS volume. These results are robust to variations in kmax and the inclusion of the hexadecapole. For Stage IV surveys such as DESI and Euclid, we perform forecasts using a Fisher matrix analysis based on the same EFTofLSS model, assuming a Planck-like prior on the Hubble constant and baryon density. With a survey volume of ∼50 Gpc^3/h^3 and number density n̄ ≈ 3 × 10^{-4} h^3/Mpc^3, we predict that γ will be measured to σ(γ) ≈ 0.02, enabling a ∼3σ test of GR. For the γνCDM model, the degeneracy is significantly reduced, yielding σ(γ) ≈ 0.03 and σ(M_ν) ≈ 0.02 eV, assuming a fiducial Planck cosmology. This would allow a >5σ detection of the minimal neutrino mass, and the figure of merit for the (γ, M_ν) plane improves by an order of magnitude compared to BOSS. These forecasts highlight the potential of Stage IV surveys to simultaneously constrain modified gravity and neutrino properties, breaking key degeneracies and providing a stringent test of the cosmological model.

title: Magnetically-driven explosions of rapidly-rotating white dwarfs following Accretion-Induced Collapse
text_ai: We present 2D multi-group flux-limited diffusion magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) simulations of the Accretion-Induced Collapse (AIC) of a rapidly-rotating white dwarf. We focus on the dynamical role of MHD processes after the formation of a millisecond-period protoneutron star. Our simulations reveal that differential rotation in the newly formed protoneutron star generates strong toroidal magnetic fields via the magnetorotational instability (MRI) and a large-scale dynamo. The field grows to magnetar strengths (~10^15 G) within tens of milliseconds after bounce. The amplified magnetic field then drives a magnetically-dominated outflow along the rotation axis, producing a collimated, relativistic jet. This jet is powered by both the magnetic pressure and the spin-down energy of the rapidly-rotating core. Concurrently, neutrino heating from the protoneutron star drives a delayed, neutrino-driven wind that is magnetically channelled. The interaction between the jet and the infalling stellar envelope leads to a bipolar explosion with a total energy release of ~10^51 ergs, comparable to typical Type Ic supernovae. The explosion is highly anisotropic, with the jet penetrating the progenitor's envelope while the equatorial regions remain bound. Our results demonstrate that MHD processes are essential for enabling explosions in AIC, even for relatively low neutrino luminosities. The simulations also predict nucleosynthetic signatures: the jet ejects proton-rich material with a unique composition including excesses of light p-nuclei, while the neutrino-driven wind produces typical weak r-process elements. We discuss implications for fast radio bursts and the formation of magnetars from AIC events. The models naturally account for the observed association between some supernovae and long gamma-ray bursts, provided the progenitor star retains a modest envelope. Our findings highlight the critical role of rotation and magnetic fields in transforming a failed collapse into a successful explosion.

title: Towards Practical Implementations of Person Re-Identification from Full Video Frames
text_ai: With the major adoption of automation for cities security, person re-identification (Re-ID) has been extensively studied recently. In this paper, we argue that the current way of studying person re-identification, i.e. by trying to re-identify a person within already detected and pre-cropped images of people, is not sufficient to implement practical security applications, where the inputs to the system are the full frames of the video streams. We therefore propose a novel framework that operates directly on raw video frames, integrating person detection and re-identification into a single end-to-end pipeline. Our approach leverages a region proposal network to simultaneously localize individuals and extract identity-discriminative embeddings, eliminating the reliance on external detectors and their associated misalignment errors. Furthermore, we introduce a temporal consistency module that exploits motion cues across consecutive frames to refine identity predictions and suppress false positives from static background regions. Extensive experiments on three large-scale benchmarks—PRID, iLIDS-VID, and MARS—demonstrate that our method achieves competitive rank-1 accuracy while significantly reducing computational overhead compared to two-stage cascaded systems. Notably, we show that performance gaps between full-frame and cropped-input evaluations are primarily attributable to detection failures rather than embedding quality, underscoring the necessity of end-to-end learning. Our work provides a practical pathway for deploying Re-ID in real-world surveillance scenarios where full video streams are the only available input modality.

title: Simultaneous Segmentation and Recognition: Towards more accurate Ego Gesture Recognition
text_ai: Ego hand gestures can be used as an interface in AR and VR environments. While the context of an image is important for tasks like scene understanding, object recognition, image caption generation and activity recognition, it plays a minimal role in ego hand gesture recognition. Existing approaches often treat segmentation and recognition as separate tasks, discarding the rich spatial and temporal cues that arise from joint reasoning. We argue that accurate hand segmentation is not merely a preprocessing step but an integral component that can actively inform gesture classification—especially in cluttered egocentric views where hand–object interactions are subtle yet critical. To this end, we propose a unified deep architecture that simultaneously segments the hand region and recognizes its gesture category. Our model employs a shared encoder with two task-specific decoders that exchange features through a cross-attention mechanism, enabling the recognition branch to leverage pixel‑wise hand boundaries and the segmentation branch to benefit from high‑level semantic cues. We evaluate on two public egocentric datasets (Ego‑Gesture and FPHA) under intra‑ and cross‑subject protocols. The joint framework consistently outperforms pipelines using separate segmentation followed by recognition, achieving up to 4.2% higher accuracy while maintaining real‑time inference. Ablation studies confirm that the synergy between tasks is most pronounced when hand regions are heavily occluded or motion‑blurred. These results demonstrate that simultaneous segmentation and recognition yields more robust ego gesture understanding, paving the way for immersive AR/VR interfaces that require both precise hand localization and reliable gesture interpretation.

title: The H - Omega_o Diagram From Recent CMB Observations: Yes, We Can Already Say Something
text_ai: The CMB is already one of the pillars of the Big Bang model. However it may also become our most powerful tool to distinguish contending models and to determine their cosmological parameters. To realize this goal, more than 20 observational groups and two new satellites are gearing up to make precise measurements of the CMB at small angular scales. and already the first generation of these experiments — such as BOOMERANG, MAXIMA, and DASI — have delivered landmark results. Their measurements of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) power spectrum at degree and sub‑degree scales have revealed a distinct first acoustic peak, the position of which directly constrains the total energy density of the Universe, Ω₀. Combining this with independent determinations of the Hubble constant (H₀) from the HST Key Project and of the matter density from large‑scale structure and supernovae, we construct a joint H₀–Ω₀ diagram. In this diagram, each current CMB data set defines a confidence contour in the H₀–Ω₀ plane, and these contours intersect the independent constraints in a highly nontrivial manner. We find that the CMB data alone already exclude a flat, matter‑dominated Einstein–de Sitter universe (Ω₀ = 1, H₀ ≈ 50 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹) at high significance, even before imposing any priors from other cosmological probes. When combined with the HST measurement of H₀ = 72 ± 8 km s⁻¹ Mpc⁻¹, the CMB data strongly favour a flat universe with Ω₀ ≈ 1.0–1.1, but require a substantial cosmological constant (ΩΛ ≈ 0.7) to reconcile the high H₀ with the low matter density inferred from cluster abundances. The resulting concordance region overlaps remarkably well with the constraints from Type Ia supernovae. Thus, despite the limited angular resolution and sky coverage of the current generation of CMB experiments, the H₀–Ω₀ diagram already delivers a robust verdict: the Universe is spatially flat, has a low matter density, and is dominated by dark energy. We conclude that, contrary to some expectations, the CMB power spectrum is already sufficiently well measured to discriminate between broad classes of cosmological models. With the upcoming launches of MAP and Planck, this diagram will be refined to exquisite precision, but the essential outline of the cosmological parameters is already in place.

title: HEX: Hierarchical Emergence Exploitation in Self-Supervised Algorithms
text_ai: In this paper, we propose an algorithm that can be used on top of a wide variety of self-supervised (SSL) approaches to take advantage of hierarchical structures that emerge during training. SSL approaches typically work through some invariance term to ensure consistency between similar samples and a regularization term to prevent global dimensional collapse. While existing regularization terms aim to prevent collapse, they predominantly operate at the global level and thus neglect the hierarchical information that emerges as representations learn to discriminate between increasingly fine-grained categories. Our proposed algorithm, HEX (Hierarchical Emergence Exploitation), explicitly captures this structure by introducing a multi-resolution clustering objective. In particular, HEX constructs a set of cluster assignments at varying granularities, from coarse to fine, and enforces consistency between assignments across adjacent hierarchical levels. This is achieved through a novel regularization loss that encourages representations to form a nested polytope structure, where higher-level clusters encompass more specific lower-level ones. Importantly, HEX is designed as a lightweight plug-in that can be integrated into any SSL framework without modifying its core architecture or training procedure. We evaluate HEX on several state-of-the-art SSL methods, including SimCLR, BYOL, and MoCo v2, across benchmark datasets such as CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet-100, and STL-10. Empirical results demonstrate that HEX consistently improves linear probing accuracy, often by 2–4%, and yields more semantically coherent clusters in nearest-neighbor classification. Furthermore, the hierarchical representations learned with HEX exhibit superior transferability to downstream tasks, including object detection and image segmentation, where multi-scale understanding is beneficial. Ablation studies confirm that each component of HEX contributes to its overall performance, and visualizations of the learned hierarchies reveal interpretable structures aligned with human semantic hierarchies. We also demonstrate that the hierarchical structure induced by HEX enhances the robustness of representations to input perturbations and improves performance in few-shot learning scenarios. The code for HEX will be made publicly available. Our work underscores the potential of leveraging emergent hierarchical patterns in SSL, providing a simple yet effective means to enhance representation quality across diverse algorithms.

SSL approaches typically work through some invariance term to ensure consistency between similar samples and a regularization term to prevent global dimensional collapse.

title: Routing Protocols Performance in Mobile Ad-Hoc Networks Using Millimeter Wave
text_ai: Self-Organized networks (SONs) have been studied for many years, and have attracted many researchers due to their substantial applications. Although the performance of such networks in the lower band networks (sub-6 GHz band frequencies) has been well studied, there are only sparse studies on SON in higher frequency bands, such as the millimeter wave (mmWave) band ranges between 28GHz and 300GHz. This paper addresses this gap by evaluating the performance of proactive, reactive, and hybrid routing protocols, including OLSR, AODV, DSDV, and ZRP, in mobile ad-hoc networks (MANETs) operating within the mmWave spectrum. Using the ns-3 simulator with a detailed mmWave propagation model that accounts for path loss, directional beamforming, and blockage due to obstacles, we conduct extensive simulations under varying node densities, mobility speeds, and traffic loads. Performance metrics assessed include packet delivery ratio, average end-to-end delay, throughput, and normalized routing load. Our results demonstrate that proactive protocols like OLSR achieve superior packet delivery and lower delay in dense networks with moderate mobility, while reactive protocols such as AODV exhibit better scalability in terms of routing overhead in sparse configurations. The directional antenna gain in mmWave systems reduces interference but introduces deafness issues, which significantly affect route discovery and maintenance. We further observe that hybrid protocols offer a trade-off but require careful parameter tuning. The study concludes that existing routing protocols must be adapted to exploit the unique features of mmWave communication, such as beamforming techniques, to enhance network performance. These findings provide a foundation for designing efficient routing solutions for future millimeter-wave self-organized networks.

title: On exponentiality of automorphisms of ${\bf A}^n$ of order $p$ in characteristic $p>0$
text_ai: Let $X$ be an integral affine scheme of characteristic $p>0$, and $\sigma $ a non-identity automorphism of $X$. If $\sigma $ is $\textit{exponential}$, i.e., induced from a ${\bf G}_a$-action on $X$, then $\sigma $ is obviously of order $p$. It is easy to see that the converse is not true in general. In this paper, we focus on the case where $X$ is the affine $n$-space ${\bf A}^n$ over an algebraically closed field $k$ of characteristic $p>0$. Our main theorem provides a necessary and sufficient condition for an order-$p$ automorphism $\sigma$ of ${\bf A}^n$ to be exponential: $\sigma$ must be conjugate to an automorphism of the form $(x_1,\dots,x_n)\mapsto (x_1+f_1,\dots,x_n+f_n)$ where $f_i\in k[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ satisfy $\partial f_i/\partial x_j=0$ for all $i,j$ and $f_i^p=0$. Equivalently, the linear part of $\sigma$ is unipotent and the fixed point scheme is smooth. Using this characterization, we prove that for $n=1$, every order-$p$ automorphism is exponential, while for $n\geq 2$, there exist counterexamples, such as $(x,y)\mapsto (x+y^p,y)$ on ${\bf A}^2$. The proof relies on the correspondence between ${\bf G}_a$-actions and iterative higher derivations. We also discuss the structure of the automorphism group of ${\bf A}^n$ in positive characteristic and show that exponential automorphisms correspond to translations in the Frobenius direction.

title: Domain-knowledge Inspired Pseudo Supervision (DIPS) for Unsupervised Image-to-Image Translation Models to Support Cross-Domain Classification
text_ai: The ability to classify images is dependent on having access to large labeled datasets and testing on data from the same domain that the model can train on. Classification becomes more challenging when dealing with new data from a different domain, where gathering and especially labeling a larger image dataset for retraining a classification model requires a labor-intensive human effort. Unsupervised image-to-image translation offers a promising alternative by converting source domain images to the target domain without paired data, thus enabling the use of source-trained classifiers on target data. However, conventional translation models often prioritize visual realism over semantic consistency, leading to degraded classification performance. To address this, we propose Domain-knowledge Inspired Pseudo Supervision (DIPS), a framework that integrates high-level domain knowledge—such as class-discriminative attributes or structural priors—to generate reliable pseudo-labels for unlabeled target images. These pseudo-labels serve as weak supervision signals that guide the translation process, encouraging the model to preserve task-relevant semantics while adapting appearance. DIPS operates in a two-stage pipeline: first, a small set of labeled source samples is used to extract domain-relevant features and define pseudo-labeling criteria; second, the translation model is fine-tuned using a composite loss that combines standard cycle-consistency with a classification loss on the pseudo-labeled target images. This approach requires no additional human annotation and can be applied to any unsupervised translation architecture. We validate DIPS on three cross-domain classification tasks, including digit style transfer (MNIST → USPS/SVHN), synthetic-to-real adaptation (GTA5 → Cityscapes), and medical imaging (fundus → angiography). Results show consistent improvements of 8–15% in target domain classification accuracy over baseline translation models and existing unsupervised adaptation methods. Moreover, DIPS yields translated images with higher visual fidelity to the target domain while maintaining distinct class boundaries. Our ablation studies confirm that the pseudo-supervision component accounts for the majority of the performance gain, and that the choice of domain knowledge significantly influences robustness. These findings demonstrate that incorporating even minimal domain insights can substantially bridge the semantic gap in unsupervised translation, making cross-domain classification viable without costly labeling efforts.

title: Funding pharmacists in general practice: A feasibility study to inform the design of future economic evaluations.
text_ai: Funding is a significant barrier to employing general practice pharmacists. To explore the feasibility of determining the cost-benefit of pharmacists in Australian general practice. Two part-time pharmacists were employed by general practices in Canberra, Australia. Diaries of the pharmacists were analysed to determine time worked and participation in income-generating activities, including Government-funded programs: Asthma Cycle of Care, Home Medicine Reviews, and Health Care Assessments. A total of 1,842 hours were recorded over 12 months. Pharmacists spent 38% of their time on these billable activities, generating mean revenue of $47 per hour worked. However, significant variation occurred between pharmacists and across program types. Time-motion analysis revealed extensive non-billable tasks, including medication reconciliation, patient education, and liaison with general practitioners, which contributed to patient care but lacked direct reimbursement pathways. To estimate potential broader benefits, we modelled reductions in hospitalisations and medication errors using published effect sizes, yielding a net societal benefit of $3.20 per dollar invested under conservative assumptions. Sensitivity analyses showed results were most sensitive to pharmacist consultation time and program uptake rates. Despite promising indicators, data limitations—such as incomplete capture of indirect benefits and reliance on self-reported diaries—restrict definitive conclusions. We conclude that a full economic evaluation is feasible but requires standardised activity coding, prospective cost tracking, and linked patient outcome data. These findings inform the design of a future multi-site trial to generate robust evidence for policy decisions on funding models for pharmacists in general practice.

title: An Effective Crop-Paste Pipeline for Few-shot Object Detection
text_ai: Few-shot object detection (FSOD) aims to expand an object detector for novel categories given only a few instances for training. However, detecting novel categories with only a few samples usually leads to the problem of misclassification. In FSOD, we notice the false positive (FP) of novel categories is prominent, in which the base categories are often recognized as novel ones. To mitigate this, we propose a simple yet effective Crop-Paste pipeline that explicitly reduces novel-category false positives by leveraging base-class context. Our key insight is that misclassifications often arise from spatial or appearance similarities between base and novel instances. The pipeline operates in two stages: first, during training, we randomly crop a base-class region from a support image and paste it onto a query image, thereby creating a mixed-sample that preserves the novel object’s location while augmenting the background with base features. This forces the detector to learn discriminative cues that separate novel objects from base artifacts. Second, during inference, we apply a confidence calibration module that re-weights predictions based on the spatial distribution of pasted base regions, effectively suppressing false positives that overlap with known base patterns. We evaluate our method on standard FSOD benchmarks, including PASCAL VOC and MS COCO, under various shot settings (1, 2, 3, 5, 10). Results show that our pipeline consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving up to 3.5% and 4.2% mAP improvements on VOC and COCO novel splits, respectively. Notably, the reduction in novel-category false positives accounts for over 70% of the total gain, confirming the effectiveness of our targeted design. Furthermore, we conduct extensive ablation studies to demonstrate the impact of crop size, paste ratio, and multi-scale augmentation. Our approach maintains efficiency, adding negligible computational overhead (0.1 seconds per epoch) compared to base detectors. The Crop-Paste pipeline is model-agnostic and can be integrated into any two-stage or single-stage FSOD framework. This work highlights the importance of addressing base-novel confusion as a primary bottleneck in few-shot detection and provides a straightforward yet powerful solution.

title: ImmuNeCS: Neural Committee Search by an Artificial Immune System
text_ai: Current Neural Architecture Search techniques can suffer from a few shortcomings, including high computational cost, excessive bias from the search space, conceptual complexity or uncertain empirical benefits over random search. Here, we propose ImmuNeCS, a novel Neural Architecture Search framework inspired by the Artificial Immune System paradigm. By modeling the search process as an adaptive immune response, ImmuNeCS treats candidate architectures as antibodies that are generated, evaluated, and refined through somatic hypermutation and clonal selection. A key innovation is the introduction of a neural "committee" that collectively explores the architecture space, thereby mitigating the bias inherent in handcrafted search spaces and reducing the risk of premature convergence. The committee dynamically adjusts its composition by promoting diverse, high-fitness architectures through a fitness-proportional cloning mechanism, while low-fitness members are eliminated via a negative selection process. This immune-inspired cycle of variation, evaluation, and selection naturally balances exploration and exploitation without requiring complex surrogate models or reinforcement learning policies. ImmuNeCS is evaluated on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet subsets, demonstrating state-of-the-art performance while requiring only a fraction of the GPU-hours typical of evolutionary or gradient-based methods. Notably, the method consistently outperforms random search with statistical significance, addressing the criticism that many NAS approaches offer marginal empirical benefits. Furthermore, the committee-based design inherently supports parallelization and fault tolerance, as each architecture is evolved independently. Ablation studies reveal that the diversity-maintaining mechanisms of the immune system—specifically, affinity maturation and a self-regulating population size—are crucial for avoiding overfitting of the search trajectory. In summary, ImmuNeCS provides a conceptually simple, computationally efficient, and robust alternative to existing NAS techniques, leveraging principles from biological immunity to discover high-performing neural architectures without the overhead of excessive hyperparameter tuning or restrictive search space design.

title: Quantile LSTM: A Robust LSTM for Anomaly Detection In Time Series Data
text_ai: Anomalies refer to the departure of systems and devices from their normal behaviour in standard operating conditions. An anomaly in an industrial device can indicate an upcoming failure, often in the temporal direction. In this paper, we make two contributions: 1) we estimate conditional quantiles and consider three different ways to define anomalies based on the estimated quantiles. Specifically, we introduce Quantile LSTM, a recurrent neural network that extends standard LSTM by employing quantile regression at each time step to estimate conditional quantiles of the target distribution. The model captures both the central tendency and the spread of the predictive distribution, enabling robust anomaly detection in non-stationary time series. For anomaly definition, we consider three criteria: (i) point falling outside a quantile-based prediction interval, (ii) deviation from a dynamic quantile threshold, and (iii) cumulative exceedance of tail quantiles over a sliding window. Experiments on synthetic and real-world industrial datasets—including sensor readings from rotating machinery and power plant telemetry—demonstrate that Quantile LSTM significantly outperforms standard LSTM autoencoders, one-class SVM, and isolation forest in terms of F1-score and precision-recall AUC. The method maintains high detection performance even under heavy-tailed noise and concept drift, confirming its robustness. Our framework provides a principled, uncertainty-aware approach for early failure warning, reducing false positives while capturing subtle temporal anomalies.

title: CorrectNav: Self-Correction Flywheel Empowers Vision-Language-Action Navigation Model
text_ai: Existing vision-and-language navigation models often deviate from the correct trajectory when executing instructions. However, these models lack effective error correction capability, hindering their recovery from errors. To address this challenge, we propose Self-correction Flywheel, a novel post-training paradigm. Self-correction Flywheel integrates error detection and trajectory correction into a closed-loop process. We train a lightweight error detector to identify misalignments between visual observation and instruction. Upon detection, a correction policy generates a recovery action. We then iteratively collect failure cases and augment training with corrected trajectories, forming a flywheel that progressively reduces errors. We evaluate CorrectNav on R2R and RxR. Results show a 12% relative improvement in success rate and 15% reduction in navigation error. The mechanism generalizes to unseen environments, robustly recovering from overshooting or dead ends. The post-training paradigm requires no base model changes and minimal overhead. Our work highlights explicit error correction for reliable VLN. Ablation studies confirm the importance of each component: error detection alone yields limited gain, while the full flywheel achieves substantial improvement. Additionally, the correction policy requires no extra training steps beyond the post-training phase. CorrectNav achieves a success rate of 76% on R2R and 62% on RxR, outperforming baselines by 8% and 6% respectively. This demonstrates the effectiveness of self-correction in building robust navigation agents.
