title: The Use of Telemedicine for Penicillin Allergy Skin Testing.
text_ai: Penicillin skin testing (PST) is increasingly used as a tool to evaluate penicillin allergy in patients with a reported history. The limited availability of allergists, however, may be an impeding factor. We sought to assess the clinical utility of telemedicine to facilitate PST. Penicillin-allergic inpatients receiving systemic antibiotics were prospectively identified between April and August 2017. Eligible patients were randomized to either a telemedicine-facilitated PST pathway (intervention) or standard allergist consultation (control). In the intervention arm, a trained non-allergist clinician performed PST under real-time remote supervision by an allergist via secure video conferencing. The primary outcome was the proportion of patients completing PST within 48 hours of enrollment. Secondary outcomes included time to PST, rate of penicillin allergy delabeling, changes in antibiotic therapy, adverse events, and length of stay. A total of 102 patients were enrolled (51 per arm). Baseline characteristics were similar between groups. PST completion within 48 hours occurred in 45 (88%) intervention patients versus 18 (35%) controls (p<0.001). Median time to PST was 6 hours (interquartile range 4–12) in the telemedicine group compared to 32 hours (IQR 24–54) in the control group (p<0.001). Among patients completing PST, negative results were obtained in 39 (87%) intervention and 16 (89%) control patients, leading to penicillin allergy delabeling in 37 (95%) and 15 (94%), respectively. Antibiotic de-escalation to a β-lactam occurred more frequently in the intervention group (33 [65%] vs. 14 [27%], p<0.001). No adverse events related to PST or telemedicine occurred. Length of stay was significantly shorter in the intervention group (median 5 days vs. 8 days, p=0.02). Telemedicine-facilitated PST is a safe, effective, and timely strategy that overcomes the barrier of limited allergist availability, enabling broader implementation of penicillin allergy evaluation in hospitalized patients.

title: Broad-band spectral study of LMXB black hole candidate 4U 1957+11 with NuSTAR
text_ai: We present here the results of broadband spectral analysis of low-mass X-ray binary and a black hole candidate 4U 1957+11. The source was observed nine times with the Nuclear Spectroscopic Telescope Array (NuSTAR) between 2018 September and 2019 November. During these observations, the spectral state of 4U 1957+11 evolved marginally. We find the source in a soft spectral state, with disk temperature 1.2–1.4 keV and photon index 2.3–2.6. Broad Fe Kα emission lines are detected, signifying relativistic reflection from the inner disk. Applying the relxill model constrains the inner disk radius to the innermost stable circular orbit for a non-spinning black hole (a* < 0.3). The 3–79 keV luminosity is (0.5–1.0)×10^38 erg s^-1 (assuming 10 kpc), corresponding to ~10% Eddington. The reflection fraction is low but varies slightly, indicating a compact corona. NuSTAR’s broad band enables robust separation of disk and coronal emission, and the reflection modeling favors a face-on geometry. The inferred parameters are consistent with a truncated disk at low spin. The marginal spectral evolution is likely due to minor changes in mass accretion rate, supporting the interpretation of 4U 1957+11 as a persistent low-mass black hole binary with low spin and high inclination.

title: Implantable LVAD infections: implications for permanent use of the device
text_ai: BACKGROUND: Infection in implantable left ventricular assist device (LVAD) patients is common and has serious implications regarding permanent use of the LVAD. METHODS: Thirty-three patients had HeartMate LVAD insertion as a bridge to heart transplantation. The mean length of hospital stay was 8 days before LVAD insertion. All patients received perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis with cefazolin. Postoperatively, driveline exit site care followed a standardized protocol. Infections were classified as pump-pocket, driveline, or bloodstream according to established definitions. Patients were followed until transplantation, death, or study end. Mean follow-up was 285 days. RESULTS: Twenty patients (61%) developed at least one infection. Driveline infections occurred in 12, pump-pocket infections in 8, and bloodstream infections in 6, with some overlapping. Median time to first infection was 68 days post-implant. Twelve patients required device exchange due to refractory infection. Among infected patients, 50% died while on support compared with 23% without infection. Notably, 14 of 20 infected patients were not bridged to transplantation because of complications from infection. CONCLUSIONS: LVAD infection dramatically impairs the likelihood of successful bridge to transplantation and raises serious concerns for permanent device use. High infection rates, frequent need for device exchange, and excess mortality suggest that current strategies to prevent and manage infection are inadequate. Without substantial improvements in device design and infection control, the permanent application of implantable LVADs remains problematic.

METHODS: Thirty-three patients had HeartMate LVAD insertion as a bridge to heart transplantation. The mean length of hospital stay was 8 days before LVAD insertion.

title: Modified Lagrangian Formulation of Gear Tooth Crack Analysis using Combined Approach of Variable Mode Decomposition (VMD) and Time Synchronous Averaging (TSA)
text_ai: This paper discusses the possible observation of an integrated gear tooth crack analysis procedure that employs the combined approach of variable mode decomposition (VMD) and time synchronous averaging (TSA) based on the coupled electromechanical gearbox (CEMG) system. This paper also incorporates the modified Lagrangian formulation to model the CEMG system by considering Rayleigh's dissipative potential. The VMD-TSA integration exploits the non-stationary, multi-component nature of vibration signals from gearboxes, where VMD decomposes raw signals into intrinsic mode functions (IMFs) with specific center frequencies, and TSA enhances periodic components associated with gear rotation. This combined approach isolates crack-induced perturbations from background noise and other sources. The modified Lagrangian formulation extends classical gear dynamics by incorporating the electromechanical coupling of the CEMG system, where electrical parameters (e.g., stator currents, magnetic flux) are coupled with mechanical degrees of freedom. Rayleigh's dissipative potential accounts for damping effects from friction, backlash, and material nonlinearity, leading to a set of differential-algebraic equations that govern the system's transient response. A time-varying mesh stiffness model, derived from crack propagation theory, is embedded within these equations to simulate progressive tooth degradation. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the proposed VMD-TSA-Lagrangian framework yields high sensitivity to incipient cracks, with detection thresholds as low as 5% tooth reduction. Compared to conventional methods (e.g., wavelet analysis or empirical mode decomposition), the approach reduces false positives by 18% and improves signal-to-noise ratio by 12 dB under varying load conditions. Experimental validation on a back-to-back gear test rig confirms that the method accurately tracks crack growth stages, from hairline cracks to complete tooth fracture. The abstract concludes that this hybrid methodology offers a robust, physics-informed diagnostic tool for electromechanical drives, enabling early fault identification and predictive maintenance scheduling without requiring extensive baseline data. Future work may extend the Lagrangian representation to planetary gear trains or incorporate machine learning for automated crack classification.

title: Aberrated optical cavities
text_ai: Optical cavities are an enabling technology of modern quantum science: from their essential role in the operation of lasers, to applications as fly-wheels in atomic clocks and interaction-enhancing components in quantum optics experiments, developing a quantitative understanding of the mode-shapes and energies of optical cavities has been crucial for the growth of the field. While ideal cavities—with perfect mirrors and alignment—exhibit well-defined Hermite-Gaussian or Laguerre-Gaussian modes, real-world implementations inevitably suffer from aberrations such as mirror surface defects, misalignment, thermal lensing, and substrate inhomogeneities. These aberrations distort the resonant mode profiles, shift eigenfrequencies, and introduce coupling between otherwise orthogonal transverse modes, degrading performance in sensitive applications. In this work, we develop a comprehensive theoretical and numerical framework to characterize the impact of arbitrary, low-order aberrations on cavity modes. Using a perturbative expansion of the paraxial wave equation with aberrations treated as a weak perturbation to the ideal resonator, we derive analytic expressions for mode frequency shifts and modifications to the transverse field distributions. We validate these results against full-wave simulations and experimental measurements on a Fabry–Pérot cavity with controlled mirror deformations. Our analysis reveals that even small aberrations can induce significant mode mixing, altering the cavity's effective finesse and spectral response. Furthermore, we show how these insights can guide the design of error-tolerant cavities and facilitate aberration compensation strategies, thereby extending the practical utility of optical resonators in quantum optics, metrology, and photonic technologies.

title: Cleavage of the SUN-domain protein Mps3 at its N-terminus regulates centrosome disjunction in budding yeast meiosis.
text_ai: Centrosomes organize microtubules and are essential for spindle formation and chromosome segregation during cell division. Duplicated centrosomes are physically linked, but how this linkage is dissolved remains unclear. Yeast centrosomes are tethered by a nuclear-envelope-attached structure called the half-bridge, whose components have mammalian homologues. Here we identify that the N-terminal cytoplasmic domain of the SUN-domain protein Mps3 is cleaved specifically during meiosis I, and this cleavage is required for timely centrosome disjunction. Using site-directed mutagenesis and biochemical assays, we map the cleavage site to a conserved region near the N-terminus and demonstrate that cleavage is catalyzed by the separase protease. Preventing Mps3 cleavage by mutating the cleavage site or depleting separase activity stabilizes the half-bridge, causing persistent centrosome linkage and severe defects in spindle pole body separation and chromosome segregation. In contrast, expression of an N-terminally truncated Mps3 fragment that mimics the cleavage product rescues these defects. Furthermore, we show that the cleavage product remains associated with the nuclear envelope and is required for subsequent meiosis II divisions. Our results reveal a previously unknown mechanism for dissolving centrosome tethering through regulated proteolysis of a conserved nuclear envelope component. This work establishes Mps3 cleavage as a key step in centrosome disjunction and suggests that analogous SUN-domain protein processing may regulate centrosome separation in higher eukaryotes.

title: Simplified Muscle-Suspension Lower Blepharoplasty by Orbicularis Hitch.
text_ai: The suspension of orbicularis oculi during lower blepharoplasty presents a logical surgical addition for further support of the lid, as well as further improvement to its contour profile. It has traditionally been performed as an extension of the skin-muscle flap procedure, but more recently, and aggressively, as a muscle strap-flap separated from the orbicularis sheet by myotomy. Here we present a simplified technique, the orbicularis hitch, which achieves effective suspension without the need for myotomy or strap-flap dissection. Rather than isolating a muscular strip, the procedure involves a single, centrally placed 5-0 polypropylene suture through the full thickness of the orbicularis muscle immediately inferior to the tarsal plate, which is then fixated to the periosteum of the lateral orbital rim at the level of the lateral canthus. This hitch maneuver recruits a broad section of the muscle sheet, providing a uniform tension vector and restoring the lid-cheek junction with minimal disruption of the normal muscle architecture. In a retrospective review of 87 consecutive patients (174 eyelids) treated over a 24-month period, the orbicularis hitch was combined with a standard transconjunctival fat excision and skin pinch. Outcomes were assessed for lower lid position, lateral canthal angle, and patient satisfaction. At a mean follow-up of 14 months, no cases of ectropion or scleral show were observed. The average improvement in lateral canthal tilt was 3.2 degrees (p < 0.001). One transient case of chemosis and two of mild dry eye were managed conservatively and resolved within 4 weeks. Patient satisfaction, measured by a 5-point Likert scale, averaged 4.7. The orbicularis hitch offers a reproducible, safe, and effective method for lower lid suspension, avoiding the complexities and potential morbidity of myotomy-based techniques. Its simplicity and consistent results make it a valuable addition to the lower blepharoplasty armamentarium.

title: The quaternionic KP hierarchy and conformally immersed 2-tori in the 4-sphere
text_ai: The quaternionic KP hierarchy is the integrable hierarchy of p.d.e obtained by replacing the complex numbers with the quaternions, mutatis mutandis, in the standard construction of the KP hierarchy equations and solutions; it is equivalent to what is often called the Davey-Stewartson II hierarchy. In this paper, we exploit the quaternionic KP hierarchy to construct conformal immersions of 2‑tori into the 4‑sphere. We show that any such torus arises from a finite‑gap solution of the hierarchy, and conversely, every finite‑gap solution yields a conformally immersed torus. The spectral curve of the solution is a hyperelliptic curve of genus one, and the immersion is determined by a pair of holomorphic line bundles on this curve. Our approach generalizes the classical correspondence between finite‑gap solutions of the KP equation and conformal immersions of tori into the 3‑sphere, now framed in the quaternionic setting. We also prove that the Willmore functional on the immersion corresponds to a certain conserved quantity of the hierarchy, establishing a direct link between integrable dynamics and the differential geometry of surfaces in the 4‑sphere. These results provide a new class of examples of Willmore tori and suggest a broader role for quaternionic integrable systems in four‑dimensional submanifold theory.

title: Image-Specific Information Suppression and Implicit Local Alignment for Text-based Person Search
text_ai: Text-based person search (TBPS) is a challenging task that aims to search pedestrian images with the same identity from an image gallery given a query text. In recent years, TBPS has made remarkable progress and state-of-the-art methods achieve superior performance by learning local fine-grained correspondence between images and texts. However, existing local alignment methods often rely on explicit part parsing or cross-modal attention, which may introduce redundant image-specific background information and suffer from misalignment due to the inherent modality gap. To address these issues, this paper proposes a novel framework that integrates Image-Specific Information Suppression (ISIS) and Implicit Local Alignment (ILA). Specifically, ISIS leverages a channel-wise gating mechanism to dynamically suppress irrelevant visual features (e.g., background clutter and non-discriminative attributes) that are specific to each image but irrelevant to identity matching, thereby enhancing the saliency of person-related cues. Meanwhile, ILA performs local alignment in an implicit manner by learning a shared semantic space where image regions and text phrases are softly aligned without requiring explicit region-phrase correspondences. This is achieved through a cross-modal contrastive loss that encourages fine-grained consistency at the token and pixel levels, while a novel distance-weighted sampling strategy ensures that hard negative pairs are effectively utilized during training. Extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets, CUHK-PEDES, ICFG-PEDES, and RSTPReid, demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches. In particular, we achieve rank-1 accuracies of 76.32%, 65.09%, and 60.87%, respectively, representing relative improvements of 2.1%, 1.8%, and 2.5% over previous best results. Ablation studies validate the effectiveness of each component, and qualitative analyses show that our framework successfully suppresses distracting background information while preserving precise local correspondences. The proposed ISIS and ILA modules are lightweight and can be readily integrated into existing TBPS pipelines, paving the way for more robust and interpretable text-based person retrieval.

title: Modelling of initially stressed solids: structure of the energy density in the incompressible limit
text_ai: This study addresses the modelling of elastic bodies, particularly when the relaxed configuration is unknown or non-existent. We adopt the theory of initially stressed materials, incorporating the deformation gradient and stress state of the reference configuration (initial stress tensor) into the response function. We focus on the incompressible limit, where the deformation is isochoric and the hydrostatic pressure becomes an indeterminate Lagrange multiplier. In this context, the strain-energy density must be a function of the initial stress tensor and of the deformation gradient, subject to the incompressibility constraint. We derive the general structure of such an energy density by imposing the principle of material objectivity and the requirement of stress compatibility in the reference state. It is shown that the energy density can be expressed in terms of a reduced set of invariants that couple the initial stress with the deformation, leading to a simplified constitutive law. The implications for the propagation of incremental waves and for the stability of prestressed solids are discussed. Moreover, we examine the restrictions imposed by the Baker–Ericksen inequalities and by the strong ellipticity condition in the presence of initial stress. Our results clarify how the incompressible limit regularises the otherwise underdetermined response and provide a rigorous framework for modelling soft tissues, rubber-like materials, and other nearly incompressible initially stressed solids. The findings are illustrated through representative examples that highlight the role of the initial stress distribution on the effective incremental moduli.

title: UCPhrase: Unsupervised Context-aware Quality Phrase Tagging
text_ai: Identifying and understanding quality phrases from context is a fundamental task in text mining. The most challenging part of this task arguably lies in uncommon, emerging, and domain-specific phrases. The infrequent nature of these phrases significantly hurts the performance of phrase mining methods that rely on sufficient phrase occurrences in the input corpus. To address this challenge, we propose UCPhrase, an unsupervised context-aware method that leverages pre-trained language models and novel phrase scoring functions to tag quality phrases without requiring any labeled data or frequent occurrence patterns. Unlike existing unsupervised approaches that rely on corpus-level statistics or shallow linguistic patterns, UCPhrase captures fine-grained contextual signals from each individual document. Specifically, we design a context-aware phrase scoring mechanism that evaluates the quality of a candidate phrase by considering its semantic coherence within the local context, its informativeness relative to the document, and its distinctiveness across the entire corpus. This is achieved through a lightweight neural architecture that encodes phrase representations using contextualized embeddings from a pre-trained language model, then scores them via a distance-based metric in the embedding space. To identify candidate phrases, we propose a simple yet effective segmentation algorithm that extracts multi-word spans without external lexicons or part-of-speech constraints, enabling detection of rare and emerging terms. We further introduce a self-supervised refinement step that iteratively adjusts phrase boundaries using a local coherence objective. Experimental results on five benchmark datasets spanning news, scientific articles, and social media show that UCPhrase consistently outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised methods, achieving up to 15% relative improvement in F1 score on rare phrase detection. Moreover, UCPhrase demonstrates strong generalization to low-resource domains and exhibits competitive performance with supervised approaches that require extensive human annotations. Our work highlights the promise of leveraging pre-trained language models for unsupervised phrase mining, providing a practical solution for real-world text understanding tasks where labeled data is scarce.

title: A new introduction rule for disjunction
text_ai: We extend Natural Deduction with a third introduction rule for the disjunction, $\vee$-i3, with a conclusion $\Gamma\vdash A\vee B$, but both premises $\Gamma\vdash A$ and $\Gamma\vdash B$. This rule is admissible in Natural Deduction. This extension is interesting in several respects. First, it provides a novel perspective on the normalization of proofs: derivations using ∨-i3 can be reduced to normal forms that are structurally distinct from those obtained using only the standard ∨-introduction rules, thereby offering a richer analysis of normalisation and the subformula property. Second, the rule clarifies the role of the disjunction in natural deduction by showing that the standard elimination rule, ∨-E, remains complete even when the introduction rules are augmented. Third, this extension highlights a deeper symmetry between conjunction and disjunction: just as ∧-I requires both conjuncts as premises, ∨-i3 requires both disjuncts, yet the latter is admissible while the former is not. We also examine the impact of ∨-i3 on the Curry–Howard correspondence, showing that it corresponds to a novel term constructor with interesting computational behaviour, namely a form of parallel composition. Finally, we discuss the philosophical implications for the interpretation of disjunction as a logical constant and suggest applications in the design of proof assistants where redundant rules may offer alternative proof search strategies.

title: Randomized Classifiers vs Human Decision-Makers: Trustworthy AI May Have to Act Randomly and Society Seems to Accept This
text_ai: As \emph{artificial intelligence} (AI) systems are increasingly involved in decisions affecting our lives, ensuring that automated decision-making is fair and ethical has become a top priority. Intuitively, we feel that akin to human decisions, judgments of artificial agents should necessarily be grounded in some moral principles. This intuition, however, may overlook a critical dimension of fairness: the role of unpredictability in preventing systematic bias and ensuring equitable outcomes across heterogeneous populations. In this paper, we challenge the prevailing assumption that deterministic, rule-based reasoning is the sole path to trustworthy AI. We argue that under conditions of irreducible uncertainty—such as when multiple equally qualified candidates compete for a scarce resource—randomized classifiers can provide a form of procedural justice that mirrors the function of lotteries in human societies. Such randomized decisions avoid the pitfalls of perpetuating historical discrimination, which even carefully calibrated deterministic models often inadvertently encode. Moreover, they distribute opportunities more evenly across groups, reducing the risk of reinforcing existing inequalities. We present results from a series of behavioral experiments designed to test public attitudes toward AI systems that occasionally make decisions by explicit randomization. Contrary to the expectation that randomness would be viewed as capricious or unfair, our participants consistently rated randomized AI decisions as more trustworthy than deterministic ones in contexts involving high stakes and ambiguous merit. Importantly, participants recognized randomness as a deliberate design choice to ensure impartiality, not as a sign of incompetence. This acceptance aligns with well-documented human practices: from jury selection to draft lotteries, society routinely endorses random procedures precisely because they are perceived as free from bias. Our findings suggest that the pursuit of trustworthy AI may require embracing stochastic decision-making as a legitimate and socially acceptable tool. By explicating the conditions under which randomization enhances rather than undermines trust, this paper contributes to a more nuanced understanding of fairness in machine learning. We conclude that, far from being a failure of reasoning, purposeful randomness can be a hallmark of principled, ethical AI.

title: An ab-initio study on engineering quantum anomalous Hall effect in compensated antiferromagnet MnBi$_{2}$Te$_{4}$
text_ai: Recently, the quantum anomalous Hall effect (QAHE) has been theoretically proposed in compensated antiferromagnetic systems by using the magnetic topological insulator model [see arXiv:2404.13305 (2024)]. However, the related and systematic study based on a realistic material system is still limited. As the only experimentally realized antiferromagnetic topological insulator, MnBi$_{2}$Te$_{4}$ becomes a vital platform for exploring various topological states. In this work, we perform first-principles density functional theory calculations to demonstrate that by introducing a symmetry-breaking perturbation, such as a vertical electric field or uniaxial strain, the compensated antiferromagnetic phase of MnBi₂Te₄ can host the QAHE. Specifically, we find that the topological phase transition occurs when the band inversion at the Γ point is tuned, leading to the emergence of chiral edge states with a quantized Hall conductance of e²/h. Furthermore, we systematically map out the phase diagram as a function of external electric field and strain, identifying a robust QAHE window with a sizable gap. Our results establish MnBi₂Te₄ as a versatile material for realizing QAHE in compensated antiferromagnets, offering a realistic pathway for experimental observation. This study not only validates the theoretical model proposed recently but also provides concrete guidelines for engineering topological phases in antiferromagnetic systems, paving the way for future experiments.

title: Sketch and Validate for Big Data Clustering
text_ai: In response to the need for learning tools tuned to big data analytics, the present paper introduces a framework for efficient clustering of huge sets of (possibly high-dimensional) data. Building on random sampling and consensus (RANSAC) ideas pursued earlier in a different (computer vision) context for robust regression, a suite of novel dimensionality and set-reduction algorithms is developed. These algorithms operate by first constructing a compact, random sketch of the data—through either random projections or stratified sampling—and then validating candidate cluster assignments via a consensus mechanism that tests the agreement among multiple subsets. The resulting procedures achieve near-linear time complexity in both the number of points and dimensions, making them scalable to terabyte-scale datasets. Extensive experiments on synthetic benchmarks and real-world data from domains such as genomics, astrophysics, and network traffic demonstrate that the proposed methods rival or exceed the clustering accuracy of standard k-means, DBSCAN, and spectral clustering, while reducing runtime by more than an order of magnitude and memory usage by several orders. The framework also naturally handles high-dimensional and noisy data, where conventional clustering often fails. We further derive theoretical bounds on the fidelity of the sketch and on the probability of correct validation under mild data sparsity and separation conditions, providing rigorous justification for the empirical findings.

title: Enhancing the Properties of Plasma Activated Water using an Air Bubble Diffuser
text_ai: In this study, the impact of an air bubbler on the properties of plasma-activated water (PAW) was investigated in different configurations. A pencil plasma jet (PPJ) using a dielectric barrier discharge (DBD) was used to prepare PAW. The air bubble diffuser was positioned either directly beneath the plasma jet or at a lateral offset to assess the effect of bubble injection location on PAW activation efficiency. Plasma treatment was performed for fixed durations (5, 10, and 15 minutes) with a constant air flow rate of 2 L/min through the diffuser, and the resulting PAW was characterized by measuring pH, electrical conductivity (EC), oxidation–reduction potential (ORP), and the concentrations of key reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (RONS), including hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂), nitrite (NO₂⁻), and nitrate (NO₃⁻). Compared to plasma treatment without bubbling, the introduction of air bubbles significantly accelerated the acidification of PAW, reducing pH from 6.8 to below 3.0 within 5 minutes, and increased EC by up to 300% after 15 minutes. ORP values exceeding 600 mV were achieved only in the bubbler-assisted configurations, indicating a stronger oxidative environment. The concentration of H₂O₂ reached 2.5 mM, while NO₂⁻ and NO₃⁻ levels were 0.8 mM and 4.2 mM, respectively, representing enhancements of 40–60% relative to the no-bubbler case. The lateral bubbler placement yielded slightly higher RONS yields than the direct placement, likely due to improved gas–liquid mixing and longer bubble residence time. Optical emission spectroscopy revealed that the air bubbler did not alter the plasma discharge characteristics but enhanced mass transfer of plasma-generated species into the bulk liquid. These findings demonstrate that an air bubble diffuser is a simple, cost-effective means to substantially improve the chemical and physical properties of PAW, rendering it more potent for applications in microbial inactivation and plasma-agriculture. The study provides practical guidance for designing efficient PAW generation systems by optimizing bubbler configuration.

title: Black Silicon with high density and high aspect ratio nanowhiskers
text_ai: Physical properties of black Silicon (b-Si) formed on Si wafers by reactive ion etching in chlorine plasma are reported in an attempt to clarify the formation mechanism and the origin of the observed optical and electrical phenomena which are promising for a variety of applications. The nanowhiskers, with densities exceeding 10⁸ cm⁻² and aspect ratios greater than 50:1, are formed through a self-masking mechanism driven by micromasking from redeposited etch products or native defects. Their sharp tips and high surface area result in broadband antireflection below 2% across the visible and near-infrared spectrum, attributed to a graded refractive index profile. Electrical characterization reveals enhanced photocurrent response and suppressed surface recombination due to optimal passivation, with conductivity dominated by the underlying crystalline substrate. The formation process is sensitive to chlorine plasma parameters—specifically pressure, power, and substrate temperature—which govern the balance between etching and passivation. The resulting b-Si exhibits tunable morphology, enabling tailored optical and electronic properties for applications in photovoltaics, photodetectors, and sensors. These findings elucidate the interplay between plasma conditions and whisker growth, offering a pathway to scalable fabrication of high-performance black silicon.

title: The effects of water temperature on gastric motility and energy intake in healthy young men.
text_ai: Although immediate pre-meal water ingestion has been shown to reduce energy intake in healthy young men, no studies are available regarding potential mechanisms underlying the effect of energy intake in response to different temperatures of pre-meal water ingestion. This study examined the effects of consuming different temperatures of water on gastric motility and energy intake in healthy young men. Twenty healthy young men (age 23.4 ± 2.8 years, BMI 22.1 ± 1.7 kg/m²) participated in a randomized, single-blind, crossover trial. On three separate mornings, after an overnight fast, participants consumed 500 mL of water at 4 °C (cold), 22 °C (room temperature), or 60 °C (warm) in a counterbalanced order. Thirty minutes later, gastric motility was assessed via real-time ultrasonography, measuring antral contraction frequency (ACF) and gastric emptying rate (GER). Participants then consumed a standardized ad libitum pasta meal, and energy intake was quantified. Visual analogue scales were used to record subjective hunger, fullness, and desire to eat throughout the protocol. Cold water ingestion significantly increased ACF (mean ± SD: cold 4.2 ± 0.6 contractions/min) compared with room temperature (3.6 ± 0.5, P = 0.008) and warm water (3.3 ± 0.4, P < 0.001). GER was accelerated for cold water (half‑emptying time 18.2 ± 3.1 min) versus warm water (22.4 ± 4.0 min, P = 0.015). Energy intake was lowest after cold water (785 ± 112 kcal), followed by room temperature (835 ± 124 kcal), and highest after warm water (892 ± 130 kcal); the cold–warm difference was significant (P = 0.002). Moreover, cold water enhanced perceived fullness (P = 0.012) and reduced desire to eat (P = 0.024) before the meal. These findings indicate that pre‑meal ingestion of cold water increases gastric motility and accelerates gastric emptying, which may enhance satiety signals and thereby reduce subsequent energy intake. The temperature of pre‑meal water appears to be a critical modulator of both gastric function and short‑term energy consumption, offering a potential non‑pharmacological strategy for appetite control in healthy young men. Further research should explore the gut‑brain signalling pathways involved.

title: Snow Globe: An Advancing-Front 3D Delaunay Mesh Refinement Algorithm
text_ai: <incorrect proofs; does not consider an important case because of which the proofs are wrong. The paper was withdrawn from submission> One of the objectives of a Delaunay mesh refinement algorithm is to produce meshes with tetrahedral elements having a bounded aspect ratio, which is the ratio between the radius of the circumscribing and inscribing spheres. Snow Globe overcomes this deficiency by introducing a robust advancing-front mechanism that explicitly handles the previously ignored case. The algorithm begins with a coarse boundary triangulation and iteratively refines it by inserting new vertices into the interior. Each insertion step ensures that the new point lies within the circumsphere of its target tetrahedron while maintaining a minimum distance from existing vertices, thereby preventing the formation of slivers. The advancing front propagates through the domain, systematically covering all regions. Theoretical analysis confirms that under mild conditions on the input boundary, the algorithm terminates and produces a mesh where every tetrahedron has an aspect ratio bounded by a constant. Experimental results on a range of three-dimensional geometries demonstrate that Snow Globe consistently achieves high element quality, with significantly fewer poorly shaped tetrahedra compared to conventional Delaunay refinement methods. The algorithm is particularly effective for domains with complex topology and non-uniform size requirements. This work resolves the issues that led to the prior withdrawal and provides a validated, correct solution for three-dimensional Delaunay mesh refinement. The robust theoretical framework and practical performance make Snow Globe a valuable tool for applications requiring high-quality tetrahedral meshes.

title: Impact of macronutrient supplements for children born preterm or small for gestational age on developmental and metabolic outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
text_ai: Nutritional supplements may improve development of infants born small (preterm or small for gestational age [SGA]) but may increase the risk of later metabolic disease. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to assess the effects of macronutrient supplements for infants born small on later development and metabolism. We searched MEDLINE, Embase, CENTRAL, and trial registries from inception to May 2024 with no language restrictions. Eligible studies were randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials that provided additional macronutrients (protein, energy, or both) via fortified human milk, preterm formula, or supplements versus standard feeding or placebo in infants born preterm (<37 weeks’ gestation) or SGA (birth weight <10th percentile). We excluded studies with ongoing postnatal growth restriction or major congenital anomalies. Primary developmental outcomes were cognitive scores (Bayley Scales, Wechsler scales) at ≥12 months; primary metabolic outcomes were body mass index (BMI) z-scores, blood pressure, and fasting insulin or glucose at ≥3 years. Secondary outcomes included motor development, catch‑up growth, and adiposity. Two reviewers extracted data and assessed risk of bias using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool. We synthesized data with random-effects meta-analysis, explored heterogeneity through I² statistics and prespecified subgroup analyses (by gestational age, SGA vs. preterm, nutrient composition, duration of supplementation), and evaluated publication bias via funnel plots and Egger’s test. Certainty of evidence was rated using GRADE. Twenty-nine trials (n=5,512) met inclusion criteria; 24 provided data for meta-analysis. Most trials (21/29) had low or unclear risk of bias; four were at high risk due to attrition or baseline imbalance. Macronutrient supplementation significantly improved cognitive scores in early childhood (mean difference [MD] 2.5 points, 95% CI 0.9 to 4.1; I²=43%; n=1,492 from 8 trials; moderate certainty), but this benefit diminished by school age (MD 0.8 points, 95% CI −1.0 to 2.6; I²=55%; n=906). For metabolic outcomes, supplementation led to a small increase in BMI z-score at ages 5–7 years (MD 0.14, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.26; I²=62%; n=2,103 from 11 trials), but not at later follow-up (≥10 years: MD 0.03, 95% CI −0.12 to 0.18). No significant effects were observed on systolic blood pressure (MD −1.1 mm Hg, 95% CI −3.0 to 0.8) or fasting insulin (standardized MD 0.07, 95% CI −0.05 to 0.19). Subgroup analyses suggested that the cognitive benefit was larger in SGA infants (MD 3.7 points) than in preterm infants (MD 1.6 points; p for interaction=0.04), and that higher protein-to-energy ratio (>3.0 g/100 kcal) was associated with greater BMI increase (MD 0.23 vs. 0.05; p=0.02). Sensitivity analyses excluding high-risk-of-bias trials did not change conclusions. Funnel plots showed no clear asymmetry for cognitive outcomes but possible small-study effects for BMI (Egger’s p=0.07). Overall certainty of evidence was moderate for early cognitive benefit and BMI increase, low for later cognitive and metabolic outcomes, due to imprecision and inconsistency. Macronutrient supplements for infants born preterm or SGA yield modest early cognitive gains but also a small increase in early childhood BMI, without clear effects on other metabolic markers. The trade-off between developmental improvement and potential long-term metabolic risk requires careful consideration, especially for SGA infants who may benefit more cognitively but also show larger BMI increases. Current evidence is limited by short follow-up, variable supplement composition, and incomplete reporting of metabolic outcomes beyond BMI. Future trials should standardize supplement regimens, include long-term metabolic profiling (e.g., adiposity, insulin resistance), and stratify by birth phenotype. Clinicians and policymakers should balance these benefits and harms when designing nutritional interventions for high-risk infants.
prefix: Nutritional supplements may improve development of infants born small (preterm or small for gestational age [SGA]) but may increase the risk of later metabolic disease. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to assess the effects of macronutrient supplements for infants born small on later development and metabolism.

title: Adaptive sports for promoting physical activity in community-dwelling adults with stroke: A feasibility study.
text_ai: Despite proven health benefits of regular participation in physical activities (PA), adults with stroke fail to achieve recommended levels of PA. Sports being an enjoyable activity is more likely to encourage participation. This study aimed to evaluate the feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary efficacy of a 12-week adaptive sports program designed to promote PA in community-dwelling adults with chronic stroke. A single-arm, pre-post feasibility design was employed. Twenty-four participants (mean age 58.7 years, 12 female, time since stroke 3.2 years) were recruited from community support groups. The intervention comprised twice-weekly, 60-minute sessions of modified wheelchair basketball and seated volleyball, led by certified adaptive sports instructors and supervised by a physiotherapist. Feasibility was assessed via recruitment, retention, attendance, and adverse event rates. Acceptability was measured using a post-intervention satisfaction questionnaire. Physical activity was objectively measured using accelerometers (ActiGraph wGT3X-BT) worn for 7 days pre- and post-intervention, and secondary outcomes included walking capacity (6-minute walk test), balance (Berg Balance Scale), and quality of life (Stroke Impact Scale). Results demonstrated high feasibility: 83% recruitment rate (24/29 approached), 92% retention (22/24 completed), and 90% session attendance. No serious adverse events occurred; two minor musculoskeletal complaints resolved with rest. Acceptability was very high (mean satisfaction score 4.7/5). Accelerometer data showed a significant increase in daily moderate-to-vigorous PA from baseline (mean 8.4 min/day) to post-intervention (mean 22.1 min/day, p<0.001). Walking capacity and balance improved significantly (p<0.05), though quality of life changes were not statistically significant. These findings suggest that adaptive sports are a feasible and well-tolerated approach to increasing PA in stroke survivors. A larger randomized controlled trial is warranted to establish efficacy and explore mechanisms.
prefix: Despite proven health benefits of regular participation in physical activities (PA), adults with stroke fail to achieve recommended levels of PA. Sports being an enjoyable activity is more likely to encourage participation.

title: Quantum Hamiltonians with weak random abstract perturbation. II. Localization in the expanded spectrum
text_ai: We consider multi-dimensional Schr\"odinger operators with a weak random perturbation distributed in the cells of some periodic lattice. In every cell the perturbation is described by the translate of a fixed abstract operator depending on a random variable. The random variables, indexed by the lattice, are assumed to be independent and identically distributed according to an absolutely continuous probability density. Using a multiscale analysis adapted to this abstract setting, we prove that the operator exhibits exponential localization in an energy interval contained within the expanded spectrum. Specifically, we show that with probability one, the spectrum is pure point in that interval and eigenfunctions decay exponentially in the spatial variable. Moreover, we establish dynamical localization: the time-averaged transition probabilities decay exponentially. The proof exploits a Wegner estimate derived from the absolute continuity of the density and a Combes–Thomas estimate for the unperturbed operator. The expanded spectrum, introduced in Part I, provides a framework to handle perturbations that are not standard potentials. Our results apply to a wide class of random perturbations, including those with nonlocal or singular single-site operators. Examples include random Schrödinger operators with magnetic fields and random Hamiltonians on periodic graphs.

The random variables, indexed by the lattice, are assumed to be independent and identically distributed according to an absolutely continuous probability density.

title: Energy-Based Flow Matching for Generating 3D Molecular Structure
text_ai: Molecular structure generation is a fundamental problem that involves determining the 3D positions of molecules' constituents. It has crucial biological applications, such as molecular docking, protein folding, and molecular design. Recent advances in generative modeling, such as diffusion models and flow matching, have made great progress on these tasks by modeling molecular conformations as a distribution. We propose Energy-Based Flow Matching (EB-FM), a generative framework that integrates energy-based models with flow matching to directly generate 3D molecular structures. Unlike standard flow matching, which learns a deterministic transport map from noise to data, EB-FM incorporates an energy function—either derived from physical force fields or learned from data—to bias the flow toward low-energy conformations. This is achieved by augmenting the learned vector field with a gradient term from the energy, ensuring generated samples respect both geometric and energetic constraints. The framework supports unconditional generation as well as conditional tasks such as ligand pocket docking. Empirically, EB-FM achieves state-of-the-art performance on the QM9, GEOM-DRUGS, and LBA benchmarks, improving stability (measured by steric clashes and bond length deviations), diversity, and coverage compared to diffusion models and prior flow-based methods. Notably, the energy guidance reduces the number of sampling steps by an order of magnitude while maintaining high-quality structures. Our results demonstrate that explicitly incorporating domain-specific energy priors into flow matching enables more physically plausible and computationally efficient molecular generation, with direct implications for drug discovery and structural biology.

It has crucial biological applications, such as molecular docking, protein folding, and molecular design. Recent advances in generative modeling, such as diffusion models and flow matching, have made great progress on these tasks by modeling molecular conformations as a distribution.

title: Duration of antibody response following vaccination against feline immunodeficiency virus.
text_ai: Objectives Recently, two point-of-care (PoC) feline immunodeficiency virus (FIV) antibody test kits (Witness and Anigen Rapid) were reported as being able to differentiate FIV-vaccinated from FIV-infected cats at a single time point, irrespective of the gap between testing and last vaccination (0-7 years). The present study aimed to characterize the duration and decay kinetics of vaccine-induced antibodies in cats vaccinated with the commercially available inactivated whole-virus FIV vaccine (Fel-O-Vax® FIV, Zoetis). Specifically, we sought to determine whether the diagnostic performance of two PoC antibody test kits (Witness® FIV, Zoetis; Anigen Rapid FIV Ab, BioNote) remained consistent across extended post-vaccination intervals, and to identify any temporal thresholds beyond which false-positive results might diminish or disappear. A cohort of 48 specific-pathogen-free domestic cats (24 males, 24 females; aged 12–16 weeks at enrollment) was vaccinated according to the manufacturer's recommended protocol: three doses at 2–3 week intervals, followed by an annual booster. Serum samples were collected at baseline (pre-vaccination), 2 weeks after the final primary dose, and then at 3, 6, 12, 18, 24, 36, 48, 60, 72, and 84 months post-booster. All samples were tested in duplicate with both PoC kits and with a reference laboratory-based ELISA (IDEXX FIV Antibody Test) and immunoblotting (FIV Western Blot, Zoetis) for confirmation. The reference assays provided quantitative signal-to-cutoff ratios and qualitative positive/negative interpretations; PoC results were recorded as visible band intensities scored on a 0–3 scale by two independent observers blinded to vaccination status. Antibody responses were detected in all vaccinated cats by 2 weeks post-primary series and persisted in 100% of animals up to 12 months post-booster, as measured by both reference assays and PoC kits. Thereafter, a gradual but heterogeneous decline was observed. By 24 months, 44/48 cats (91.7%) remained positive by reference ELISA, while Witness and Anigen Rapid identified 42/48 (87.5%) and 40/48 (83.3%) as positive, respectively. At 48 months, positivity rates dropped to 70.8% (reference), 64.6% (Witness), and 58.3% (Anigen Rapid); by 84 months, only 12.5% of cats remained positive by reference methods, and 10.4% and 8.3% by Witness and Anigen Rapid, respectively. Importantly, all samples that tested positive by PoC kits also tested positive by reference methods at the same time point, yielding 100% specificity for both kits at all time points when compared against a gold standard of FIV infection (field isolates from naturally infected cats, n=30). However, the sensitivity of both PoC kits relative to the reference assays decreased over time, falling below 90% at 24 months and dropping to approximately 85–90% at later intervals. These findings indicate that the duration of vaccine-induced antibody response following recommended Fel-O-Vax® FIV vaccination is highly variable among individuals, with a median duration of approximately 3–4 years before seroreversion begins. Importantly, the two PoC kits demonstrated excellent specificity (>99%) throughout the entire 7-year follow-up period when tested against true FIV infection. However, their sensitivity to detect vaccination history diminished over time, meaning that a negative PoC result does not rule out prior vaccination, especially beyond 2–3 years post-booster. The clinical utility of these kits for differentiating vaccinated from infected cats therefore depends on the time elapsed since last vaccination; a positive result at any interval is highly indicative of vaccination, but a negative result should be interpreted cautiously in cats with an unknown or distant vaccination history. Further studies with larger sample sizes and longer follow-up are warranted to refine seroreversion curves and to evaluate the impact of booster dose timing on diagnostic accuracy.

title: Minimization based formulations of inverse problems and their regularization
text_ai: The conventional way of formulating inverse problems such as identification of a (possibly infinite dimensional) parameter, is via some forward operator, which is the concatenation of the observation operator with the parameter-to-state-map for the underlying model. However, this direct operator inversion typically yields ill-posed problems, due to the compactness or smoothing nature of the forward operator, especially when the parameter space is infinite-dimensional. Regularization becomes essential to obtain stable and meaningful solutions. Minimization-based formulations recast the inverse problem as an optimization task: one seeks a parameter that minimizes a sum of a data fidelity term, measuring the discrepancy between observed and predicted data, and a regularization functional that encodes prior knowledge or promotes desirable properties such as smoothness or sparsity. This variational approach unifies many classical and modern methods: Tikhonov regularization employs a quadratic penalty, while total variation regularization preserves edges, and ℓ1-type penalties enforce sparsity in a suitable basis. The choice of regularization functional and its associated parameter (the regularization strength) critically influences the solution and its stability. Moreover, the formulation naturally extends to infinite-dimensional settings, where functional analysis tools guarantee existence, stability, and convergence of regularized solutions as the noise level tends to zero. Source conditions and regularity of the forward operator play a key role in deriving convergence rates. An alternative perspective interprets the minimization as performing maximum a posteriori estimation under a Bayesian prior, linking deterministic regularization to statistical inversion. This paper reviews the core principles of minimization-based approaches for inverse problems, focusing on the interplay between the forward operator, the regularization functional, and the geometry of the parameter space. We discuss common choices, their theoretical properties, and practical considerations such as efficient numerical optimization strategies, including gradient-based methods and proximal algorithms. We also highlight recent developments like learned regularizers and deep plug-and-play priors that marry data-driven techniques with variational frameworks. The goal is to provide a concise yet comprehensive overview of why minimization formulations are foundational for the regularization of inverse problems.

title: Properties of the $\eta_q$ leading-twist distribution amplitude and its effects to the $B/D^+ \to\eta^{(\prime)}\ell^+ \nu_\ell$ decays
text_ai: The $\eta^{(\prime)}$-mesons in the quark-flavor basis are mixtures of two mesonic states $|\eta_{q}\rangle=|\bar u u+\bar d d\rangle/\sqrt 2$ and $|\eta_{s}\rangle=|\bar s s\rangle$. In the previous work, we have made a detailed study on the $\eta_{s}$ leading-twist distribution amplitude. Therefore, in this paper we extend our investigation to the $\eta_q$ leading-twist distribution amplitude $\phi_{2;\eta_q}(x,\mu)$, employing the same QCD sum rule approach within the framework of the background field method. We compute its first few nontrivial Gegenbauer moments $a_2^{\eta_q}$, $a_4^{\eta_q}$ at the typical scale $\mu=1$ GeV, and observe that they deviate significantly from those of the $\eta_s$ counterpart due to the different quark content. The derived $\phi_{2;\eta_q}$ exhibits a double-humped shape with a distinct suppression at the endpoints. Subsequently, we incorporate this distribution amplitude into the light-cone sum rules to calculate the transition form factors for the $B\to\eta^{(\prime)}$ and $D^+\to\eta^{(\prime)}$ semileptonic decays. Our results indicate that the $\eta_q$ component provides the dominant contribution to $\eta$ and a subleading but non-negligible contribution to $\eta^\prime$ decays. The predicted differential branching fractions $d\mathcal{B}(B\to\eta^{(\prime)}\ell\nu_\ell)/dq^2$ are in good agreement with the available LHCb and BaBar measurements. We also make predictions for the $D^+\to\eta^{(\prime)}\ell\nu_\ell$ channels, which await future experimental verification. A detailed error analysis stemming from the uncertainties of the distribution amplitude moments is presented, confirming the robustness of our approach.
prefix: The $\eta^{(\prime)}$-mesons in the quark-flavor basis are mixtures of two mesonic states $|\eta_{q}\rangle=|\bar u u+\bar d d\rangle/\sqrt 2$ and $|\eta_{s}\rangle=|\bar s s\rangle$. In the previous work, we have made a detailed study on the $\eta_{s}$ leading-twist distribution amplitude.

title: Next generation testing strategy for assessment of genomic damage: A conceptual framework and considerations.
text_ai: For several decades, regulatory testing schemes for genetic damage have been standardized where the tests being utilized examined mutations and structural and numerical chromosomal damage. This has served the genetic toxicity community well when most of the substances being tested were amenable to such assays. However, the evolving landscape of chemical and pharmaceutical development, coupled with a deeper understanding of genomic instability and its myriad manifestations, has exposed the limitations of this traditional paradigm. Conventional assays, such as the Ames test, in vitro micronucleus test, and chromosomal aberration assay, while robust for detecting specific lesions under controlled conditions, are increasingly recognized as insufficient for comprehensive hazard identification across diverse chemical classes and exposure scenarios. They often fail to capture non-coding DNA damage, epimutations, aneuploidies without micronuclei, complex rearrangements, and low-frequency events that may nonetheless drive carcinogenesis or heritable genetic risk. Moreover, their reliance on immortalized rodent cell lines or bacterial systems raises questions about human relevance, metabolic competence, and the ability to recapitulate tissue-specific responses or chronic low-dose exposures typical of real-world human environments. The high cost, labor intensity, and animal welfare concerns associated with in vivo follow-up tests further underscore the need for a transformative shift. This paper presents a conceptual framework for a next-generation testing strategy (NGTS) aimed at assessing genomic damage in a more holistic, human-relevant, and resource-efficient manner. The proposed NGTS integrates emerging technologies and mechanistic insights from toxicogenomics, advanced cellular models, and computational biology. At its core lies a tiered, weight-of-evidence approach that moves beyond the binary positive/negative classification toward a probabilistic characterization of genotoxic potential across multiple dimensions of genomic integrity. The first tier leverages high-content screening platforms, such as multiplexed reporter assays for DNA damage signaling pathways (e.g., γH2AX, 53BP1 foci), coupled with transcriptomic profiling of DNA damage response gene sets. These assays provide broad coverage of genotoxic modes of action (MOAs) – including clastogenicity, aneugenicity, oxidative stress, and topoisomerase inhibition – in metabolically competent human cell lines or induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived models. Dose-response modeling and benchmark concentration approaches replace traditional dose-level comparisons, enabling detection of subtle perturbations at low concentrations. The second tier incorporates genome-wide analysis via next-generation sequencing (NGS) to directly characterize induced mutations, structural variants, and copy number alterations. Error-corrected duplex sequencing and single-molecule real-time sequencing allow interrogation of rare mutational events in nuclear and mitochondrial genomes, while optical genome mapping resolves large structural changes invisible to conventional karyotyping. Integration of epigenetic marks, such as DNA methylation and histone modification patterns, further expands the definition of genomic damage to include transmissible alterations not captured by sequence changes alone. A critical element of this framework is the explicit incorporation of toxicokinetic considerations and in vitro-to-in vivo extrapolation (IVIVE) using physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) models. Traditional genotoxicity tests typically treat cells with fixed concentrations without regard for tissue-specific exposure, metabolism, or clearance. The NGTS proposes that test concentrations be informed by in silico predictions of human internal exposure levels, derived from chemical structure, physicochemical properties, and existing toxicokinetic data. This alignment with real-world exposure scenarios enhances the biological plausibility of positive findings and reduces the rate of false positives arising from supraphysiological doses. Furthermore, the inclusion of organotypic culture systems—such as 3D liver spheroids, gut-on-a-chip, or lung microtissues—enables assessment of tissue-specific metabolism, cell–cell interactions, and chronic exposure regimes that better mimic the in vivo milieu. These systems can be coupled with high-throughput omics profiling to generate mechanistic signatures that distinguish between direct DNA reactivity and indirect genotoxicity through oxidative stress or inflammatory mediators. The conceptual framework also addresses the pressing need for standardization and validation of novel assays to facilitate regulatory acceptance. We propose a pre-validation pathway that uses a curated set of reference chemicals with well-characterized in vivo genotoxicity profiles, covering diverse MOAs, potencies, and chemical classes. Performance metrics such as sensitivity, specificity, transferability, and reproducibility are defined a priori, with statistical frameworks for inter-laboratory comparisons. Importantly, the NGTS advocates for a paradigm shift from method-driven testing to hypothesis-driven assessment. Rather than prescribing a fixed battery of assays, the strategy recommends a flexible, case-by-case approach where the choice of endpoints and models is guided by prior chemical knowledge, use scenario, and intended human exposure. For example, a food additive with negligible systemic absorption might require only Tier 1 screening, whereas a therapeutic with chronic dosing and potential for metabolite accumulation would warrant full Tier 2 profiling with NGS and long-term organotypic cultures. Additional considerations include the integration of in silico models—such as quantitative structure-activity relationships (QSARs), read-across, and mechanistic alerts—as initial filters to prioritize chemicals for experimental testing. Machine learning algorithms trained on large-scale toxicogenomics datasets can provide probabilistic genotoxicity scores with confidence intervals, reducing animal use and experimental burden. However, the framework acknowledges that computational models require rigorous validation against human-relevant endpoints and should not be used in isolation for risk characterization until their predictive accuracy reaches parity with experimental data. Ethical considerations are embedded throughout: the NGTS explicitly aims to replace, reduce, and refine animal testing by relying on human cell-based assays and computational methods wherever feasible. This aligns with the 3Rs principles and facilitates adoption in regulatory jurisdictions with growing emphasis on non-animal alternatives. A key challenge lies in the interpretation and communication of complex multi-dimensional data. Traditional binary classifications are simple but may miss nuanced patterns of genomic damage that have different implications for human risk. The NGTS proposes a hazard classification system based on integrated evidence streams, using a modified version of the genotoxicity MOA framework recommended by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and the International Conference on Harmonisation (ICH). Each line of evidence—from transcriptomic signatures to NGS mutational spectra—is assigned a confidence level, and a weight-of-evidence algorithm calculates the overall likelihood of genotoxicity under human-relevant exposure. This probabilistic output conveys both the nature (e.g., aneugenic vs. clastogenic) and the potency, facilitating quantitative risk assessment rather than merely hazard identification. Visual analytics, such as heatmaps and integrated network diagrams, are employed to present findings to regulators in an intuitive manner. Finally, the paper outlines specific recommendations for implementation in regulatory contexts. These include pilot programs with select chemical inventories (e.g., pesticide actives, cosmetic ingredients) to generate proof-of-concept data; establishment of an open-access database for NGTS results with raw omics data to enable cross-study comparisons; and development of international guidelines under the auspices of the OECD Test Guidelines Programme to harmonize protocols and accelerate acceptance. Practical considerations such as cost, equipment requirements, and technician training are addressed by proposing a modular design where Tier 1 screens are affordable and widely accessible, while Tier 2 NGS analyses are centralized in specialized laboratories. Over time, advances in single-cell sequencing, long-read technologies, and microfluidic culture platforms are expected to further reduce costs and enhance throughput. In conclusion, the next-generation testing strategy for genomic damage assessment represents a necessary evolution from a rigid, endpoint-limited system to a flexible, mechanistically informed, and human-relevant framework. By integrating high-content in vitro assays, genome-wide sequencing, computational toxicology, and advanced culture models, the NGTS promises to improve the sensitivity and specificity of genotoxicity testing while reducing animal use and regulatory burden. The conceptual framework presented herein serves as a foundation for collaborative efforts among academia, industry, and regulators to define and validate the specific methodologies, data interpretation standards, and decision criteria that will operationalize this vision. Widespread adoption will require sustained investment in research, validation studies, and stakeholder dialogue, but the potential benefits – more accurate risk assessment, accelerated product development, and enhanced protection of human health and the environment – justify the considerable effort. The time is ripe to transition from conventional methods to a genomic-scale, evidence-based paradigm that can meet the challenges of the twenty-first century chemical landscape.

title: A brain proteomic investigation of rapamycin effects in the Tsc1+/- mouse model.
text_ai: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) is a rare monogenic disorder characterized by benign tumors in multiple organs as well as a high prevalence of epilepsy, intellectual disability and autism. TSC is caused by inactivating mutations in the TSC1 or TSC2 genes. The resulting hyperactivation of the mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) complex 1 (mTORC1) drives many of the pathological features, making mTOR inhibitors such as rapamycin a promising therapeutic candidate. However, the molecular consequences of chronic mTORC1 hyperactivity in the brain, and the extent to which rapamycin reverses them, remain incompletely understood. Here, we performed an unbiased, quantitative proteomic analysis of cerebral cortex from adult Tsc1+/- mice—a model that recapitulates aspects of the neurological phenotype—and wild-type littermates, both with and without chronic rapamycin treatment (6 mg/kg daily for 4 weeks). Using tandem mass tag (TMT) labeling coupled with liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), we identified and quantified over 6,000 proteins across four experimental groups (WT-vehicle, WT-rapamycin, Tsc1+/−-vehicle, Tsc1+/−-rapamycin; n = 4–5 per group). Differential expression analysis (fold-change > 1.2, adjusted p < 0.05) revealed that Tsc1 heterozygosity altered the abundance of 347 proteins relative to WT-vehicle, with a striking enrichment of proteins involved in synaptic signaling, cytoskeletal organization, and mitochondrial function. Specifically, we observed upregulation of several postsynaptic density components (e.g., Homer1, Dlg4/PSD-95) and downregulation of astrocytic glutamate transporters (Glt1/Slc1a2, Glast/Slc1a3), suggesting a synaptic–glial imbalance. Rapamycin treatment of Tsc1+/- mice normalized 62% of these differentially expressed proteins, including key synaptic and glial markers, but also induced 89 unique changes not seen in WT-rapamycin controls. Notably, proteins involved in autophagy-lysosome pathway (e.g., Sqstm1/p62, Lamp1) were increased in Tsc1+/- cortex and further elevated by rapamycin, indicating incomplete blockade of mTORC1-mediated suppression of this degradative route. Pathway analysis using Gene Ontology and Ingenuity Pathway Analysis confirmed that mTORC1-related signatures (e.g., protein synthesis, ribosome biogenesis) were partially reversed, but also uncovered a sustained perturbation of oxidative phosphorylation and tricarboxylic acid cycle enzymes (e.g., Ndufs1, Sdha, Idh3a). These metabolic alterations were accompanied by reduced ATP levels and increased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species in Tsc1+/- cortical synaptosomes, which rapamycin only modestly ameliorated. Our findings demonstrate that the Tsc1+/- brain proteome is broadly disrupted, with synaptic, glial, and mitochondrial components most vulnerable. Chronic rapamycin treatment provides substantial, but incomplete, proteomic normalization; persistent changes in metabolic and autophagic pathways may contribute to residual neurological deficits observed in TSC models and patients. This dataset serves as a comprehensive resource for identifying novel targets and combinatorial strategies to more fully correct mTORC1-driven brain pathology.
prefix: Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) is a rare monogenic disorder characterized by benign tumors in multiple organs as well as a high prevalence of epilepsy, intellectual disability and autism. TSC is caused by inactivating mutations in the TSC1 or TSC2 genes.

title: Dynamical Majorana Neutrino Masses and Axions II: Inclusion of Axial Background and Anomaly Terms
text_ai: We extend the study of a previous publication \cite{amsot} on Schwinger-Dyson dynamical mass generation for fermions and pseudoscalar fields (axion-like particles (ALP)), in field theories containing Yukawa type interactions between the fermions and ALPs, by incorporating anomaly terms and/or (constant) axial background fields. As in \cite{amsot}, we use Schwinger-Dyson equations in the rainbow approximation to derive coupled gap equations for fermion and ALP self-energies. The anomaly induces an effective ALP mass via topological susceptibility; the axial background acts as a chiral chemical potential. We find that the axial background can generate a dynamical fermion mass even without Yukawa coupling, above a critical threshold. Anomaly terms stabilize the ALP mass. We analyze the phase diagram in coupling, background, and anomaly space. In the strong-coupling regime, we observe a crossover from symmetric to dynamically massive phase; axial background lowers the critical coupling and may induce a first-order transition. We discuss implications for QCD axion: axial background as dark matter condensate or neutrino asymmetry, anomaly from axion-gluon coupling. Our results show natural dynamical mass generation for neutrinos and axions, with consequences for neutrino masses, dark matter, and strong CP problem. We compare with lattice and previous work, finding qualitative agreement. Our analysis extends the previous work \cite{amsot} to more general settings and provides a unified framework for understanding dynamical mass generation in the presence of anomalies and background fields.

title: Challenges in the thermal modeling of highly porous carbon foams
text_ai: The heat pulse experiment is a well-known method for determining thermal diffusivity. However, neither the measurement nor the evaluation methodologies are straightforward for heterogeneous, highly porous materials. In the present paper, we focus on two open-cell carbon foam types, differing in their porosity but having the same size. Both foams exhibit porosities above 85% (specifically 90% and 95%) and complex pore structures. Standard analytical solutions of the heat equation, assuming homogeneity, fail to capture the transient thermal response accurately. We combine experimental heat pulse measurements using laser heating and infrared thermography with finite element simulations that explicitly model the foam’s microstructure. The simulations reveal that conventional data analysis underestimates thermal diffusivity by up to 30% because it neglects radiative transfer across pores and the detailed conductive paths through the struts. We also examine the influence of pore size distribution and strut connectivity on the measured signal. Based on these findings, we propose a modified evaluation methodology that incorporates porosity and radiative contributions, yielding more reliable diffusivity estimates. The results demonstrate that accurate thermal characterization of highly porous carbon foams requires accounting for their intricate morphology. Our framework improves interpretation of heat pulse experiments on similar heterogeneous materials.
prefix: The heat pulse experiment is a well-known method for determining thermal diffusivity. However, neither the measurement nor the evaluation methodologies are straightforward for heterogeneous, highly porous materials. In the present paper, we focus on two open-cell carbon foam types, differing in their porosity but having the same size.

title: Clinical and functional outcome of open primary repair of triangular fibrocartilage complex tears associated with distal radius fractures
text_ai: PURPOSE: We evaluate the clinical and functional outcome of open primary repair of acute TFCC tears in distal radius fracture, when there is gross intraoperative distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ) instability after fixation of the distal radius, in the absence of an ulnar styloid fracture or when the ulnar fracture fragment is too small to be fixed. METHODS: A consecutive series of patients with distal radius fractures treated by open reduction and internal fixation between 2015 and 2020 were retrospectively reviewed. Inclusion criteria were acute TFCC tears confirmed intraoperatively, gross DRUJ instability after stable radial fixation, and either an absent ulnar styloid fracture or a nonfixable styloid fragment (<2 mm or comminuted). Exclusion criteria were prior wrist surgery, concomitant ipsilateral upper extremity fractures, and chronic DRUJ instability. Thirty-two patients (mean age 42 years; 21 males) met criteria. All underwent open primary TFCC repair using transosseous sutures through the ulnar fovea or capsular repair, supplemented by temporary K-wire transfixion of the DRUJ for 4 weeks. Postoperative rehabilitation included progressive range of motion starting at 6 weeks. Outcomes at mean 24-month follow-up included DRUJ stability (ballottement test, stress radiographs), range of motion, grip strength, visual analog scale for pain, QuickDASH score, and modified Mayo Wrist Score. RESULTS: At final follow-up, DRUJ was stable in 30 of 32 patients (94%). Mean flexion-extension arc was 89% of the contralateral side, grip strength 86%. Median QuickDASH score was 8 (IQR 2–18), and mean Mayo score was 82 (range 65–100). Two patients developed transient ulnar nerve paresthesias that resolved. No reoperations for instability or implant removal were required. One patient had mild residual DRUJ instability but declined further intervention. CONCLUSIONS: In distal radius fractures with intraoperative DRUJ instability not attributable to an ulnar styloid fragment, open primary repair of acute TFCC tears reliably restores stability and yields favorable clinical and functional outcomes with low complication rates. This approach should be considered when DRUJ instability persists after adequate radial fixation.
prefix: PURPOSE: We evaluate the clinical and functional outcome of open primary repair of acute TFCC tears in distal radius fracture, when there is gross intraoperative distal radioulnar joint (DRUJ) instability after fixation of the distal radius, in the absence of an ulnar styloid fracture or when the ulnar fracture fragment is too small to be fixed.

title: Immunofluorescence Capillary Imaging Segmentation: Cases Study
text_ai: Nonunion is one of the challenges faced by orthopedics clinics for the technical difficulties and high costs in photographing interosseous capillaries. Segmenting vessels and filling capillaries are critical in understanding the obstacles encountered in capillary growth. In this study, we present a novel segmentation framework for immunofluorescence capillary imaging aimed at addressing these challenges. The framework combines deep learning-based vessel detection with morphological post-processing to accurately delineate capillary networks from high-resolution images. We applied this method to three representative cases of nonunion: atrophic, hypertrophic, and infected nonunions. For each case, we evaluated segmentation performance using Dice similarity coefficient and precision-recall metrics. Results demonstrate that our approach achieves Dice scores above 0.85 across all cases, significantly outperforming traditional thresholding methods. Furthermore, the segmentation enabled quantification of capillary density, branching angles, and vessel tortuosity, revealing distinct microvascular patterns corresponding to each nonunion type. In the atrophic case, sparse and disconnected capillaries were observed, while the hypertrophic case showed excessive but disorganized vessel growth. The infected case exhibited irregular capillary morphology with microvascular leakage. These findings suggest that automated segmentation of immunofluorescence capillary images can provide valuable biomarkers for diagnosing nonunion subtypes and monitoring therapeutic interventions. This case study underscores the potential of advanced image analysis to overcome the technical and cost barriers in orthopedics, facilitating routine clinical assessment of interosseous capillaries.
