title: An Optimal Algorithm for Computing the Spherical Depth of Points in the Plane
text_ai: For a distribution function $F$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$ and a point $q\in \mathbb{R}^d$, the \emph{spherical depth} $\SphD(q;F)$ is defined to be the probability that a point $q$ is contained inside a random closed hyper-ball obtained from a pair of points from $F$. The spherical depth $\SphD(q;S)$ is also defined for an arbitrary data set $S\subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ and $q\in \mathbb{R}^d$. In this paper, we restrict attention to the planar case $d=2$ and present an optimal algorithm for computing the spherical depth $\SphD(q;S)$ of a given query point $q$ with respect to a data set $S$ of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Recall that $\SphD(q;S)$ is defined as the fraction of unordered pairs $\{p_1,p_2\}\subseteq S$ such that $q$ lies inside the closed disk having $\overline{p_1p_2}$ as its diameter. As noted, this containment occurs exactly when the condition $(p_1-q)\cdot(p_2-q)\le 0$ holds, which is equivalent to the angle $\angle p_1 q p_2$ being at least $90^\circ$. This geometric fact allows a reduction to a one-dimensional problem. Translating $q$ to the origin, we radially project each point $p\in S$ onto the unit circle, assigning it an angular coordinate $\theta(p) \in [0,2\pi)$. The depth then becomes the proportion of unordered pairs of angles $(\theta_1,\theta_2)$ whose circular distance modulo $\pi$ is at least $\pi/2$. This is precisely the number of points falling in a moving half-circle window on the circle. Sorting the angles and performing a linear scan gives an $O(n\log n)$-time algorithm using $O(n)$ space. We prove optimality by showing that even deciding whether $\SphD(q;S)\ge 1/2$ requires $\Omega(n\log n)$ comparisons, via a reduction from sorting. Furthermore, we show how to preprocess $S$ in $O(n\log n)$ time so that subsequent queries can be answered in $O(\log n)$ time each. Experiments on both synthetic and real data confirm the theoretical performance and highlight the practical benefits compared to the brute-force $O(n^2)$ method. This work closes the gap between the combinatorial definition of spherical depth and its efficient computation, providing a tool that can be integrated into larger robust statistical procedures.

The spherical depth $\SphD(q;S)$ is also defined for an arbitrary data set $S\subseteq \mathbb{R}^d$ and $q\in \mathbb{R}^d$.

title: Patient Insurance Status Is Associated With Care Received After Transfer Among Pediatric Patients in the Emergency Department.
text_ai: To determine whether frequency of interfacility transfer varied by insurance status among pediatric emergency department (ED) patients. Secondarily, we tested for an association between insurance status and odds of transfer with discharge from the second ED without observation or admission. We used the 2016 New York State ED and Inpatient Databases to identify all patients <18 years. We classified insurance as public, private, or uninsured. Multivariable logistic regression modeled the association between insurance and transfer status, adjusting for age, sex, severity of illness (using All Patient Refined Diagnosis Related Groups), trauma designation, weekend arrival, and hospital characteristics. Among 827,361 pediatric ED visits, 2.3% resulted in interfacility transfer. Overall, 18.5% of transfers were discharged from the receiving ED without observation or admission. Compared with privately insured patients, uninsured pediatric patients had significantly lower odds of transfer (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 0.67, 95% CI 0.61–0.74), whereas publicly insured patients had slightly higher odds (aOR 1.08, 95% CI 1.04–1.12). Among transferred patients, uninsured children had higher odds of discharge without further care (aOR 1.22, 95% CI 1.08–1.38) compared with privately insured peers. Public insurance was not associated with this outcome. These findings suggest that insurance status influences both the decision to transfer and the necessity of the transfer. Uninsured children may face barriers to transfer, yet when transferred, they are more likely to be discharged after minimal evaluation, implying potentially avoidable transfers or differential care intensity. Publicly insured children are transferred more frequently but with comparable downstream resource use. Further research should explore mechanisms underlying these disparities and their impact on patient outcomes and healthcare costs.

title: A Review on the Applications of Transformer-based language models for Nucleotide Sequence Analysis
text_ai: In recent times, Transformer-based language models are making quite an impact in the field of natural language processing. As relevant parallels can be drawn between biological sequences and natural languages, the models used in NLP can be easily extended and adapted for various applications in bioinformatics. This review systematically examines the adaptation and performance of Transformer architectures—including BERT, GPT, and their biological variants (e.g., DNABERT, Nucleotide Transformers)—across diverse nucleotide sequence tasks. We categorize applications into sequence representation learning, functional element annotation, variant effect prediction, and genome assembly. Key findings indicate that self-supervised pretraining on large-scale genomic corpora enables models to capture syntactic and semantic features analogous to natural language, such as k-mer composition and regulatory grammar. However, we also identify critical limitations: computational cost for long-range dependencies, bias from non-uniform training data, and difficulty in integrating structural information like chromatin accessibility. We further discuss emerging strategies to address these challenges, including efficient attention mechanisms, hybrid architectures with convolutional or recurrent components, and transfer learning from cross-species data. By synthesizing over 80 recent studies, this review provides a structured taxonomy of approaches and benchmarks, highlights gaps in current evaluation metrics, and proposes directions for future research, such as multimodal models combining sequence and epigenetic features. Ultimately, we argue that Transformer-based models represent a paradigm shift in nucleotide analysis, yet rigorous validation and domain-specific architectural refinements remain essential for clinical and synthetic biology applications.
prefix: In recent times, Transformer-based language models are making quite an impact in the field of natural language processing. As relevant parallels can be drawn between biological sequences and natural languages, the models used in NLP can be easily extended and adapted for various applications in bioinformatics.

title: Third-order analysis of pseudopotential lattice Boltzmann model for multiphase flow
text_ai: In this work, a third-order Chapman-Enskog analysis of the multiple-relaxation-time (MRT) pseudopotential lattice Boltzmann (LB) model for multiphase flow is performed for the first time. The leading terms on the interaction force, consisting of an anisotropic and an isotropic term, are successfully identified in the third-order macroscopic equation recovered by the lattice Boltzmann equation (LBE), and then new mathematical insights into the pseudopotential LB model are provided. Specifically, it is demonstrated that the third-order contributions introduce corrections to the pressure tensor and the viscous stress tensor, which are crucial for maintaining thermodynamic consistency and reducing spurious currents. By analytically deriving the third-order error terms, the mechanism underlying the coupling between the discrete lattice effects and the interaction force is clarified. Moreover, a systematic comparison between the single-relaxation-time (SRT) and MRT models at third order reveals that the MRT model offers enhanced control over the spurious velocity magnitude through tunable relaxation parameters. The analysis further shows that the isotropic term of the interaction force at third order is responsible for an effective surface tension correction, while the anisotropic term leads to directional deviations that degrade the isotropy of the interface. Based on these insights, an optimized forcing scheme is proposed to minimize third-order errors. Numerical simulations of a static droplet and a two-phase flow in a shear flow confirm the theoretical predictions, demonstrating reduced spurious currents and improved interface isotropy compared to the standard pseudopotential approach. The third-order analysis thus provides a rigorous framework for improving the accuracy and reliability of multiphase LB simulations.

title: MOSEv2: A More Challenging Dataset for Video Object Segmentation in Complex Scenes
text_ai: Video object segmentation (VOS) aims to segment specified target objects throughout a video. Although state-of-the-art methods have achieved impressive performance (e.g., 90+% J&F) on existing benchmarks such as DAVIS and YouTube-VOS, these datasets primarily contain salient, dominant, and isolated objects, limiting their generalization to real-world scenarios. To address these limitations, we introduce MOSEv2, a significantly more challenging dataset designed to push the boundaries of VOS research. Unlike existing benchmarks, MOSEv2 focuses on complex scenes featuring heavy occlusions, small or non-salient objects, rapid camera and object motion, low contrast, and cluttered backgrounds. The dataset comprises 4,478 high-resolution video clips spanning 78 categories, with dense per-frame instance-level annotations and a rigorous test set that eschews easy samples. Each video contains multiple interacting objects, frequent disappearances and reappearances, and ambiguous boundaries, forcing models to rely on long-term temporal reasoning and robust appearance cues rather than simple spatial salience. We benchmark over 20 state-of-the-art VOS methods on MOSEv2 and observe a significant performance drop compared to DAVIS and YouTube-VOS—the top methods achieve only 72.3% J&F, a gap of nearly 20 percentage points. This reveals the dataset's increased difficulty and its capacity to expose model weaknesses, such as poor handling of small objects, failure under severe occlusion, and sensitivity to distractors. Furthermore, we analyze failure modes and propose a new evaluation protocol that separately measures segmentation quality under different challenge factors. Our results demonstrate that MOSEv2 provides a more realistic and demanding testbed for VOS, encouraging the development of methods that generalize beyond simple scenarios. We believe this dataset will catalyze progress toward robust video understanding and serve as a crucial benchmark for future work.

title: Discovering momentum-dependent magnon spin texture in insulating antiferromagnets: Role of the Kitaev interaction
text_ai: We theoretically show that the Kitaev interaction generates a novel class of spin texture in the excitation spectrum of the antiferromagnetic insulator found in the Kitaev-Heisenberg-$\Gamma$ model. In conducting electronic systems, there is a series of vortex type of spin texture along the Fermi surface induced by Rashba and Dresselhaus spin-orbit coupling. but we reveal that in the insulating regime, the Kitaev interaction yields a momentum-dependent spin texture in the magnon Bloch states, distinct from its electronic counterpart. This texture arises from the bond-dependent anisotropic exchange, which breaks inversion symmetry in the spin sector and induces a synthetic spin-orbit field for magnons. Using linear spin-wave theory, we compute the magnon spectrum of the Kitaev-Heisenberg-Γ model on a honeycomb lattice and extract the spin polarization of each magnon band. We find that the spin texture exhibits rich momentum-space vortices and antivortices, with winding numbers that can be controlled by the relative strength of Kitaev, Heisenberg, and off-diagonal Γ couplings. Notably, the Berry curvature associated with the magnon bands acquires nontrivial peaks at the vortex centers, leading to finite thermal Hall conductivity and magnon Nernst effect. Our results demonstrate that insulating antiferromagnets with Kitaev interactions host a new platform for spin-texture physics, where the absence of charge carriers does not preclude the emergence of momentum-space topological features. This work opens pathways for exploring spin transport and topological magnonics in strongly correlated insulators, and suggests that the Kitaev material candidates – such as α-RuCl3 – can exhibit measurable spin-texture signatures in inelastic neutron scattering and optical probes.

title: A DNN Based Post-Filter to Enhance the Quality of Coded Speech in MDCT Domain
text_ai: Frequency domain processing, and in particular the use of Modified Discrete Cosine Transform (MDCT), is the most widespread approach to audio coding. However, at low bitrates, audio quality, especially for speech, degrades drastically due to the lack of available bits to directly code the transform coefficients. To address this issue, we propose a deep neural network (DNN) based post-filter that operates entirely in the MDCT domain, directly enhancing the decoded transform coefficients prior to the inverse transform. The network architecture is designed as a lightweight convolutional autoencoder that learns to suppress coding artifacts while preserving spectral details. Training is performed using a perceptually motivated loss function combining mean squared error with a spectral distance metric, leveraging a large corpus of clean and coded speech pairs. Objective evaluations across multiple bitrates and codecs demonstrate consistent improvements in both PESQ and STOI scores, with subjective listening tests confirming a statistically significant reduction in perceived distortions. The post-filter introduces minimal algorithmic delay and computational overhead, making it suitable for real-time communication systems. Moreover, its domain-agnostic formulation allows integration with existing MDCT-based codecs without requiring modifications to the encoder or bitstream. These results indicate that DNN-based post-filtering in the MDCT domain offers a practical and effective solution for enhancing low-bitrate coded speech quality.

title: Negative-Tension Branes and Tensionless 1/2 Brane in Boundary Conformal Field Theory
text_ai: In the framework of boundary conformal field theory we consider a flat unstable D$p$-brane in the presence of a large constant electromagnetic field. We show that the constant electromagnetic field modifies the boundary conformal field theory by introducing a constant \(B\)-field background, which can be absorbed into a deformation of the boundary conditions. This deformation leads to a family of exact boundary states parameterized by the field strength. In the limit of large field, the effective tension of the brane decreases and can become negative, signaling a transition to a novel phase. Remarkably, at a critical value of the electromagnetic field, the brane tension exactly vanishes, yielding a tensionless 1/2 brane. This state is characterized by a half-integer grading of the boundary condition and corresponds to a topological defect in the worldsheet theory. We compute the boundary entropy and the overlap with closed-string states, confirming the consistency of these exotic branes. Our results provide a concrete realization of negative-tension branes within string theory and suggest a connection to the \({\cal N}=2\) supersymmetric extension of boundary conformal field theory. The tensionless 1/2 brane may serve as a building block for constructing new brane configurations with fractional tension, with potential applications to tachyon condensation and the description of D-brane decay in strong electric fields. Furthermore, we discuss the interpretation of the negative-tension branes as orientifold-like objects and their role in the open-string tachyon potential.

title: Spatiotemporal model of a key step in endocytosis: SNX9 recruitment via phosphoinositides
text_ai: Clathrin mediated endocytosis (CME) is an ubiquitous cellular pathway that regulates central aspects of cell physiology such as nutrient uptake, modulation of signal transduction, synaptic transmission and membrane turn-over. Endocytic vesicle formation depends on the timed production of specific phosphoinositides and their interactions with various endocytic proteins. Here we present a spatiotemporal model describing the recruitment of the BAR domain protein SNX9 to sites of clathrin-coated pit maturation. SNX9 is a key endocytic adaptor that couples phosphoinositide recognition to membrane curvature sensing and actin nucleation, yet the precise timing and mechanisms governing its arrival remain poorly understood. Our model integrates the dynamics of phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2) and phosphatidylinositol 3,4-bisphosphate (PI(3,4)P2) turnover with the cooperative membrane binding and curvature-dependent oligomerization of SNX9. Using partial differential equations solved on a deformable membrane patch, we simulate the spatiotemporal evolution of phosphoinositide gradients and SNX9 density during early CME. We find that local PIP2 depletion, driven by phospholipase C activity and the conversion to PI(3,4)P2 via class I phosphoinositide 3-kinase, creates a dynamic window that enables SNX9 to accumulate specifically at the invaginating pit rim. The model predicts that SNX9 binding is enhanced by membrane curvature, which in turn amplifies local SNX9 clustering and stabilizes the neck of the budding vesicle. Crucially, we show that a delay in PI(3,4)P2 production or a reduction in SNX9's affinity for PIP2 disrupts the spatial coordination, leading to inefficient vesicle scission. Our results provide a quantitative framework for understanding how phosphoinositide metabolism and curvature sensing cooperate to orchestrate protein recruitment with sub-second precision during endocytosis, and offer testable predictions for experimental perturbations of the SNX9-phosphoinositide axis.

title: Nature of excitons bound to inversion domain boundaries: Origin of the 3.45-eV luminescence lines in spontaneously formed GaN nanowires on Si(111)
text_ai: We investigate the 3.45-eV luminescence band of spontaneously formed GaN nanowires on Si(111) by photoluminescence and cathodoluminescence spectroscopy. This band is found to be particularly prominent for samples synthesized at comparatively low temperatures. At the same time, these samples exhibit a peculiar morphology, namely, isolated long nanowires are interspersed within a dense matrix of short ones. By combining spatially resolved cathodoluminescence mapping with temperature-dependent photoluminescence, we identify that the 3.45-eV emission originates from excitons bound to inversion domain boundaries (IDBs). The line shape and energy position are consistent with a bound exciton transition, exhibiting a characteristic thermal quenching behavior with an activation energy of 26 meV. Time-resolved photoluminescence measurements reveal a biexponential decay with a fast component of 0.5 ns attributed to free exciton recombination in the nanowire cores and a slower component of 2.8 ns assigned to the IDB-bound exciton. Transmission electron microscopy confirms the presence of IDBs exclusively in the short nanowires of the dense matrix, while the long nanowires are defect-free. These IDBs act as efficient radiative recombination centers, capturing excitons from the surrounding volume. The dominance of the 3.45-eV band at lower growth temperatures is explained by the increased density of IDBs due to the higher incorporation of oxygen impurities or growth instabilities that promote polarity inversion. Our results unambiguously link the 3.45-eV luminescence to excitons bound at inversion domain boundaries, resolving a long-standing debate about the origin of this ubiquitous emission in GaN nanostructures. This understanding is crucial for engineering the optical properties of GaN nanowires for optoelectronic applications.

title: Interacting Q-balls
text_ai: We study non-topological solitons, so called Q-balls, which carry a non-vanishing Noether charge and arise as lump solutions of self-interacting complex scalar field models. Explicit examples of new axially symmetric non-spinning Q-ball solutions that have not been studied so far are constructed numerically. We then investigate the interactions of these axially symmetric Q-balls and their fundamental (spherically symmetric) counterparts. By employing a relaxation method and explicit time evolution, we simulate head-on collisions and analyze the outcome as a function of the relative phase and impact parameter. For in-phase collisions, we observe the formation of a compound Q-ball with enhanced charge, while out-of-phase collisions lead to repulsion and elastic scattering. At intermediate phases, the Q-balls can merge into an excited, non-spinning bound state that eventually decays by emitting scalar radiation. The charge exchange between interacting Q-balls is shown to be mediated by the coherent superposition of the scalar fields in the overlap region. Our results reveal that the new axially symmetric Q-balls exhibit distinct interaction dynamics compared to their spherically symmetric siblings, opening avenues for studying multi-soliton systems with nontrivial topology. The findings extend the known parameter space of Q-ball interactions and provide a foundation for exploring higher-dimensional generalizations.

title: Modelling Population-Level Hes1 Dynamics: Insights from a Multi-Framework Approach
text_ai: Mathematical models of living cells have been successively refined with advancements in experimental techniques. A main concern is striking a balance between modelling power and the tractability of the associated mathematical analysis. In this work we model the dynamics for the transcription factor Hairy and enhancer of split-1 (Hes1), whose expression oscillates during neural development, and which critically enables stable fate decision in the embryonic brain. We employ a multi-framework strategy that integrates delayed differential equations, stochastic simulations, and agent-based models to capture population-level Hes1 heterogeneity. Our analysis reveals that noise in gene expression and cell-to-cell variability are critical for maintaining oscillatory coherence across a tissue. By comparing frameworks, we identify that deterministic models alone fail to replicate observed desynchronisation, while stochastic models reproduce key features of in vivo data. This work demonstrates that hybrid approaches provide a more complete picture of Hes1 regulation, offering insights into how population-level dynamics ensure robust neural progenitor maintenance. Our findings underscore the necessity of multi-scale modelling in developmental biology.

title: Terminal Brain Damage: Exposing the Graceless Degradation in Deep Neural Networks Under Hardware Fault Attacks
text_ai: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have been shown to tolerate "brain damage": cumulative changes to the network's parameters (e.g., pruning, numerical perturbations) typically result in a graceful degradation of classification accuracy. However, the limits of this natural resilience are not well understood in the presence of small adversarial changes to the DNN parameters' underlying memory representation, such as bit-flips that may be induced by hardware fault attacks. In this paper, we systematically expose this vulnerability by introducing the concept of terminal brain damage: the abrupt, irreversible collapse of DNN accuracy induced by a minimal number of precisely targeted bit-flips. Unlike random or pruned perturbations, which degrade performance slowly, we demonstrate that as few as one bit-flip in a highly sensitive parameter—such as a weight in the first layer or a bias in a critical neuron—can reduce top-1 accuracy on ImageNet from over 76% to below 1%. Through a comprehensive analysis across multiple architectures (ResNet, VGG, Transformer), we identify a small set of "critical bits" whose corruption yields catastrophic failure. We further show that these bits are not uniformly distributed but cluster in layers with high dynamic range or low redundancy. Our findings expose a graceless degradation regime that existing fault tolerance mechanisms—including error-correcting codes and retraining—fail to mitigate. We argue that hardware fault attacks exploiting such terminal brain damage pose a serious security threat, and we propose directions for developing DNNs that are truly robust to memory-level perturbations. This work bridges the gap between algorithmic resilience and hardware security, revealing that the natural grace of DNN degradation is a fragile illusion.

title: Current laboratory performance of starlight suppression systems, and potential pathways to desired Habitable Worlds Observatory exoplanet science capabilities
text_ai: We summarize the current best polychromatic (10 to 20 % bandwidth) contrast performance demonstrated in the laboratory by different starlight suppression approaches and systems designed to directly characterize exoplanets around nearby stars. We present results obtained by internal coronagraph and external starshade experimental testbeds using entrance apertures equivalent to off-axis or on-axis telescopes, either monolithic or segmented. These results reveal that current laboratory contrasts typically reach between 1×10⁻⁹ and 1×10⁻⁸ at inner working angles of 3–4 λ/D over 10–20% bandwidths, depending on the aperture type and coronagraph architecture. For the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO), which targets Earth-like exoplanets at 10⁻¹⁰ contrast over a 20% bandpass with a 6–8 m segmented telescope, a gap of one to two orders of magnitude remains. We discuss key pathways to close this gap, focusing on advances in wavefront sensing and control—particularly for low-order aberrations and mid-spatial-frequency segment errors—and in coronagraph design, such as optimised phase-induced amplitude apodisation or vector vortex masks with broadened chromatic tolerance. For starshades, improving petal-shape manufacturing tolerances and edge-scattering mitigation is critical. Hybrid approaches combining internal coronagraphy with external starshade pre-filtering may also relax individual system requirements. Furthermore, we emphasise the importance of end-to-end modelling with realistic telescope jitter and thermal drift, as well as the need for dedicated testbeds that replicate HWO’s on-axis segmented aperture. Coordinated investment in these areas, alongside risk-reduction demonstrations at the required contrast and bandwidth, is essential to establishing a credible technology foundation for HWO’s exoplanet science mission. The laboratory progress to date provides optimism, but targeted, systematic engineering advances remain necessary to meet the ambitious performance thresholds required for direct imaging of habitable-zone Earth analogs.

title: Testing Sparsity Assumptions in Bayesian Networks
text_ai: Bayesian network (BN) structure discovery algorithms typically either make assumptions about the sparsity of the true underlying network, or are limited by computational constraints to networks with a small number of variables. While these sparsity assumptions can take various forms, frequently the assumptions focus on an upper bound for the maximum in-degree of the underlying graph $\nabla_G$. We develop a formal framework for testing whether a given bound on $\nabla_G$ is consistent with observed data. Our approach leverages properties of the marginal likelihood under a parameterized prior that encodes the sparsity constraint, enabling a hypothesis test that does not require enumerating all networks within the bound. Through theoretical analysis, we characterize the asymptotic behavior of the test and derive conditions under which it is consistent. Extensive simulations across a range of true graph structures and sample sizes demonstrate that our test reliably detects violations of the assumed in-degree bound, while maintaining low false-positive rates when the bound holds. Applied to several real-world datasets, the method reveals that commonly assumed sparsity levels are often too restrictive, suggesting that many empirical Bayesian network analyses may underestimate network complexity. These results underscore the importance of validating sparsity assumptions before relying on structure discovery algorithms that depend on them.

title: Galactic Stellar and Substellar Initial Mass Function
text_ai: We review recent determinations of the present day and initial mass functions in various components of the Galaxy, disk, spheroid, young and globular clusters. As a general feature, the IMF is well described by a power-law form for $m\ga 1 \msol$ and a lognormal form below. We discuss the universality of this shape across different environments, noting that the high-mass power-law index is consistent with the Salpeter slope of $x=1.35$ ($\xi(m)\propto m^{-x}$) for the disk and spheroid, while young clusters and the Galactic center exhibit modest variations that may reflect differing initial conditions or dynamical evolution. The low-mass lognormal component peaks near $0.1\msol$ and extends into the substellar regime down to planetary masses, with a steep decline below $0.03\msol$ that implies a deficit of free-floating planets relative to earlier predictions. We highlight the challenges in determining the IMF in the substellar domain, where completeness limits and binary contamination bias observations, and where theoretical models of opacity-limited fragmentation and disk accretion yield different predictions. For globular clusters, we show that the present-day mass function is significantly depleted in low-mass stars due to dynamical evaporation, but the initial IMF—reconstructed from white dwarf and neutron star populations and from main-sequence turnoff fitting—again agrees with the universal form, though with a possible flattening at the lowest masses. We conclude that the stellar IMF appears to be remarkably invariant across Galactic components and epochs, with only subtle systematic variations that may be linked to metallicity or cloud temperature. The substellar IMF, however, remains less certain and may be more sensitive to local conditions. We discuss implications for star formation theory, the budget of baryonic dark matter, and the interpretation of extragalactic integrated light.

title: Addressing UX Practitioners' Challenges in Designing ML Applications: an Interactive Machine Learning Approach
text_ai: UX practitioners face novel challenges when designing user interfaces for machine learning (ML)-enabled applications. Interactive ML paradigms, like AutoML and interactive machine teaching, lower the barrier for non-expert end users to create, understand, and use ML models, but their application to UX practice is largely unstudied. This paper addresses this gap by investigating how interactive ML can be repurposed to support UX practitioners in their design workflows. We conducted a mixed-methods study with 18 professionals, combining semi-structured interviews and a design probe involving a custom interactive ML tool. Findings reveal three primary challenges: translating user behavior into model specifications, iterating on model behavior without coding, and communicating ML uncertainty to stakeholders. Our interactive ML approach—a visual teachable interface with real-time feedback—enabled practitioners to create and refine ML models autonomously, reducing reliance on data scientists. Evaluation showed significant improvements in perceived control over model outcomes and a 40% reduction in iteration time. We argue that interactive ML, when adapted to UX-specific tasks, can lower barriers to designing ML-infused interfaces. The paper contributes empirical insights into practitioners' struggles, a design framework for interactive ML in UX, and practical guidelines for tool builders seeking to democratize ML within user experience teams.

Interactive ML paradigms, like AutoML and interactive machine teaching, lower the barrier for non-expert end users to create, understand, and use ML models, but their application to UX practice is largely unstudied.

title: Dimensions of Higher Order Factor Analysis Models
text_ai: The factor analysis model is a statistical model where a certain number of hidden random variables, called factors, affect linearly the behaviour of another set of observed random variables, with additional random noise. The main assumption of the model is that the factors and the noise are Gaussian random variables. However, in many applications, the factors themselves exhibit a hierarchical structure, necessitating higher-order factor analysis models. This paper investigates the dimensionality of such models, focusing on parameter count and identifiability. We derive analytical expressions for the effective number of dimensions as a function of the numbers of first- and second-order factors and indicators per factor. We characterize identification conditions and discuss implications for model selection criteria such as AIC and BIC. Additionally, we address rotational indeterminacy in higher-order models and present a new algorithm for estimating loading matrices under identification constraints. Simulation studies across various parameter settings validate the theoretical findings. Our results provide a comprehensive framework for understanding dimensionality in higher-order factor analysis and offer practical guidance for applied researchers in psychometrics.

title: Optimizing Geometric Multigrid Methods with Evolutionary Computation
text_ai: For many linear and nonlinear systems that arise from the discretization of partial differential equations the construction of an efficient multigrid solver is a challenging task. Here we present a novel approach for the optimization of geometric multigrid methods that is based on evolutionary computation, a generic program optimization technique inspired by the principle of natural evolution. Specifically, we employ a genetic algorithm to search the space of multigrid components, including smoothing strategies, restriction and prolongation operators, and cycle types. The fitness function is defined as the asymptotic convergence rate measured via the spectral radius of the multigrid operator. We test the method on a variety of elliptic problems, including Poisson equations with anisotropic coefficients and discontinuous permeability fields. In all cases, the evolved solvers achieve convergence rates comparable to or better than carefully hand-tuned classical multigrid methods, while requiring no expert knowledge. Furthermore, analysis of the evolved configurations reveals that the algorithm tends to prefer certain combinations, such as block smoothers for anisotropic problems, providing interpretable design rules. Extensions to nonlinear systems via Newton–multigrid frameworks are also discussed. These results demonstrate that evolutionary computation can effectively automate the optimization of geometric multigrid solvers, opening the door to self-tuning numerical algorithms.

title: WhisperFuzz: White-Box Fuzzing for Detecting and Locating Timing Vulnerabilities in Processors
text_ai: Timing vulnerabilities in processors have emerged as a potent threat. As processors are the foundation of any computing system, identifying these flaws is imperative. Recently fuzzing techniques, traditionally used for detecting software vulnerabilities, have shown promising results for uncovering vulnerabilities in large-scale hardware designs, such as processors. However, existing hardware fuzzing approaches primarily focus on functional correctness or security logic bugs, often overlooking timing side-channel vulnerabilities that arise from microarchitectural state or speculative execution. To address this gap, we propose WhisperFuzz, a white-box fuzzing framework that systematically explores processor microarchitectures to detect and precisely locate timing vulnerabilities. WhisperFuzz leverages a novel combination of dynamic information flow tracking and cycle-accurate simulation to identify instructions that cause measurable timing variations dependent on secret data. It incorporates a custom coverage metric that captures microarchitectural timing paths, enabling targeted generation of test inputs that expose subtle timing channels. Unlike prior black-box approaches, WhisperFuzz has full visibility into internal microarchitectural events, allowing it to not only detect timing differences but also attribute them to specific hardware components. The coverage metric is defined over state transitions that correlate with timing differences, and the framework is fully automated, requiring no manual annotation of vulnerable patterns. Furthermore, it employs a failure localization technique based on differential timing analysis across multiple runs, pinpointing the exact pipeline stages, cache levels, or buffer structures responsible for the vulnerability. We evaluate WhisperFuzz on two open-source RISC-V processors—Rocket (in-order) and BOOM (out-of-order)—and demonstrate its effectiveness in detecting known timing vulnerabilities such as those exploitable via Spectre variants and Flush+Reload attacks, as well as three previously unknown timing channels. WhisperFuzz achieves high coverage of timing-sensitive microarchitectural states, up to 85% across tested designs, and locates the root-cause microarchitectural structures with an average precision of 92%. These results show that white-box fuzzing with fine-grained microarchitectural feedback is a viable and scalable methodology for pre-silicon detection and localization of timing vulnerabilities in complex processors.

title: RIDCP: Revitalizing Real Image Dehazing via High-Quality Codebook Priors
text_ai: Existing dehazing approaches struggle to process real-world hazy images owing to the lack of paired real data and robust priors. In this work, we present a new paradigm for real image dehazing from the perspectives of synthesizing more realistic hazy data and introducing more robust priors into the network. Specifically, we design a data synthesis strategy that utilizes real-world depth maps and atmospheric light distributions derived from natural scenes, producing hazy images that faithfully mimic the complex scattering and non-uniform haze found in authentic captures. For robust priors, we construct a high-quality codebook via vector quantization on a large corpus of pristine outdoor images, where each code represents a compact yet expressive latent feature spanning textures, edges, and color statistics. The dehazing network adopts an encoder–decoder architecture with a codebook lookup module: the encoder maps a hazy input to latent features, which are then replaced by the nearest code from the codebook to inject clean priors, and the decoder reconstructs the haze-free output. This retrieval process is differentiable and jointly optimized with the synthesis pipeline. A novel contrastive loss further aligns the synthesized haze distribution with real ones. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks (e.g., HazeRD, O-HAZE, and real-world images) show that RIDCP consistently achieves superior perceptual quality and higher PSNR/SSIM than state-of-the-art methods, while reducing artifacts and color shifts. Ablation studies confirm the necessity of both realistic data synthesis and codebook priors. Our paradigm effectively revitalizes real image dehazing by overcoming the twin challenges of scarce paired data and weak priors.
prefix: Existing dehazing approaches struggle to process real-world hazy images owing to the lack of paired real data and robust priors. In this work, we present a new paradigm for real image dehazing from the perspectives of synthesizing more realistic hazy data and introducing more robust priors into the network.

title: One for the Future: measuring the mass transfer rate in the ULX M82 X-2 by using orbital period changes will take millenia
text_ai: Bachetti et al. (2021) have recently claimed to measure the mass transfer rate in the pulsing ULX system M82 X-2 by following the change of its orbital period over 7 yr. However, we demonstrate that the required baseline for a reliable measurement of the secular orbital period derivative is several orders of magnitude longer than the 7 yr span used. The observed period derivative is dominated by short-term variations—likely arising from tidal interactions or stochastic accretion torques—rather than the secular mass transfer. Using population synthesis and detailed binary evolution models, we show that the intrinsic mass transfer rate in M82 X-2 implies an orbital period change on timescales of thousands of years, not decades. Consequently, the claim by Bachetti et al. conflates a short-term fluctuation with a secular trend, and their derived mass transfer rate is not physically meaningful. To accurately constrain the mass transfer rate in this ULX pulsar, monitoring over at least several centuries is required, rendering the method impractical with current observational capabilities. Future X-ray observatories with long-term stability may eventually succeed, but for now the orbital evolution remains an open question.
prefix: Bachetti et al. (2021) have recently claimed to measure the mass transfer rate in the pulsing ULX system M82 X-2 by following the change of its orbital period over 7 yr.

title: Fully On-board Low-Power Localization with Multizone Time-of-Flight Sensors on Nano-UAVs
text_ai: Nano-size unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) hold enormous potential to perform autonomous operations in complex environments, such as inspection, monitoring or data collection. Moreover, their small size allows safe operation close to humans and agile flight. An important part of autonomous flight is localization, which is a computationally intensive task especially on a nano-UAV that usually has strong constraints in sensing, processing and memory. In response to these constraints, we propose a fully on-board localization method that leverages a commercial multizone time-of-flight (ToF) sensor, which provides low-resolution depth maps at very low power consumption—typically under 100 mW. By exploiting the spatial structure of the depth readings across multiple zones, our algorithm extracts a lightweight geometric signature of the environment, such as range discontinuities and relative distances to nearby surfaces. A key innovation is the use of a particle filter that operates directly on this signature, requiring only a few kilobytes of memory and minimal CPU cycles, thus making it feasible for resource-limited nano-UAV platforms. We demonstrate the approach on a custom 65-mm hexacopter equipped with a 4×4 ToF array and a low-power microcontroller. Experimental validation in structured indoor environments—including corridors, rooms, and a cluttered lab—shows that the system achieves mean localization errors below 0.2 m with a processing loop running at 10 Hz, while drawing less than 1.5 W total for sensing and computation. The method is completely self-contained, requires no external infrastructure, and integrates seamlessly with basic flight controllers. These results represent a significant step toward truly autonomous nano-UAVs capable of navigating in GPS-denied spaces with minimal hardware. Our work highlights how careful choice of sensing modality and algorithm design can overcome the severe limitations of nano-scale robots.

title: Higher-order conservation laws for the non-linear Poisson equation via the characteristic cohomology
text_ai: We study higher-order conservation laws of the non-linearizable elliptic Poisson equation $ \frac{{\partial}^2 u}{\partial z \partial \bar{z}} = -f(u) $ as elements of the characteristic cohomology of the associated exterior differential system. The theory of characteristic cohomology determines a normal form for differentiated conservation laws by realizing them as elements of the kernel of a linear differential operator. We explicitly compute this kernel using the method of characteristics on the exterior differential system. This yields the characteristic cohomology groups. The computation relies on the Spencer resolution of the exterior differential system. These results demonstrate the power of characteristic cohomology for nonlinear PDE analysis. The kernel solves a linear PDE on the jet bundle. For general $f$, the space of conservation laws is finite-dimensional, with dimension given by a formula in terms of $f$ and its derivatives. When $f$ is linear or Liouville type, nontrivial higher-order laws exist; otherwise, only zero-order and first-order laws appear. We also show that all higher-order conservation laws can be generated from a finite set. The cohomological approach relates conservation laws to symmetries. We provide explicit examples for $f(u)=e^u$ and $f(u)=u^p$. This classification extends previous results for the linear case.

title: The EXP pair-potential system. I. Fluid phase isotherms, isochores, and quasiuniversality
text_ai: The exponentially repulsive EXP pair potential defines a system of particles in terms of which simple liquids' quasiuniversality may be explained [A. K. Bacher et al., Nat. Commun. 5, 5424 (2014); J. C. Dyre, J. Phys. Condens. Matter 28, 323001 (2016)]. This paper and its companion present a detailed simulation study of the EXP system. We report extensive molecular dynamics simulations of the EXP system across a broad range of densities and temperatures, mapping out its fluid-phase equation of state. Isotherms are accurately described by a simple two-parameter analytic form, while isochores exhibit a striking linear dependence on temperature above the freezing line. The data confirm that the EXP system obeys quasiuniversality: its reduced structure and dynamics closely match those of other simple liquids after appropriate scaling. In particular, we quantify the effective hard-sphere diameter from the structural properties and demonstrate that the EXP system’s virial potential-energy correlation coefficient exceeds the standard Rosenfeld–Tarazona threshold, confirming isomorph theory predictions. The companion paper extends this analysis to the solid phase.

Commun. 5, 5424 (2014); J. C. Dyre, J. Phys. Condens. Matter 28, 323001 (2016)]. This paper and its companion present a detailed simulation study of the EXP system.

title: Intra-abdominal hypertension and the abdominal compartment syndrome
text_ai: The pressure within the abdominal cavity is normally little more than atmospheric pressure. However, even small increases in intra-abdominal pressure can have adverse effects on renal function, cardiac output, hepatic blood flow, respiratory mechanics, splanchnic perfusion and intracranial pressure. and may eventually culminate in the life-threatening condition known as abdominal compartment syndrome. Intra-abdominal hypertension is defined as a sustained or repeatedly elevated intra-abdominal pressure of ≥12 mmHg, while abdominal compartment syndrome represents a further progression to sustained pressures >20 mmHg that is associated with new or worsening organ dysfunction. The pathophysiology is complex, involving direct mechanical compression of organs and vessels as well as systemic inflammatory responses. Common causes include massive fluid resuscitation, abdominal trauma, pancreatitis, intra-abdominal hemorrhage, or ascites. Early recognition is critical because delayed treatment leads to high morbidity and mortality. Diagnosis relies on measuring bladder pressure as a surrogate for intra-abdominal pressure, coupled with clinical signs of organ failure. Management follows a stepwise approach: non-operative measures such as improving abdominal wall compliance, evacuating intraluminal contents, and optimizing fluid balance; then, if refractory, surgical decompression via laparostomy. Failure to promptly relieve pressure can result in irreversible renal, respiratory, cardiovascular, and neurologic compromise. This abstract reviews the epidemiology, pathogenesis, diagnostic criteria, and evidenced-based management strategies for intra-abdominal hypertension and abdominal compartment syndrome, highlighting the importance of routine pressure monitoring in critically ill patients. Understanding these concepts enables clinicians to intervene early and improve patient outcomes in the intensive care unit and surgical settings.

title: Windows over a New Low Energy Axion
text_ai: We outline some general features of possible extensions of the Standard Model that include anomalous U(1) gauge symmetries, a certain number of axions and their mixings with the CP-odd Higgs sector. As previously shown, after the mixing one of the axions becomes a physical pseudoscalar (the axi-Higgs) that can take the role of a modified QCD axion. We then focus on the minimal realization of this framework, featuring a single anomalous U(1) and two axion-like fields, one of which emerges from the Higgs sector. The resulting low-energy effective theory contains a single physical axion—the “low-energy axion”—whose mass and couplings are determined by both the anomaly and the Higgs vacuum expectation values. Remarkably, its mass can be significantly suppressed relative to the standard QCD axion for the same anomaly coefficient, opening a new window for axion searches. We compute the axion-photon coupling and show that it can be enhanced or suppressed depending on the mixing angles, leading to distinct experimental signatures. Phenomenological constraints from astrophysics, laboratory searches, and cosmology are examined. The axion can evade current bounds while remaining detectable in upcoming experiments such as ALPS II, IAXO, and cavity haloscopes. Furthermore, the axi-Higgs component modifies the axion-nucleon coupling, potentially affecting supernova cooling bounds. We also discuss the cosmological abundance, noting that the low-energy axion can be produced via misalignment and topological defects, with a relic density that may differ from the standard scenario. This framework thus provides a viable and testable realization of a light axion from symmetry-breaking sectors beyond the Standard Model.

title: Topological Cycle Graph Attention Network for Brain Functional Connectivity
text_ai: This study, we introduce a novel Topological Cycle Graph Attention Network (CycGAT), designed to delineate a functional backbone within brain functional graph--key pathways essential for signal transmissio--from non-essential, redundant connections that form cycles around this core structure. We first introduce a cycle incidence matrix that establishes an independent cycle basis within a graph, mapping its relationship with edges. By leveraging this basis, CycGAT computes cycle-aware attention scores that distinguish edges participating in the backbone from those involved in cyclic redundancy, effectively filtering noise while preserving critical communication pathways. The model aggregates node features through a message-passing scheme that incorporates topological cycle information, enabling it to learn representations that are robust to spurious correlations in functional connectivity networks. We evaluate CycGAT on resting-state fMRI data from the Human Connectome Project, comparing against baseline GNNs and traditional graph-theoretic methods for tasks including sex classification and cognitive trait prediction. Our results demonstrate that CycGAT achieves statistically significant improvements in accuracy and robustness, particularly in scenarios with high edge density or noisy connectivity estimates. Ablation studies confirm that the cycle-aware attention mechanism is key to these gains, and further analysis of learned attention weights reveals biologically plausible backbone structures aligned with known functional hubs. This work provides a principled framework for incorporating topological cycle structure into graph neural networks, advancing the analysis of brain functional connectivity.

title: Optimized quantum implementation of elliptic curve arithmetic over binary fields
text_ai: Shor's quantum algorithm for discrete logarithms applied to elliptic curve groups forms the basis of a "quantum attack" of elliptic curve cryptosystems. To implement this algorithm on a quantum computer requires the efficient implementation of the elliptic curve group operation. Such an implementation requires we be able to compute inverses in the underlying field. Binary fields $\mathbb{F}_{2^n}$ are attractive for quantum implementation due to the absence of carry propagation, enabling more efficient addition and multiplication circuits. We present a fully optimized quantum circuit for elliptic curve point addition and doubling over $\mathbb{F}_{2^n}$ in affine coordinates. Our design leverages a normal basis representation, which makes squaring a simple cyclic shift and inversion implementable via a linear-depth, low-qubit version of the Itoh–Tsuji algorithm. We provide a detailed quantum circuit for field multiplication based on a Karatsuba scheme that reduces the number of Toffoli gates and ancilla qubits compared to previous schoolbook approaches. For the coordinate inversion required at each step of the group operation, we adapt the linear-reconstruction technique to eliminate excessive ancilla reuse, achieving a constant factor overhead reduction. The complete point addition circuit is synthesized using the Clifford+T gate set, with particular attention to T-count minimization. We report resource estimates for elliptic curves of cryptographic relevance (e.g., n=163, 233, 283) and show that our circuits improve on the best known quantum implementations by up to 30% in total T-count and 20% in qubit footprint. These optimizations substantially lower the overall cost of Shor’s algorithm for elliptic curve discrete logarithms, bringing post-quantum security assessments for binary-field-based cryptosystems, such as those standardized by NIST and SECG, closer to practical feasibility on future fault-tolerant quantum computers.

title: Kinks scattering in deformed $\varphi^6$ model
text_ai: The deformed model $\tilde{\varphi}^{(6)}$ is introduced based on the $\varphi^4$ model using a deformation functional $F[\varphi]$ including a free parameter $a$. The kink solutions in different sectors and their internal modes are obtained as functions of the deformation parameter and their characteristics are evaluated as well. In particular, we study kink-antikink collisions in the two topological sectors using both a collective coordinate approximation and direct numerical simulations. The scattering outcomes are highly sensitive to the deformation parameter \(a\): the critical velocity for capture, the structure of resonance windows, and the emergence of chaotic regimes all exhibit a pronounced dependence on \(a\). We analyze the normal mode spectrum around the kinks, showing how the internal mode frequencies shift with \(a\) and correlating these shifts with modifications in the resonant energy transfer during collisions. The interpolation between the limiting cases of \(\varphi^4\) (\(a\to0\)) and the standard \(\varphi^6\) model is explicitly demonstrated, and we identify the parameter ranges where the fractal scattering pattern characteristic of \(\varphi^4\) is replaced by the simpler two-bounce windows of \(\varphi^6\). Our findings provide a comprehensive understanding of how deformation alters kink dynamics and highlight the pivotal role of internal modes in determining scattering behavior.

The kink solutions in different sectors and their internal modes are obtained as functions of the deformation parameter and their characteristics are evaluated as well.

title: Electric generation and ratcheted transport of contact-charged drops.
text_ai: We describe a simple microfluidic system that enables the steady generation and efficient transport of aqueous drops using only a constant voltage input. Drop generation is achieved through an electrohydrodynamic dripping mechanism by which conductive drops grow and detach from a grounded nozzle in response to an electric field. After detachment, each drop acquires a net charge through contact electrification with the nozzle and the surrounding fluid, enabling subsequent electrostatic manipulation. The drops are then transported across a dielectric surface by a ratcheting mechanism: an array of interdigitated electrodes beneath the surface generates a spatially periodic, time-asymmetric electric field that induces directed motion without external pumps or moving parts. We characterize the dependence of drop size, generation frequency, and transport velocity on the applied voltage and flow rate, showing that steady operation is maintained over a wide range of conditions. The contact charge is measured and found to scale linearly with the drop volume, while the transport speed increases quadratically with the field strength. This passive, electrically driven system offers a robust platform for digital microfluidics, requiring only a single DC power supply and eliminating the need for pulsed or AC voltages. Potential applications include droplet-based assays, sample handling, and lab-on-a-chip devices where simplicity and reliability are paramount. The coupling of generation and ratcheted transport in one device represents a step toward fully autonomous droplet manipulation.

Drop generation is achieved through an electrohydrodynamic dripping mechanism by which conductive drops grow and detach from a grounded nozzle in response to an electric field.

title: The Density-Potential Mapping in Quantum Dynamics
text_ai: This work studies in detail the possibility of defining a one-to-one mapping from charge densities as obtained by the time-dependent Schr\"odinger equation to external potentials. Such a mapping is provided by the Runge-Gross theorem and lies at the very core of time-dependent density functional theory. While the Runge-Gross theorem establishes this mapping formally under assumptions of analyticity in time, its practical inversion remains subtle. We examine the rigorous conditions under which the density uniquely determines the external potential, focusing on the role of the initial many-body state and the time-differentiability of the density. By constructing explicit counterexamples, we delineate the boundaries of the mapping: degeneracies arise when the initial state is not a single Slater determinant or when the density exhibits non-analytic temporal behavior. Furthermore, we propose a constructive inversion scheme based on the continuity equation and the force-balance relation, demonstrating that, for a broad class of analytic densities, the potential can be reconstructed uniquely up to a purely time-dependent function. This reconstruction is validated numerically for one-dimensional model systems. Our analysis clarifies the precise scope of the density–potential mapping, highlighting both its power and its limitations in practical time-dependent density functional theory calculations. Implications for the development of approximate exchange-correlation functionals that respect the mapping are discussed.

Such a mapping is provided by the Runge-Gross theorem and lies at the very core of time-dependent density functional theory.

title: Seismic hazard assessment in Menton, France: Topographical site effect zoning considering a semi-empirical approach and a Machine Learning scheme
text_ai: The presence of topography influences the seismic ground motion and may result in strong amplifications, generally at the top of hills and reliefs. The increasing urbanization of hills requires an accurate estimation of these effects even in areas of moderate seismicity. This study presents a comprehensive methodology for regional-scale topographical site effect zoning, applied to the city of Menton (French Riviera), characterized by steep coastal relief and moderate seismic activity. A semi-empirical approach is first employed, combining one-dimensional numerical simulations of soil columns with empirical topographic amplification factors derived from a database of instrumented hills. This yields a preliminary amplification map at a 50 m resolution. To refine the zoning, a Machine Learning scheme is implemented—specifically, a random forest regressor trained on a dataset of over 10,000 synthetic topographical profiles and their associated spectral amplification ratios computed via 2D finite-difference modeling. The model learns the non-linear relationship between morphological attributes (slope, curvature, normalized height, and aspect) and frequency-dependent site amplification. Application to Menton’s high-resolution digital elevation model produces a continuous amplification map for the 2–10 Hz frequency band. Results reveal that topographical effects can locally double ground motion intensity relative to flat-ground conditions, particularly at ridge crests and convex slope breaks. The combined semi-empirical and ML approach successfully captures first-order amplification patterns while remaining computationally efficient for hazard assessment. The resulting zoning informs local seismic risk mitigation strategies and urban planning regulations.

title: Vegetarianism and veganism compared with mental health and cognitive outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
text_ai: Vegetarian and vegan diets are increasing in popularity. Although they provide beneficial health effects, they may also lead to nutritional deficiencies. Cognitive impairment and mental health disorders have a high economic burden. A meta-analysis was conducted to examine the relationship between vegan or vegetarian diets and cognitive and mental health. Medline, PsycINFO, and Embase were systematically searched from inception to December 2023 for observational and interventional studies comparing vegetarian or vegan diets with omnivorous diets on cognitive and mental health outcomes. Eligible studies included validated measures of depression, anxiety, stress, or cognitive function (e.g., Mini-Mental State Examination, memory tests). Data were extracted independently by two reviewers; random-effects meta-analyses were conducted with odds ratios (OR) or standardized mean differences (SMD) and 95% confidence intervals (CI). Of 4,213 records screened, 38 studies (n = 241,214) met inclusion criteria: 31 on mental health and 7 on cognitive outcomes. For depression, vegetarians/vegans had significantly higher odds compared with omnivores (OR 1.31, 95% CI 1.14–1.50, I² = 62%), with similar results for anxiety (OR 1.27, 95% CI 1.08–1.49). Subgroup analyses revealed no difference between vegetarians and vegans. For cognitive outcomes, no significant overall difference was observed (SMD –0.04, 95% CI –0.13 to 0.05), but studies reporting low vitamin B12 intake among vegans showed poorer cognitive performance (SMD –0.39, 95% CI –0.62 to –0.16). Heterogeneity was moderate to high, and sensitivity analyses indicated that adjustment for confounders attenuated but did not eliminate mental health associations. These findings suggest that vegetarian and vegan diets are associated with a modest increased risk of depression and anxiety, whereas cognitive impairment appears limited to those with insufficient nutritional supplementation. Clinicians should screen for mental health symptoms and ensure adequate intake of vitamin B12, iron, and omega-3 fatty acids. Future longitudinal research with detailed dietary assessments is warranted to clarify causality and protective factors.

title: Curvature Perturbations from a Massive Vector Curvaton
text_ai: We study a ghost-free model of massive vector curvaton proposed in the literature, where the quick decrease of the vector background expectation value is avoided by a suitable choice of kinetic and mass functions. We then compute the power spectrum of curvature perturbations generated by the vector curvaton field during inflation. By solving the linearized perturbation equations, we show that the vector field can source a nearly scale-invariant spectrum of adiabatic perturbations, despite its inherent anisotropic nature. The amplitude and tilt of the power spectrum are determined by the model parameters, including the coupling functions that control the background dynamics. We find that for a broad range of parameters, the predicted spectral index and tensor-to-scalar ratio are consistent with current cosmic microwave background observations. Furthermore, we discuss the possible signatures of non-Gaussianity arising from the vector curvaton mechanism, highlighting distinctive features such as a significant anisotropic bispectrum. Our results demonstrate that the massive vector curvaton provides a viable and testable alternative to the standard scalar curvaton scenario.

title: Preschool Gender-Typed Play Behavior at Age 3.5 Years Predicts Physical Aggression at Age 13 Years.
text_ai: Gender differences in play behavior and physical aggression have been consistently reported. Theoretical perspectives concerning evolutionary, social, and social-cognitive mechanisms suggest that male-typical play behavior during childhood increases subsequent physical aggression. The evidence supporting these connections is limited, however. The present longitudinal study addressed this gap by examining whether gender-typed play behavior at age 3.5 years predicts physical aggression at age 13 years in a large, community-based sample (N = 1,835; 50.2% boys). Parents reported children’s play preferences using the Pre-School Activities Inventory (PSAI) at age 3.5, yielding a continuous masculinity–femininity score. Physical aggression at age 13 was assessed via multiple informants (mother, teacher, and child self-report) using validated scales. Covariates included child sex, verbal skills, and baseline aggressive behavior at age 3.5, as well as family socioeconomic status and maternal education. Hierarchical multiple regression analyses revealed that more male-typical play at age 3.5 significantly predicted higher levels of physical aggression at age 13, even after controlling for all covariates (β = .09, p < .01). This effect remained robust when examining boys and girls separately, though it was slightly stronger for boys. Moreover, the predictive association held for both overt and relational forms of aggression, indicating specificity to physically aggressive acts. These findings provide rare, prospective evidence linking early gender-typed play to later aggression, supporting theoretical accounts positing that male-typical play fosters aggressive behavioral patterns through mechanisms such as reinforcement of rough-and-tumble play, exposure to aggressive peer contexts, and internalization of masculine norms. The results suggest that early play-based interventions targeting gender-typed behavioral trajectories may mitigate later aggression, particularly for boys exhibiting highly masculine play. Future research should examine mediating processes and the role of parental socialization in this developmental pathway.

title: Two-year follow-up of mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists for chronic central serous chorioretinopathy.
text_ai: To evaluate the long-term oral mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRa) treatment in chronic central serous chorioretinopathy (CSC). Patients with chronic non-resolving CSC (defined as foveal subretinal fluid (SRF) lasting >4 months with retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) alterations) treated with MRa only (eplerenone or spironolactone) for at least 6 months were retrospectively included. A total of 48 eyes from 43 patients (32 male; mean age 48.5±9.2 years) met inclusion criteria. Treatment duration averaged 18.3 months (range 6–24). Mean best-corrected visual acuity significantly improved from 0.38±0.21 logMAR at baseline to 0.21±0.18 logMAR at 12 months (P<0.001) and remained stable at 0.19±0.17 logMAR at 24 months (P=0.002 vs baseline). Central retinal thickness decreased from 423±57 μm to 310±44 μm at 12 months (P<0.001) and 295±41 μm at 24 months (P<0.001). Complete SRF resolution was achieved in 33 eyes (68.8%) by 12 months and in 38 eyes (79.2%) by 24 months. Among eyes with resolution, 6 (15.8%) experienced recurrence within the follow-up period, successfully managed with continued MRa therapy. No significant differences were observed between eplerenone (n=30) and spironolactone (n=18) groups regarding any outcome (P>0.05). Adverse events were mild, including transient hyperkalemia (5.2%) and gynecomastia (4.2%), none requiring treatment discontinuation. Conclusion: Long-term MRa therapy (≥6 months) demonstrates sustained anatomical and functional benefits in chronic CSC, with high rates of SRF resolution and favorable safety profile over 2-year follow-up. These findings support MRa as a durable treatment option for non-resolving disease.

title: A Generic Framework for Clustering Vehicle Motion Trajectories
text_ai: The development of autonomous vehicles requires having access to a large amount of data in the concerning driving scenarios. However, manual annotation of such driving scenarios is costly and subject to the errors in the rule-based trajectory labeling systems. To address these limitations, this paper presents a generic framework for clustering vehicle motion trajectories that operates independently of predefined rules or manual segmentation. The framework first extracts robust trajectory features—including spatial, temporal, and kinematic attributes—through a learned representation that captures both local motion patterns and global path characteristics. These features are then input into a scalable clustering module that supports multiple algorithms (e.g., DBSCAN, hierarchical clustering, spectral clustering) with automatic parameter selection based on trajectory distribution metrics. The output produces semantically meaningful clusters corresponding to distinct driving scenarios such as lane changes, intersection turns, or highway merging. We evaluate the framework on three public trajectory datasets (highD, NGSIM, and nuScenes) and compare against state-of-the-art rule-based labeling systems. Results demonstrate that our generic approach achieves comparable or superior scenario coverage while reducing labeling effort by over 90% and eliminating human annotation biases. The framework is modular, extensible, and requires no domain-specific tuning, making it suitable for diverse autonomous driving development pipelines.

title: The formation of astrophysical Mg-rich silicate dust
text_ai: We present new results for ground-state candidate energies of Mg-rich olivine (MRO) clusters and use the binding energies of these clusters to determine their nucleation rates in stellar outflows, with particular interest in the en- vironments of core-collapse supernovae (CCSNe). We performed systematic quantum chemical calculations using density functional theory to identify the global minima for (MgO)_x(SiO_2)_y clusters with sizes up to x+y=6, providing the first comprehensive set of ground-state energies for MRO stoichiometries. From these energies, we derive binding energies per monomer and cluster size-dependent surface free energies, which are then incorporated into classical nucleation theory modified for cluster evaporation fluxes. We find that the critical cluster size for MRO nucleation in typical CCSN ejecta ranges from 1 to 4 monomers, depending on the local gas temperature and supersaturation ratio, with nucleation rates peaking at temperatures near 1100 K. Our results predict that MRO dust can nucleate efficiently in the C-rich ejecta zones of CCSNe, provided that sufficient Mg and Si are available in the gas phase, consistent with recent observations of silicate dust in young supernova remnants. The derived nucleation rates are orders of magnitude higher than previously estimated using bulk thermodynamic properties, underscoring the importance of cluster-specific binding energies. This work thus provides a robust microphysical foundation for modeling dust formation in astrophysical outflows.

title: Forced-induced desorption of a polymer chain adsorbed on an attractive surface - Theory and Computer Experiment
text_ai: We consider the properties of a self-avoiding polymer chain, adsorbed on a solid attractive substrate which is attached with one end to a pulling force. The conformational properties of such chain and its phase behavior are treated within a Grand Canonical Ensemble (GCE) approach. We show that the GCE method allows us to derive exact recursion relations for the generating function of the chain, from which we obtain the force-extension curve and the fraction of adsorbed monomers as functions of the pulling force and the surface attraction strength. The phase diagram in the force–temperature plane reveals a first-order desorption transition at a critical force that scales with the adsorption energy per monomer. In the weak-adsorption regime, the chain undergoes a continuous transition from a three-dimensional coil to a two-dimensional self-avoiding walk on the surface, followed by a sharp desorption under tension. Using extensive Monte Carlo simulations with the pruned-enriched Rosenbluth method (PERM), we verify the theoretical predictions and extract universal exponents. For strong adsorption, the desorption force exhibits a logarithmic dependence on chain length, consistent with the prediction of a marginal scaling regime. The GCE approach further yields the exact form of the desorption force as a function of the adsorption energy, which compares favorably with simulation data. Our results bridge the gap between mean-field theories and numerical experiments, providing a comprehensive picture of force-induced desorption in self-avoiding polymers. The implications for single-molecule manipulation experiments are discussed.

title: TractoSCR: A Novel Supervised Contrastive Regression Framework for Prediction of Neurocognitive Measures Using Multi-Site Harmonized Diffusion MRI Tractography
text_ai: Neuroimaging-based prediction of neurocognitive measures is valuable for studying how the brain's structure relates to cognitive function. However, the accuracy of prediction using popular linear regression models is relatively low. We propose a novel deep regression method, namely TractoSCR, that allows full supervision for contrastive learning in regression tasks using diffusion MRI tractography. TractoSCR extracts fiber bundle-specific features from tractography and employs a dual-loss objective: a mean squared error regression loss and a supervised contrastive loss that pulls together embeddings of samples with similar cognitive scores while pushing apart those with dissimilar scores. This contrastive regularization is fully supervised by the continuous target, using a Gaussian kernel to define pairwise similarities. To handle multi-site variability, we incorporate a harmonization module based on ComBat or adversarial learning, ensuring site-invariant representations. We evaluate TractoSCR on the ABCD and HCP datasets, predicting individual cognitive composite scores from whole-brain tractography. Compared to elastic net, kernel regression, and standard deep regression, TractoSCR achieves up to 15% lower root mean squared error and higher correlation with observed scores. Ablation studies confirm the contribution of each component. Our framework demonstrates that supervised contrastive learning, originally designed for classification, can be effectively adapted to regression in high-dimensional neuroimaging, offering a principled way to leverage continuous label structure for improved predictive performance. TractoSCR thus provides a robust tool for linking brain connectivity to cognition across diverse populations and scanning protocols.

title: Discontinuous Galerkin Methods for Hypersonic Flows
text_ai: In recent years, high-order discontinuous Galerkin (DG) methods have emerged as an attractive approach for numerical simulations of compressible flows. This paper presents an overview of the recent development of DG methods for compressible flows with particular focus on hypersononic flows. First, we survey state-of-the-art DG methods for computational fluid dynamics. We then discuss the specific challenges posed by hypersonic regimes, including strong shocks, severe gradients, high-temperature gas effects, and chemical non-equilibrium. In this context, we highlight the critical role of shock-capturing techniques, such as artificial viscosity, limiters, and modal filtering, in maintaining robustness and accuracy. Next, we review advanced DG formulations tailored for hypersonic flows: the use of entropy-stable and kinetic-energy-preserving schemes to enhance stability, and the integration of flux reconstruction and hybridizable DG methods for improved efficiency. We also examine temporal integration strategies, from explicit Runge–Kutta methods to implicit–explicit approaches, necessary for resolving disparate time scales inherent in reacting flows. Furthermore, we summarize recent progress in adaptive mesh refinement and parallel implementation, which are essential for resolving complex multi-scale physics. Finally, we provide a perspective on open research directions, including the coupling of DG with high-fidelity physical models for turbulence and radiation, and the development of machine-learning-augmented closures. This overview aims to serve as a comprehensive reference for practitioners and to stimulate further innovation in DG methods for hypersonic applications.

title: On Triangulation as a Form of Self-Supervision for 3D Human Pose Estimation
text_ai: Supervised approaches to 3D pose estimation from single images are remarkably effective when labeled data is abundant. However, as the acquisition of ground-truth 3D labels is labor intensive and time consuming, recent attention has shifted towards semi- and weakly-supervised learning. Generating an effective form of supervision with little annotations still poses major challenge in crowded scenes. We address this by leveraging multi-view triangulation as a form of self-supervision. Our key idea is to use off-the-shelf 2D pose detectors to obtain 2D keypoints from multiple camera views, then triangulate them into 3D poses that serve as pseudo-ground-truth labels. Unlike traditional multi-view supervision which requires synchronized cameras with known calibration, we automatically calibrate the cameras using a novel robust triangulation procedure that minimizes reprojection error across unlabeled images. This self-supervised signal is especially beneficial in crowded scenes, where occlusions and ambiguities hinder existing methods. We further introduce a consistency loss that encourages the predicted 3D pose from a single view to match the triangulated pseudo-label, while also enforcing temporal smoothness across frames. Experiments on three challenging datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms fully-supervised baselines using only a fraction of labeled data, and significantly improves accuracy in crowded settings. The triangulation-based self-supervision is simple, scalable, and requires no additional annotation effort.
